docs.title: init
docs.content:
# init

`stacktape init` reads the project you already have and writes a Stacktape configuration for it.

It opens a wizard in your browser and reads your code **on your machine** using a coding agent you
already have installed — Claude Code or Codex. It does not interview you: where your code does not say,
it picks the sensible answer, then shows you what it picked and the line behind every resource it
proposes, so you can change any of it. No source, filenames, or configuration contents are sent to
Stacktape, and no account is needed.

To be precise about where your code goes: an agent works the way it always does — it sends the file
contents it chooses to read to its own model provider, under the account you already have with it, with
read-only tools (it cannot run scripts or install anything). If you would rather no AI read the code at
all, pick **Files only** — the built-in scanner reads manifests locally and sends nothing anywhere.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape init
```

Run it in the directory of the project you want to deploy. The command prints a `http://127.0.0.1:…`
address and opens it; the wizard runs there and the terminal keeps the session alive until you close it
with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
## What happens, in order

1. **Start.** The wizard opens with nothing read yet. It shows which directory it will read and which
   agents it found, and waits. Reading starts when you press the button — never before.
2. **Read.** The agent opens files and you watch it happen: every file it reads appears as it reads it.
   Only the *names* of your environment variables are ever kept or shown. Before the agent starts, a
   deterministic pass has already read the manifests that state the deployment most clearly:
   Docker Compose, Dockerfiles and Procfiles; Render, Fly.io and Heroku app manifests; and literal
   declarations in Serverless Framework, SAM, SST, CDK and Terraform. It also notices when one of
   those tools already deploys the project.
3. **Review.** Every resource, with the reason it exists, the line of your code behind it, and what it
   costs — a real monthly estimate per resource and in total, priced from AWS list prices. Anything
   the code could not settle was decided for you, listed under "Decided for you", and can be changed
   with one click — the configuration is rebuilt from your choice, and the price updates with it.
   Nothing blocks. You choose YAML or TypeScript, and the file is written.
4. **Try it locally (optional).** With your explicit click, the wizard can build and start supported
   services in Docker. Building may download dependencies and run their install hooks. The started
   app receives throwaway settings and has no network. Every result says whether the service passed,
   failed, was inconclusive, or could not be checked. A proven startup failure holds the Deploy
   button until you fix it or explicitly set the result aside; a skipped check is never shown as a
   pass.
5. **Deploy.** The wizard checks that the CLI is signed in to Stacktape. The first click is read-only:
   a short-lived CLI process resolves the same connected AWS account or profile that deploy will use,
   then shows the exact account, region and stack name. You separately confirm creating a new stack or
   updating a specific existing Stacktape stack. Foreign, mismatched and unsafe stacks are blocked. The
   deploy child checks that target again before it creates secrets or changes AWS, then reports progress,
   warnings and typed HTTPS URLs. This step is optional and clearly marked as the one that costs money.
   If your Stacktape organization has multiple connected AWS accounts and no saved default, start with
   `stacktape init --aws-account <account-name>`. That account selection is carried through the target check,
   deploy, and typed URL lookup.
   If the deploy fails for a reason that could be our reading of your code — a wrong start
   command, a missing build step — the agent re-reads the project against the actual error, the
   configuration is rebuilt, and the deploy runs again. At most twice, and never for problems with the
   AWS account itself.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
## Who reads your code

`init` drives a coding agent that is already installed and already paid for — your subscription, your
machine. It never sends your code to Stacktape.

The preview has no Stacktape-hosted AI fallback. If neither local agent is available, the **No agent**
mode below performs deterministic file analysis instead of uploading source or snippets elsewhere.

| Agent | How it is used |
|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Every built-in tool is switched off; the only tools it has are the ones Stacktape gives it, all read-only. You can pick the model. |
| **Codex** | Runs read-only in a scratch working directory, because its patch tool cannot be disabled. |
| **No agent** | Reads package manifests, Compose, Dockerfiles, Procfiles, Render/Fly.io/Heroku manifests, supported IaC declarations, lockfiles, environment-variable names, and whatever already deploys the project. Free, instant, and leans on defaults more often. |

An imported deployment file describes what the project expects; it does not give `init` access to
the provider account or prove that the deployment is currently running. The Review step says when it
found such a file. A Stacktape deploy creates a separate stack: it does not take over, change or delete
resources managed by the existing tool.

The agent cannot write to your repository, cannot reach the network through us, and cannot put words in
front of you: it reports findings from a fixed list of kinds, and every word you read in the wizard is
written by Stacktape.

docs.title: init
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--coding-agent`

Which agent reads the project. `auto` (the default) takes the best one installed. Naming one that is not
installed fails rather than quietly using another.

```bash
stacktape init --coding-agent claude-code
stacktape init --coding-agent none          # static analysis only
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--headless`

Runs the whole thing in the terminal instead of opening a browser. Use it over SSH, in a container, or in
CI. Nothing prompts: the terminal prints what was decided for you, and the configuration is written.

```bash
stacktape init --headless
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--no-browser`

Starts the wizard and prints its address without opening anything. Use it when the browser you want is not
this machine's default, or when the port is forwarded from somewhere else.

```bash
stacktape init --no-browser
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--infrastructure-type`

How much infrastructure to create: `low-cost`, `standard` (the default), or `production`. It sets every
size and safety setting in the generated configuration, and it is the only thing reading your code
cannot tell us.

- **low-cost** — one small copy of everything. Trying it out, a side project, staging.
- **standard** — room for real traffic, a week of backups, deletion protection on your database.
- **production** — two copies of your app so one failure changes nothing, and a standby database in a
  second datacentre.

```bash
stacktape init --infrastructure-type production
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--config-format`

`yaml` (the default) or `typescript`. In the browser this is chosen on the Review step instead, once you
have seen what is in the file.

```bash
stacktape init --headless --config-format typescript
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--project-directory`

The project to read. Defaults to the current directory.

```bash
stacktape init --project-directory ./my-app
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--starter-id`, `--starter-project`

Initialize from a ready-made project instead of reading yours. These skip the wizard entirely.

```bash
stacktape init --starter-id lambda-api-postgres
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### `--initialize-project-to`

Where a starter project's files are placed.


> **Warning:** If the directory is not empty, its contents are deleted first. Point it at a new or empty directory.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
## Existing and generated configuration files

Init preserves `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml` and `stacktape.ts`. When one exists, it writes `stacktape.generated.yml` or `.ts` beside it, replacing any previous file at that generated path. Review or save edits to an existing generated file before rerunning init. For a TypeScript config in a project with `package.json`, init also adds or updates the `stacktape` dependency to match the CLI and prints the install command; it does not run the package manager. Deploy the generated config with `--config`, or merge it yourself:

```bash
stacktape deploy \
  --config stacktape.generated.yml \
  --project <project-name> \
  --stage dev \
  --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
## Examples

Read the project with Claude Code's most careful model:

```bash
stacktape init --coding-agent claude-code
```

No agent, no browser, cheapest infrastructure — a configuration in one step:

```bash
stacktape init --headless --coding-agent none --infrastructure-type low-cost
```

docs.title: init
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) — deploy the configuration `init` wrote.
- [`dev`](/cli/dev) — run the project locally against a minimal dev stack.
- [`delete`](/cli/delete) — remove everything a deploy created.

docs.title: init
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: init
headingPath: Does my code leave my machine?
docs.content:
### Does my code leave my machine?

If you choose Claude Code or Codex, that local agent sends the file contents it selects to its own
model provider under your account, just as it normally does. Stacktape receives no source, file names,
or configuration contents. If you choose **Files only**, no AI provider receives code either.

Stacktape does receive anonymous outcome statistics — which frameworks were detected, whether the
deploy succeeded, how long the analysis took — so we can see where generation fails and fix it. Set
`STP_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` to turn that off. [What the CLI sends](/getting-started/deploy-your-first-stage#what-does-the-cli-send-to-stacktape)
lists everything else.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### What about my .env files?

Only the *names* are kept. `DATABASE_URL` tells the analysis that a database exists — and its value is
looked at once, in memory on your machine, for two things and two things only: whether the scheme says
`postgres://` or `mysql://`, and whether the host belongs to a provider like Supabase, so we do not
propose replacing a database that is already live. Both reduce to a single word before anything is
stored. The value itself is never written to the facts, never quoted in a citation, never logged and
never shown — every citation from an environment file stops at the `=`.

docs.title: init
headingPath: Do I need an AWS account before running init?
docs.content:
### Do I need an AWS account before running init?

Not to run it. You need one to deploy. The wizard can use local AWS credentials or an AWS account
connected to your Stacktape organization. Before any AWS change it resolves the same credentials the
deploy command will use and shows the exact account, region and stack target for confirmation.

docs.title: init
headingPath: Do I need a Stacktape account?
docs.content:
### Do I need a Stacktape account?

Not to analyze your project or to get the file — that all happens on your machine, with no account
and nothing sent to us. Deploying from the wizard does go through Stacktape, so the Deploy step
checks whether this machine is signed in and tells you to run `stacktape login` if it is not.

docs.title: init
headingPath: What does “Try it here first” run?
docs.content:
### What does “Try it here first” run?

Only after you click it, `init` runs your project's build and start commands using disposable Docker
images and containers. The image build may access the network to download dependencies and may run
package-manager install hooks from the project. The started application receives throwaway values
instead of your secrets and has no network access. This is not supported for every packaging and
resource type yet: the wizard labels each service **Passed**, **Failed**, **Inconclusive**, or **Not
checked** and never presents a skipped check as proof. Docker is optional; if it is missing, your
generated file is unaffected and the wizard says that AWS would be the first full run.

docs.title: init
headingPath: How do I run init non-interactively, in CI or from an AI coding agent?
docs.content:
### How do I run init non-interactively, in CI or from an AI coding agent?

`--headless`, optionally with `--agent` for JSONL output. Nothing prompts: everything the code cannot
answer is decided, and the terminal prints what was decided.

docs.title: init
headingPath: Why does it barely ask me anything?
docs.content:
### Why does it barely ask me anything?

Because almost nothing needs asking. Where your code does not say, there is nearly always an answer a
careful person would pick — so it picks it, shows you on the Review step, and lets you change it. The
one real question is how big the infrastructure should be, which is why it is shown alongside the
resources and monthly estimate on the Review step.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### Which agent should I choose?

Whichever you already have. Claude Code and Codex both produce a better result than static analysis,
because they read the code rather than pattern-matching over it. If you have neither, "Files only" still
produces a working configuration — it just falls back to defaults more often.

docs.title: init
headingPath: What happens when the deploy fails?
docs.content:
### What happens when the deploy fails?

The failure is read first. If it is about your AWS account — expired credentials, a missing
permission, a quota — it is shown to you plainly, because no change to the configuration can fix it.
If it could be about the code, the same agent that read your project reads it again with the actual
error in hand, corrects what we believed, and the deploy runs again with the rebuilt configuration.
The wizard names exactly which resources the repair rewrote, and the file in your project is always
the version that deployed. It stops after two repairs and shows the real error rather than looping.
If you chose "Files only", nothing is ever handed to an agent — the deploy just fails, plainly.

docs.title: init
docs.content:
### Does init deploy anything?

Only after two explicit actions on the last step: a read-only target check, then confirmation to create
the absent stack or update the exact existing StackId that was shown. The deploy child repeats that check
and stops if the account, region, name, ownership, status or StackId changed. Everything before the final
confirmation is a file on your disk or a read-only AWS check.

docs.title: init
headingPath: Will init overwrite files in my project?
docs.content:
### Will init overwrite files in my project?

Init preserves canonical config files but can replace a previous `stacktape.generated.yml` or `.ts` and update the `stacktape` dependency in `package.json`; see [existing and generated configuration files](#existing-and-generated-configuration-files). The `--initialize-project-to` flag empties the target directory before placing a starter project there.

docs.title: login
docs.content:
# login

The `stacktape login` command authenticates the Stacktape CLI on the current system. For local development, run it interactively: you approve the sign-in in your browser, and the CLI keeps the local auth state. For CI/CD, use a dedicated Stacktape API key stored in your CI provider's secret store.

docs.title: login
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape login
```

In interactive mode (the default), the command asks how you want to sign in:

- **Sign in with the browser** (recommended). The CLI prints an address and a code, and opens the address in your browser. Sign in to the Stacktape Console there with any sign-in method, or create an account. Check that the Console shows the same code as your terminal, then approve. The CLI continues by itself. Never approve a code that someone else sent you.
- **Enter API key manually**. Paste an API key created in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/api-keys).

Over SSH, in a container or on a machine without a browser, the browser sign-in still works: open the printed address on any device. Pass `--no-browser` to only print it. If your account belongs to several organizations, the CLI asks which one this machine works in. After successful authentication, Stacktape displays your user name and organization.

For CI/CD, prefer setting `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` as a masked secret in the runner environment. If you need an explicit login step, pass the key from the CI secret variable. Never paste an API key into an AI chat, issue tracker, shell transcript, or log.

```bash
stacktape login --api-key "$STACKTAPE_API_KEY" --agent
```

You can create CI keys from the [Stacktape Console's API keys page](/stacktape-console/api-keys). Manual API keys are bearer secrets and should be treated as shown-once credentials.

docs.title: login
docs.content:
## What happens during login

Stacktape performs these steps when you run `login`:

1. **Authenticates you** — through the browser sign-in, which the CLI exchanges for a CLI session for the organization you choose, or by verifying the API key supplied by a CI secret. The short-lived sign-in from the browser is never stored.
2. **Stores local auth state** — keeps the CLI session in the operating system's credential store (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager or the Linux Secret Service). Where that store is unavailable, as is common in WSL, SSH sessions and containers, the session is kept in `~/.stacktape/persisted-state.json`, readable only by your user. Set `STACKTAPE_CREDENTIAL_STORE=file` to always use the file, for example on a machine whose credential store asks for a password on every command.
3. **Verifies access** — calls the Stacktape API to confirm your user, organization, and permissions.
4. **Displays your identity** — prints your user name and the organization the current auth state belongs to.

If the API key is invalid, Stacktape clears the key it attempted to save and reports an authentication error.

An interactive login creates a CLI session for the organization you choose. It ends 90 days after login, or after 30 days without use, whichever comes first; the CLI then asks you to run `stacktape login` again. [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout) ends it immediately. Console-made API keys for CI keep the expiration chosen when they were created.


> **Info:** The `login` command itself does not require an existing API key — it is one of the commands that can run without prior authentication.

docs.title: login
docs.content:
## Non-interactive login

For CI/CD pipelines and automated scripts, set `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` as a masked CI secret. The CLI can read this environment variable directly, so an explicit `login` step is often unnecessary. If your workflow does use `login`, pass the key from the secret variable and combine with `--agent` for programmatic output.

```bash
stacktape login --api-key "$STACKTAPE_API_KEY" --agent
```

Do not hardcode the key in workflow YAML. Reference the CI secret.

```bash
stacktape login --api-key "$STACKTAPE_API_KEY" --agent
```

docs.title: login
docs.content: ## Flags reference

docs.title: login
docs.content:
## CLI Options: `stacktape login`

| Option | Required | Type | Description | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--api-key` | no | `string` | API Key — Your Stacktape API key. Use this only in your own terminal or CI secret store. Do not paste API keys into chat transcripts, shell history, or logs. For local interactive use, prefer `stacktape login`. | - |
| `--aws-account` | no | `string` | AWS Account — The name of the AWS account to use for the operation. The account must first be connected in the [Stacktape Console](https://console.stacktape.com/aws-accounts). Without it, the account is chosen by `--profile`, `AWS_PROFILE` or AWS credentials in environment variables, then by your saved default, then by your organization's only connected account. `--aws-account` takes precedence over all of them, but AWS credentials in environment variables must then belong to that account. | - |
| `-h, --help` | no | `string` | Show Help — If provided, the command will not execute and will instead print help information. | - |
| `--log-level` | no | `string` | Log Level — The level of logs to print to the console. • `info`: Basic information about the operation. • `error`: Only errors. • `debug`: Detailed information for debugging. | `info`, `debug`, `error` |
| `--no-browser` | no | `boolean` | No Browser — If `true`, prints the address instead of opening a browser: `init` still starts the wizard, and `login` still waits for you to approve the sign-in. Use this when the browser you want is not this machine's default, on another device, or behind a forwarded port. | - |
| `-p, --profile` | no | `string` | AWS Profile — The AWS profile to use for the command. You can manage profiles using the `aws-profile:*` commands and set a default profile with `defaults set`. For commands that use a connected AWS account, `--profile` (or `AWS_PROFILE`) selects the connected account the profile belongs to, unless `--aws-account` is set. The command fails if that account is not connected. | - |
| `--quiet` | no | `boolean` | Quiet — Hide progress, banners, success messages and hints. Command output, warnings and errors are still printed. | - |

docs.title: login
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: login
docs.content:
### Interactive login

Run `login` with no flags to start the interactive authentication flow. Choose the browser sign-in, or enter an API key manually.

```bash
stacktape login
```

docs.title: login
headingPath: Login with an API key in CI
docs.content:
### Login with an API key in CI

Pass the API key directly, typically from a CI secret or environment variable.

```bash
stacktape login --api-key "$STACKTAPE_API_KEY"
```

docs.title: login
docs.content:
### Verify your identity after login

After logging in, use [`whoami`](/cli/info-whoami) to verify your local Stacktape CLI authentication state and display the current user, organization, connected AWS accounts, and accessible projects.

```bash
stacktape whoami
```

docs.title: login
headingPath: Switch to a different user or organization
docs.content:
### Switch to a different user or organization

For local development, run `stacktape login` again and choose the user or organization you want to use. In CI, update the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret to a key from the target organization.

```bash
stacktape login
```

docs.title: login
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`logout`](/cli/logout) — removes Stacktape authentication state from the current system.
- [`whoami`](/cli/info-whoami) — displays the current user, organization, and connected AWS accounts.
- [`org create`](/cli/org-create) — creates a new organization and returns organization credentials.
- [`org list`](/cli/org-list) — lists all organizations accessible with your current user.

docs.title: login
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: login
headingPath: Where do I find my Stacktape API key?
docs.content:
### Where do I find my Stacktape API key?

Create CI/API keys from the [Stacktape Console's API keys page](https://console.stacktape.com/api-keys). Manual keys are scoped to an organization, expire by default, and are shown only once. See [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) for details on managing keys.

docs.title: login
headingPath: Do I need an explicit `login` step in CI/CD?
docs.content:
### Do I need an explicit `login` step in CI/CD?

Usually no. If you store a dedicated API key as a CI secret and expose it as `STACKTAPE_API_KEY`, the CLI reads that environment variable directly, so commands like `deploy` work without a separate `login` step. If your workflow does use `login`, pass the key from the secret variable and combine with `--agent` for output optimized for programmatic consumption. See the [custom CI/CD guide](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd) for full pipeline setup.

docs.title: login
headingPath: What happens if I log in with an invalid API key?
docs.content:
### What happens if I log in with an invalid API key?

If verification fails during `login`, Stacktape clears the API key it attempted to save and reports an authentication error. You can then retry with the correct key.

docs.title: login
headingPath: How do I switch between organizations?
docs.content:
### How do I switch between organizations?

For local development, run `stacktape login` again and choose the desired account or organization. For CI, create a key in the target organization and update the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret. Use [`org list`](/cli/org-list) to list organizations accessible with the current Stacktape user.

docs.title: login
docs.content:
### Does login expire?

Yes. A CLI session from an interactive login ends 90 days after login, or after 30 days without use, whichever comes first. Manual API keys used in CI expire according to the key's expiration setting. Use [`logout`](/cli/logout) to end the CLI session and remove local auth state.

docs.title: login
docs.content:
### Does `login` connect my AWS account?

No. The `login` command only authenticates the Stacktape CLI with Stacktape. AWS account connection is separate from login; see [connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for details. Deploying is handled by [`deploy`](/cli/deploy).

docs.title: login
headingPath: Should team members share one API key?
docs.content:
### Should team members share one API key?

No. Use a separate key per integration point and prefer individual interactive login on developer machines. Sharing a key makes attribution, rotation, and revocation harder. Treat local auth state as credential material — don't read it into chat, copy it into scripts, or use it to hand-build `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` values — and remove it with [`logout`](/cli/logout) when no longer needed.

docs.title: logout
docs.content:
# logout

The `stacktape logout` command ends the CLI session that [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) created: Stacktape revokes it, so it stops working everywhere, and the CLI removes it from your system. The command takes no required flags. After logging out, commands that require a Stacktape API key need credentials configured again via [`stacktape login`](/cli/login). Use `logout` when switching accounts, removing credentials from a shared machine, or before storing a different API key.

docs.title: logout
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape logout
```

`stacktape logout` revokes the stored CLI session, removes it from this system and prints a confirmation.

- When Stacktape cannot be reached, the CLI still removes the session from this system and says so. The session then stays valid until it expires or you revoke it on the Console's [API keys page](/stacktape-console/api-keys).
- When the stored key is a Console-made API key passed to `login --api-key`, the CLI only removes it from this system. The key stays valid for the pipelines that use it; revoke it in the Console if you no longer need it.

docs.title: logout
docs.content:
## When to use

Run `logout` when switching between Stacktape accounts or organizations, when removing local credentials from a shared machine, or before storing a different API key with `login`. If you need to verify which account is currently configured, use [`stacktape whoami`](/cli/info-whoami) before logging out.

docs.content:
# logs

The `stacktape logs` command fetches logs from a deployed resource's CloudWatch log group. It operates in two modes: standard mode retrieves recent log events with optional start-time and pattern filtering, while Insights mode runs a CloudWatch Logs Insights query for aggregation and structured analysis. The command requires a Stacktape configuration file and a deployed stack.

If the resource uses `logging.logClass: infrequent-access`, the ordinary command automatically runs a bounded Logs Insights snapshot and preserves the usual formatted or JSON event shape. CloudWatch does not support live tail or filter-pattern reads for this class, so the command exits after the snapshot. Use `--query` instead of `--filter` when you need to narrow an Infrequent Access group.


> **Info:** This command requires a Stacktape configuration file (set via `--config` or auto-detected in the working directory). The configuration is used to resolve the deployed stack and locate the correct CloudWatch log group for the specified resource.

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
## Usage

Fetch the last hour of logs from a resource named `myApi`.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

Fetch logs from a container workload. Use `--container` to specify which container's log group to target.

```bash
stacktape logs myService --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --container main
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content: ## Two modes

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### Standard mode

Standard mode fetches recent log events from the resource's CloudWatch log group. By default it returns up to 100 events from the last hour. Narrow results with `--since`, `--filter`, and `--limit`.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since "2h" --filter "ERROR" --limit 50
```

The command resolves log streams for the target log group, fetches matching events, and either formats them for terminal display or outputs JSON when `--raw` or `--agent` is set.

In an interactive terminal, the command shows the same newest events (up to `--limit`, 100 by default) and then follows the log group, printing new events that match `--filter` as they arrive until you press Ctrl+C. It sends at most two CloudWatch Logs requests per second, so following a busy production log group stays within the account's request quota. When the output is piped or redirected, or with `--raw` or `--agent`, the command prints the events once and exits. `--follow=false` does the same in a terminal.

`--follow` keeps following without a terminal, for example in a coding agent's shell or in CI. Each log line is written as plain text as soon as it arrives (with `--agent`, as NDJSON records; see below). The command ends on Ctrl+C or `SIGTERM`, and when the reading end of its output closes, as with `| head -20`: it notices on the next line it writes. `--follow` cannot be combined with `--raw`.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --follow --filter "ERROR" > api-errors.log &
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### Insights mode

Pass a `--query` flag to run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query instead. Insights mode lets you aggregate, sort, and transform log data using the [Logs Insights query language](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CWL_QuerySyntax.html). When `--query` is provided, the command calls CloudWatch Logs Insights and prints the returned results.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --query "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20"
```

In Insights mode, non-agent output prints each result row with a highlighted timestamp and message. In agent mode, that JSON payload is text in a `type: "log"` record's `message` within the CLI NDJSON stream; the final `result` record is separate.

docs.title: logs
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### startTime

Controls how far back to fetch logs. Accepts two formats:

- **Relative shorthand** — a number followed by a unit: `1h` (1 hour), `30m` (30 minutes), `1d` (1 day), `5s` (5 seconds). This counts back from `--until`, or now when it is omitted.
- **Absolute date** — any string the JavaScript `Date` constructor accepts, such as `2026-05-28T14:00:00Z`.

When omitted, defaults to 1 hour ago.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since "6h"
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### filter

A CloudWatch Logs filter pattern applied server-side before events are returned. Supports simple text matching and structured JSON filter syntax. See the [AWS filter pattern documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html) for the full syntax. This flag applies in standard mode only.

Match any log line containing the word "ERROR".

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --filter "ERROR"
```

Match structured JSON logs where the `level` field equals `"error"`.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --filter "{ $.level = \"error\" }"
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### query

A CloudWatch Logs Insights query string. When provided, the command switches to Insights mode. Insights queries support aggregation (`stats count(*)`), pattern matching (`parse`), and field extraction — useful for understanding error rates, latency distributions, or any structured analysis across large volumes of logs.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --query "stats count(*) by bin(5m) as period"
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### limit

Maximum number of log events to return in standard mode. Defaults to 100. Increase for deeper debugging sessions; keep low for quick checks.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --limit 500
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### container

Specifies which container's log group to target. This flag is optional in the CLI schema and is passed to the log group resolver. Use it when the deployed resource has more than one container (e.g., a [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload)) and Stacktape needs a container name to identify the correct log group.

```bash
stacktape logs myWorkload --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --container sidecar
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### raw

Outputs logs as JSON instead of the default formatted view. In standard mode, the output is a JSON object with `logGroup` and `events` fields, where each event has `timestamp`, `message`, and `logStream`. Useful for piping into `jq` or other tools.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --raw
```

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### agent

Without `--follow`, `--agent` uses the CLI NDJSON protocol. The log payload is JSON text inside a `type: "log"` record's `message`; the final `type: "result"` record is separate and has `result: null`. Standard-mode payloads contain `logGroup` and `events`; Insights payloads contain `logGroup`, `query` and `results`. Parse both the protocol and the message payload, or use MCP `stacktape_cli`, which extracts it. Do not parse all stdout as one log object.

With `--agent --follow`, every line of stdout stays an NDJSON record. Each batch of new events is a `type: "log"` record whose `message` holds the same `logGroup`/`events` JSON as the one-shot payload, so the same parser reads both. The final `result` record follows when following ends.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

`--until` bounds the one-shot fetch, Insights queries and the initial follow backlog, and anchors a relative `--since`. Following continues beyond that time.

docs.title: logs
logs
docs.content:
## How log group resolution works

The command initializes the deployed stack and resolves the CloudWatch log group for the resource name you pass as the first argument. The optional `--container` flag is forwarded to the resolver so it can target the intended container when the resource has multiple containers.

The resolver works with compute resources that write to CloudWatch Logs. For container resources with multiple containers, pass `--container` so the resolver can identify the correct log group.

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
## Examples

Fetch the last 30 minutes of logs.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since "30m"
```

Fetch only error-level logs from the last day.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since "1d" --filter "ERROR"
```

Run a Logs Insights query to count errors by 5-minute window.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --query "filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count(*) by bin(5m)"
```

Get raw JSON output for piping into another tool.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --raw | jq '.events[] | select(.message | contains("timeout"))'
```

Fetch logs from a specific container in a multi-container workload.

```bash
stacktape logs myWorkload --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --container worker --since "2h" --limit 200
```

Use agent mode for structured output in a CI script.

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --agent --since "30m" --filter "ERROR"
```

docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: logs
headingPath: How do I filter logs for errors only?
docs.content:
### How do I filter logs for errors only?

Use `--filter "ERROR"` for simple text matching, or `--filter '{ $.level = "error" }'` for structured JSON logs. The filter runs server-side in CloudWatch, so only matching events are returned — faster and cheaper than fetching all logs and filtering locally. See the [AWS filter pattern syntax](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html) for the full query language. The `--filter` flag applies in standard mode only; for Insights mode, use filter clauses inside the `--query` string.

docs.title: logs
headingPath: What is the difference between --filter and --query?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between --filter and --query?

The `--filter` flag applies a CloudWatch Logs filter pattern in standard mode — it returns individual log events that match the pattern. The `--query` flag runs a CloudWatch Logs Insights query, which supports aggregation, sorting, field extraction, and statistical analysis across your logs. Use `--filter` for quick searches like "show me lines containing ERROR". Use `--query` when you need to compute counts, percentiles, group results by time window, or extract fields from structured logs.

docs.title: logs
headingPath: How far back can I fetch logs?
docs.content:
### How far back can I fetch logs?

The `--since` flag controls how far back the command looks — there is no hard limit in the CLI itself, only what CloudWatch has retained for the log group's retention period. When omitted, `--since` defaults to 1 hour ago. It accepts relative shorthand (`1h`, `30m`, `1d`, `5s`) or any string the JavaScript `Date` constructor parses, such as `2026-05-28T14:00:00Z`.

docs.title: logs
docs.content:
### Does stacktape logs live-tail?

Yes. In a terminal, `stacktape logs` shows the newest events and then prints new ones as they arrive until you press Ctrl+C. Without a terminal it prints the events once, unless you pass `--follow`. For log viewing in the browser, see [Logs](/observability/logs).

docs.title: logs
headingPath: How much does CloudWatch Logs cost?
docs.content:
### How much does CloudWatch Logs cost?

CloudWatch Logs pricing depends on ingestion, storage, retrieval, and query/analysis usage. Logs Insights queries (via `--query`) charge per GB of data scanned. For most development workloads, costs are minimal. High-throughput production services should consider setting log retention limits or using [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) to cheaper storage. Check the [AWS CloudWatch pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/pricing/) for current rates.

docs.title: logs
headingPath: What is the difference between --raw and --agent?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between --raw and --agent?

`--raw` prints the standard `logGroup`/`events` payload as JSON. `--agent` without `--follow` wraps that payload as JSON text inside a log record's `message` in the CLI NDJSON protocol, followed by a separate result record. Parse both layers, or use MCP `stacktape_cli`. With `--agent --follow`, each batch of new events arrives as its own log record with the same payload. In Insights mode, `--raw` is not honored; use `--agent` to receive the `logGroup`, `query` and `results` payload inside that protocol.

docs.title: mcp add
docs.content:
# mcp add

`stacktape mcp add` connects your coding agents to Stacktape. For each agent you pick, it adds the Stacktape MCP server ([`stacktape mcp`](/cli/mcp)) for your user, then starts the server once to check that it works. Neither `mcp add` nor `mcp` needs a Stacktape API key.

docs.title: mcp add
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape mcp add
```

In a terminal, `mcp add` lists every supported agent with the ones installed on this machine preselected. Confirm the selection and it sets them up, prints what it changed and tells you how to reload each agent. Then ask your agent: “Use Stacktape to show what this project deploys.”

docs.title: mcp add
docs.content:
## Supported agents

| Agent | How the server is added |
|-------|-------------------------|
| Claude Code (`claude-code`) | `claude mcp add --scope user` |
| Codex (`codex`) | `codex mcp add`, or `~/.codex/config.toml` when the `codex` command is missing |
| Cursor (`cursor`) | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| VS Code with GitHub Copilot (`vscode`) | The user `mcp.json` of your default profile |
| GitHub Copilot CLI (`copilot`) | `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` |
| Windsurf, now Devin Desktop (`windsurf`) | The existing `mcp_config.json`, or `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenCode (`opencode`) | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` or `opencode.json` |

An agent counts as installed when its command is on your PATH, or its app or settings folder exists. The name in brackets is the value for `--coding-agents`.

docs.title: mcp add
docs.content:
## Behavior details

**User level only.** `mcp add` never writes into your project, so nothing reaches your repository or your teammates. Claude Code's `~/.claude.json` is changed only through `claude mcp add`.

**Edits in place, with a backup.** In JSON and JSONC files only the `stacktape` entry changes; comments, other servers and formatting stay. The previous file is kept as `<file>.bak.<timestamp>`. A file that cannot be parsed is left untouched and reported as failed.

**Safe to repeat.** Entries that already match are reported as already set up and not touched. Run `mcp add` again to add another agent or after moving the CLI.

**The command it writes.** When `stacktape` is on your PATH, agents run `stacktape mcp`. When you installed Stacktape with the install script, they run `~/.stacktape/bin/stacktape mcp` by its full path, which keeps working for agents started from the Dock or Start menu. In any other case `mcp add` writes the running binary's full path and tells you to run it again if that file moves.

**Connection check.** After writing, `mcp add` starts the configured command, completes an MCP handshake and lists the tools. If the server does not start, it prints the server's error output and exits with an error.

**Project entries.** If the current project has its own Stacktape entry for a configured agent (for example a committed `.mcp.json`), that agent uses it inside this project. `mcp add` names the file so you can decide whether to keep it.

docs.title: mcp add
docs.content:
## Examples

Set up two agents without the question:

```bash
stacktape mcp add --coding-agents claude-code,cursor
```

Set up every installed agent, for example from a dotfiles script:

```bash
stacktape mcp add --yes
```

With `--yes` or `--agent`, `mcp add` sets up every installed agent. When it finds none, it changes nothing and exits with an error.

docs.content:
# mcp

The `stacktape mcp` command starts a local MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes Stacktape tools and documentation to AI coding agents. The server communicates over stdio and is spawned automatically by MCP-compatible clients like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and VS Code Copilot.

docs.title: mcp
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape mcp
```

You typically do not run this command directly. Instead, configure your AI coding agent to spawn it as an MCP server. The [`mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) command automates this setup for supported clients.

docs.title: mcp
docs.content:
## CLI Options: `stacktape mcp`

docs.title: mcp
docs.content:
## What the server provides

The MCP server exposes five focused tools that AI agents use to investigate incidents, search docs, inspect projects, plan or run CLI commands, and control dev mode:

| Tool                 | Purpose                                                                                          |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `stacktape_incident` | Fetch an incident's context (`action: "show"`) or find incidents (`action: "list"`)                |
| `stacktape_docs`     | Search docs (`action: "search"`) or fetch exact docs (`action: "get"`)                           |
| `stacktape_project` | Inspect the local workspace for Stacktape config files, package scripts, and inferred defaults |
| `stacktape_cli`     | List, describe, plan, or run Stacktape CLI commands with validation and safety gates           |
| `stacktape_dev`     | Plan, start, inspect, rebuild, and stop dev mode sessions; query, reset and seed local databases |

docs.title: mcp
docs.content:
## How it works

When an MCP-compatible client starts the server, Stacktape registers the five tools and begins listening over stdio immediately, then initializes its bundled documentation index asynchronously. Incident context (`stacktape_incident`) comes from the same `incident show` and `incidents` commands you can run yourself. Infrastructure operations and diagnostics (`stacktape_cli`) execute Stacktape CLI commands with validation and safety gates. Documentation queries (`stacktape_docs`) search the local lexical index. Project scanning (`stacktape_project`) reads local config files and package scripts. Dev-mode follow-up operations like status checks, log reading, rebuilds, local database queries, resets and stop (`stacktape_dev`) communicate with the dev agent API started by [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev).

`stacktape mcp` itself does not require an API key. Operations that run Stacktape CLI commands requiring account access — such as deploy, delete, diagnostics, and starting dev mode — need credentials configured with [`stacktape login`](/cli/login).

docs.title: mcp
mcp
docs.content:
## Examples

Start the MCP server with debug-level logging for troubleshooting connection issues:

```bash
stacktape mcp --debug
```

docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: mcp
docs.content:
### Which AI clients support MCP?

[`stacktape mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) sets up Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, GitHub Copilot CLI, Windsurf and OpenCode. Any other client that can start a local stdio MCP server works too.

docs.title: mcp
headingPath: Do I need an API key to use the MCP server?
docs.content:
### Do I need an API key to use the MCP server?

The `stacktape mcp` command itself does not require an API key, so docs search and project inspection work with no credentials. Operations that run CLI commands requiring account access — such as deploy, delete, diagnostics, and starting dev mode — need credentials configured with [`stacktape login`](/cli/login).

docs.title: mcp
headingPath: Can the MCP server modify my infrastructure?
docs.content:
### Can the MCP server modify my infrastructure?

Yes. The `stacktape_cli` tool can run non-interactive CLI commands with `action: "run"`, such as `deploy`, `delete`, `rollback`, `secret set`, and `logs`. Mutating commands require `confirm: true` before they run. Destructive commands also require direct user confirmation through MCP elicitation when the client supports it; otherwise they fail closed.

For deployment preparation, agents should use `stacktape_cli` with `action: "plan"` and `command: "deploy"` first. Planning is read-only and returns the recommended run arguments, matched package script, inferred config path, working directory, and confirmation requirement without starting a deployment.

docs.title: mcp
headingPath: Do I need to start `stacktape mcp` myself?
docs.content:
### Do I need to start `stacktape mcp` myself?

No. The MCP-compatible client spawns the server automatically over stdio when it starts, and the process exits when the client disconnects — you do not manage its lifecycle. Run [`stacktape mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) once to add the server entry to your client config; you rarely run `stacktape mcp` by hand except with `--debug` to troubleshoot a connection.

docs.title: metrics
docs.content:
# metrics

The `stacktape metrics` command fetches CloudWatch metrics for a deployed resource and displays time-series data as a chart in your terminal. Use it to check invocation counts, error rates, CPU usage, database connections, or API latency without leaving your CLI or opening the AWS Console.

docs.title: metrics
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape metrics myApi Invocations --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

The command sends a CloudWatch `GetMetricData` query with the chosen statistic and period, then renders the returned datapoints as a terminal chart. With `--agent`, the command disables the interactive chart and prints machine-readable metric data containing `resource`, `metric`, `period`, `stat`, `unit`, and `datapoints`.

docs.title: metrics
docs.content:
## Supported resource types and metrics

The `metrics` command supports four resource types. Each type exposes a fixed set of CloudWatch metrics. Passing a resource whose deployed type is not in this list produces an error listing the supported types.

| Resource type | Metrics |
|---|---|
| Lambda function (`function`) | `Invocations`, `Errors`, `Duration`, `Throttles`, `ConcurrentExecutions` |
| Multi-container workload (`multi-container-workload`) | `CPUUtilization`, `MemoryUtilization` |
| Relational database (`relational-database`) | `CPUUtilization`, `DatabaseConnections`, `FreeStorageSpace`, `ReadLatency`, `WriteLatency` |
| HTTP API Gateway (`http-api-gateway`) | `Count`, `4XXError`, `5XXError`, `Latency`, `IntegrationLatency` |

For a supported resource type, passing an invalid metric name returns an error with a remediation line such as `Available metrics: ...` listing the valid metric names. For an unsupported resource type, the error lists the supported resource-type keys instead.

docs.title: metrics
docs.content:
## Important flags

**`<metric>`** (required, second positional argument) — the CloudWatch metric name to fetch. Must match one of the supported metrics for the target resource type (see table above). Examples: `Invocations`, `CPUUtilization`, `DatabaseConnections`.

**`<resource-name>`** (required, first positional argument) — the name of the resource as defined in your Stacktape configuration. The command looks up the resource in the deployed stack to determine its type and the correct CloudWatch dimension.

**`--period`** — aggregation period in seconds. Defaults to `300` (5 minutes). Use shorter periods like `60` for higher-resolution data during active debugging, or longer periods like `3600` for broader trends.

**`--stat`** — the statistic to compute for each period. Defaults to `Average`. Supported values include `Sum`, `Average`, `Maximum`, `Minimum`, and percentiles like `p99`. Use `Sum` for count-based metrics like `Invocations` or `Errors`, `Average` or `Maximum` for utilization metrics, and `p99` for latency tail analysis.

**`--since`** — how far back to look. Accepts relative shorthand (`1h`, `30m`, `1d`, `30s`) or any value the JavaScript `Date` constructor accepts (e.g. `2025-01-15T10:00:00Z`). Defaults to 1 hour ago.

docs.title: metrics
docs.content:
## Examples

Check the invocation count for a Lambda function over the last hour, aggregated in 5-minute windows.

```bash
stacktape metrics myApi Invocations --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat Sum
```

Check error count for the last 24 hours with 1-hour aggregation.

```bash
stacktape metrics myApi Errors --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat Sum --since 1d --period 3600
```

Check CPU utilization for a multi-container workload.

```bash
stacktape metrics myBackend CPUUtilization --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat Average
```

Check tail latency (p99) for an HTTP API Gateway over the last 30 minutes.

```bash
stacktape metrics myGateway Latency --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat p99 --since 30m
```

Check database connections on a relational database.

```bash
stacktape metrics mainDatabase DatabaseConnections --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat Maximum --since 6h
```

Get machine-readable output for use in scripts or AI agents.

```bash
stacktape metrics myApi Duration --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --agent
```


> **Info:** With `--agent`, the command prints metric data containing `resource`, `metric`, `period`, `stat`, `unit`, and an array of `datapoints` (each with `timestamp` and `value`). This is useful for piping into monitoring scripts or feeding to AI coding assistants.

docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: metrics
docs.content:
### What resource types support metrics?

The `stacktape metrics` command supports four deployed resource types: `function` (Lambda functions), `multi-container-workload`, `relational-database`, and `http-api-gateway`. If you pass a resource whose deployed type is not one of these, the command returns an error listing the supported type keys. Other Stacktape resource types such as [web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [private services](/resources/compute/private-service), and [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service) are not currently listed in the command's metric configuration.

docs.title: metrics
headingPath: What is the default time range and aggregation period?
docs.content:
### What is the default time range and aggregation period?

By default, the command fetches the last 1 hour of data with a 300-second (5-minute) aggregation period. Use `--since` to look further back (e.g. `--since 1d` for 24 hours) and `--period` to change the granularity. Shorter periods give more data points but may return empty values for low-traffic resources.

docs.title: metrics
headingPath: Which `--stat` should I use for a given metric?
docs.content:
### Which `--stat` should I use for a given metric?

The default is `Average`, but that is wrong for counts: use `--stat Sum` for count-based metrics like `Invocations`, `Errors`, and `Throttles`, otherwise totals get averaged into misleading per-period values. Keep `Average` (or `Maximum`) for utilization metrics like `CPUUtilization` and `MemoryUtilization`, and use `p99` for latency tail analysis on `Duration` or `Latency`.

docs.title: metrics
headingPath: Can I fetch metrics for resources in a private VPC?
docs.content:
### Can I fetch metrics for resources in a private VPC?

Yes. The `metrics` command queries AWS CloudWatch directly — it does not connect to the resource itself. No [bastion tunnel](/cli/bastion-tunnel) is needed for metric queries, regardless of VPC configuration.

docs.title: metrics
headingPath: How do I see all available metrics for my resource?
docs.content:
### How do I see all available metrics for my resource?

For a supported resource type, pass an invalid metric name and the error remediation includes a line listing the valid metrics (e.g. `Available metrics: Invocations, Errors, Duration, Throttles, ConcurrentExecutions`). For an unsupported resource type, the error lists the supported resource-type keys instead.

docs.title: metrics
headingPath: When should I use metrics vs logs?
docs.content:
### When should I use metrics vs logs?

Use `stacktape metrics` to check aggregate trends — invocation counts, error rates, CPU utilization, latency percentiles. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to inspect individual request details, error stack traces, and application output. Metrics tell you *something is wrong*; logs tell you *what went wrong*.

docs.title: org create
docs.content:
# org create

The `org create` command creates a new organization in your Stacktape account and returns a new API key scoped to it. Organizations are the account boundary Stacktape uses for projects, connected AWS accounts, and user access. Use `org create` when you need a separate organization and API key for a team or workspace.

docs.title: org create
docs.content:
## Usage

Run `org create` to create a new organization and receive an API key scoped to it.

```bash
stacktape org create
```

In interactive mode, Stacktape prompts you for the organization name. To skip the prompt, pass the organization name as an argument (`org create <organization-name>`).

```bash
stacktape org create my-team
```

For programmatic or AI-agent usage, pass `--agent` to disable interactive prompts. In agent mode, the organization name is required — the command exits with an error if it is missing.

```bash
stacktape org create my-team --agent
```


> **Info:** You must be logged in before running this command. Use [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) to configure your API key.

docs.title: org create
docs.content:
### What the command returns

On success, `org create` outputs three pieces of information:

- **Organization name** — the name you provided.
- **Organization ID** — a unique identifier assigned by Stacktape.
- **Organization API key** — a new API key scoped to the created organization. Use this key with [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) to switch your CLI context to the new organization.

In agent mode, Stacktape does not prompt for the organization name, so the organization name argument is required. Use `--json` if you need machine-readable NDJSON output.

docs.title: org create
docs.content:

All flags accepted by `org create` are listed below. None are required in interactive mode.

| `--organization-name (positional 1)` | no | `string` | Organization Name — The name of the Stacktape organization. | - |

```bash
stacktape org create production-team --debug
```

docs.title: org delete
docs.content:
# org delete

The `stacktape org delete` command deletes the organization your API key belongs to. Use it when you no longer need an organization you own. The command enforces two safety constraints before proceeding: all other non-service users must already be removed, and all AWS accounts must be disconnected from the organization. Deleting the organization revokes its API keys, including the one you used.

An API key acts in one organization, so the command can delete only that organization. To delete another organization you own, run [`login`](/cli/login) with an API key of that organization first.

docs.title: org delete
docs.content:
## Usage

Run `org delete` without flags for the interactive flow, or pass `--agent` and the organization ID for non-interactive use in CI and agent workflows.

```bash
stacktape org delete
```

In interactive mode, the command names the organization and asks you to confirm. In agent mode, pass the ID of your API key's organization as confirmation (`org delete <organization-id>`). Any other ID is refused.

```bash
stacktape org delete "org_abc123" --agent
```

docs.title: org delete
docs.content:
## Prerequisites

Before you can delete an organization:

1. Remove all non-service users (other team members must be removed first).
2. Disconnect all AWS accounts from the organization.
3. You must be the organization OWNER.
4. You must be a member of at least one other organization.

If any of these conditions are not met, the operation will fail.


> **Warning:** Deleting the organization cannot be undone. Make sure you have another way to access anything you still need before continuing.

docs.title: org delete
docs.content:

docs.content:
# org list

The `org list` command displays all organizations accessible with your current Stacktape API key. Use it to see which organizations you belong to, your role in each, and which one is currently active for CLI operations.

docs.title: org list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape org list
```

When organizations are found, the command prints a table with the following columns. If you have no organizations, it prints "No organizations found for this user."

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Organization | The organization name |
| Role | Your organization role, such as Owner, Admin, Developer, or Viewer. Unrecognized roles are displayed as returned by Stacktape |
| Connected AWS | Number of AWS accounts connected to the organization |
| Current | Whether this organization is the active one for your API key |
| ID | The organization's unique identifier |

No flags are required. The command uses the API key configured via [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) to authenticate and fetch your organization list.

docs.title: org list
docs.content:
## Output formats

When Stacktape detects an interactive terminal (TTY), `org list` renders a table. In CI or other non-TTY contexts, the output format is auto-detected. Use `--json` or `--agent` for machine-readable output.

Machine-readable JSONL output:

```bash
stacktape org list --json
```

Agent mode (JSONL output with no interactive UI):

```bash
stacktape org list --agent
```

docs.title: package
docs.content:
# package

The `package` command packages your compute resources and prepares them for deployment without actually deploying. Use it to run the same packaging step that [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) uses — useful for catching packaging or build failures early, before committing to a full deployment.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The command loads your Stacktape configuration, initializes packaging, and packages all compute resources for the target stack. A valid Stacktape configuration file is required — by default Stacktape looks for one in the current directory.

To use a configuration file in a different location, pass `--config`.

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```


> **Info:** The `package` command runs packaging with caching disabled, so every invocation produces a fresh build from the current state of your source code.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
## Examples

Package all compute resources for a staging stage in `us-east-1`:

```bash
stacktape package --stage staging --region us-east-1
```

Package with debug logging to see detailed build output:

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --debug
```

Package using a specific AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape package --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

Package using a configuration file in a subdirectory:

```bash
stacktape package --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: package
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) — creates or updates your stack on AWS. Use `deploy` when you want to deploy; `package` runs the packaging step independently.
- [`synth`](/cli/synth) — compiles your configuration into a CloudFormation template without packaging compute resources. Use `synth` when you only need to inspect the infrastructure template.
- [`validate`](/cli/validate) — validates your configuration and optionally includes workload packaging checks with `--with-package`.
- [`diff`](/cli/diff) — previews what would change in your stack if you deployed. Useful alongside `package` for a full pre-deploy review.

docs.title: package
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: package
headingPath: When should I use `package` instead of just running `deploy`?
docs.content:
### When should I use `package` instead of just running `deploy`?

Use `package` when you want to verify that your compute resources package correctly before committing to a deployment — for example, catching build errors, confirming dependencies resolve, or validating that container images build successfully. In normal workflows, [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) handles packaging as part of its pipeline, so `package` is primarily a pre-deploy verification tool.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
### How is `package` different from `validate --with-package`?

[`validate`](/cli/validate) validates your configuration, resolves resources, and synthesizes the CloudFormation template in memory. Adding `--with-package` also validates workload packaging. Use `validate --with-package` when you want configuration validation combined with packaging checks. Use `package` when you specifically want to run the packaging step on its own.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
### Does `package` use caching?

No. The `package` command runs packaging with caching disabled, so every invocation produces a fresh build from the current state of your source code. This ensures the output accurately reflects your code at the time of the run.

docs.title: package
docs.content:
### Does `package` require AWS credentials?

Only when your configuration reads something from AWS. `package` builds on your machine, so a typical project packages without AWS credentials and without any request to AWS. Credentials are loaded when packaging needs them: for a directive such as [`$Secret`](/configuration/directives), `$StackOutput` or `$AwsAccountId`, or for a web framework build whose environment references deployed resources. Stacktape then uses the profile selected with `--profile` or `AWS_PROFILE`, or the standard AWS credential chain.

docs.title: package
headingPath: Can I package only specific workloads?
docs.content:
### Can I package only specific workloads?

By default, the `package` command packages all compute resources in your configuration. To target a subset, pass `--only-workloads` with a comma-separated list of workload names (for example, `--only-workloads myFunction,myContainer`). Other workloads are skipped.

docs.title: package
headingPath: What is the difference between `package` and `synth`?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between `package` and `synth`?

[`synth`](/cli/synth) compiles your Stacktape configuration into a CloudFormation template — it produces the infrastructure definition but does not build any application code. `package` is the inverse: it builds your compute resources (according to each resource's [packaging mode](/packaging/overview)) but does not produce the infrastructure template. Run both before a deploy when you want a complete pre-deploy review.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
# param get

Retrieve the runtime value of a [referenceable parameter](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) from a resource in a deployed stack. Use `param get` to fetch URLs, connection strings, ARNs, and other outputs directly from the CLI — without opening the AWS Console or parsing CloudFormation outputs. The three required arguments are `--region`, `--resource-name`, and `--param-name`.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape param get myApi url --region eu-west-1
```

The command does not require a local Stacktape configuration file. The command takes the resource name and the parameter name as positional arguments (`param get <resource-name> <param-name>`) and requires `--region`; optional stack-selection arguments such as `--stage` or `--project` can still be used when needed to identify the target stack. `--stage` is optional; pass it when you need to target a specific stage explicitly.

Common scenarios for `param get`:

- Feed an endpoint URL into a local script or test harness.
- Retrieve a database connection string for a one-off migration tool.
- Read a resource ARN to pass into another CLI command or CI step.
- Verify the actual deployed value of a parameter after a deploy completes.

If you need a broader overview of all stack outputs and resources at once, use [`status`](/cli/info-stack) instead.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
## Examples

Retrieve a parameter from a deployed resource.

```bash
stacktape param get api url --region us-east-1
```

Pass `--stage` when you want to target a specific stage explicitly. Include it unless you have set a default stage via [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure).

```bash
stacktape param get mainDatabase connectionString --region eu-west-1 --stage production
```

For programmatic consumption in scripts or CI steps, use `--agent` or `--json` to get machine-readable JSONL output. The default interactive output includes formatting that is not suitable for shell variable capture.

```bash
stacktape param get api url --region eu-west-1 --agent
```


> **Info:** The available parameter names depend on the resource type. See [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) for the full list grouped by resource type.

docs.title: param get
docs.content:
## Error handling

If the resource name does not exist in the deployed stack overview, the command throws the missing-resource error (`e77`) for that stack and resource lookup. Double-check that the resource name matches the key used in your Stacktape configuration.

If the parameter name is not found for the given resource, the command throws the invalid-parameter error (`e78`) and passes the resource type plus the available referenceable parameter names to the error handler. This makes it straightforward to discover the correct parameter name without leaving the terminal.

docs.title: param get
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: param get
headingPath: How do I find the available parameter names for a resource?
docs.content:
### How do I find the available parameter names for a resource?

Each Stacktape resource type exposes a specific set of referenceable parameters. The full list is documented at [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters). You can also trigger the `e78` error intentionally by passing an invalid `--param-name` — the error output includes the valid parameter names for that resource type.

docs.title: param get
headingPath: Does param get require a deployed stack?
docs.content:
### Does param get require a deployed stack?

Yes. The command queries a deployed stack to read the parameter's runtime value. If the stack has not been deployed yet, there is nothing to retrieve. Deploy first with [`deploy`](/cli/deploy), then use `param get` to read outputs.

docs.title: param get
headingPath: How do I capture the value in a shell script or CI step?
docs.content:
### How do I capture the value in a shell script or CI step?

Pass `--agent` or `--json` to get machine-readable JSONL output (one JSON object per line). The default interactive output includes colors and formatting that are not suitable for capturing into a shell variable or parsing in a pipeline step.

docs.title: param get
headingPath: What is the difference between param get and status?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between param get and status?

[`param get`](/cli/param-get) retrieves a single parameter value from a single resource — ideal for scripting and automation. [`status`](/cli/info-stack) returns a broader overview of all outputs and AWS resources in the stack — better for exploration and discovery after a deployment.

docs.content:

- [`synth`](/cli/synth) — compile your Stacktape configuration into a CloudFormation template for inspection before deployment.
- [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure) — set default region and stage so you can omit them from repeated commands.

# project create

The `project create` command creates a new project in the current Stacktape organization. Use it before deploying stages under a new project name, or in automation when you need to create the project non-interactively. You must be logged in with a valid API key before running this command.

```bash
stacktape project create
```

```bash
stacktape project create my-api
```

In agent mode (`--agent`), you must provide the project name as an argument (`project create <project>`). You can also pass an optional `--region` when creating the project.

docs.content:
# project list

The `project list` command lists all projects in your current organization along with their deployed stages, deployment status, and monthly costs. Use it to review projects in your organization, see deployed and undeployed stage counts, spot in-progress or errored stages, and compare current and previous month costs.

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape project list
```

The command requires no arguments. You must be [logged in](/cli/login) to Stacktape, and the output reflects the organization your CLI session is scoped to. Run [`whoami`](/cli/info-whoami) to verify which organization you're authenticated against.

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## Output

The `project list` command prints a summary table followed by per-project detail. The summary table includes these columns:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| **Project** | The project name. |
| **Stages** | Total stage count with deployed count in parentheses — e.g. `3 (2 deployed)`. |
| **In Progress** | Number of stages with a deployment currently running. |
| **Errored** | Number of stages in an error state. |
| **This Month** | Aggregated cost across all stages for the current month. |
| **Prev Month** | Aggregated cost across all stages for the previous month. |

Projects are sorted by most recent stage activity first, then alphabetically by name. Costs use the currency code returned with stage cost data; when no current-month currency code is present, the command falls back to USD.

docs.title: project list
docs.content:
## CI and agent usage

In CI pipelines or when consumed by AI coding agents, pass `--agent` to get machine-readable JSONL output instead of the interactive table. The `--output-format` flag provides finer control over formatting.

List projects as JSONL for scripting:

```bash
stacktape project list --agent
```

Use plain text output (no colors or animations):

```bash
stacktape project list --output-format plain
```

docs.content:
# query dynamodb

The `query dynamodb` command lets you inspect data in a deployed [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) directly from the command line. It supports five read-only operations — `sample`, `scan`, `query`, `get`, and `schema` — so you can check table structure, look up items by key, or browse data without leaving the terminal.

Use this command as your first tool when you need to verify data in a deployed DynamoDB table. The command resolves your Stacktape `DynamoDbTable` resource by name and runs read-only operations against the deployed table, so there's no risk of accidental writes.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb <tableName> --stage <stage> --region <region> --operation <operation>
```

The resource name argument must match the name of a `DynamoDbTable` resource in your Stacktape configuration. If you omit `--operation`, the command defaults to `sample`. When `--limit` is omitted, the command uses a default limit of 100.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Operations

The `query dynamodb` command supports five operations. All are read-only.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### sample

The `sample` operation returns items from the table — useful for a quick sanity check that data exists and looks right. This is the default operation when `--operation` is omitted. Use `--limit` to control how many items are returned.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation sample
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### schema

The `schema` operation returns schema information for the table. Run this first when you're unfamiliar with a table — use the returned metadata to choose values for `--pk`, `--sk`, or `--index`.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation schema
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### scan

The `scan` operation reads items from the table without filtering by key. Use `--limit` to control how many items are returned (defaults to 100 when omitted). Scans read the table sequentially, so they consume read capacity proportional to the data scanned — keep `--limit` reasonable on large tables.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation scan --limit 20
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### query

The `query` operation fetches items matching a specific partition key, optionally filtered by sort key. Requires `--pk` with a JSON object mapping the partition key name to its value. Use `--sk` to narrow results by sort key, and `--index` to query a global secondary index instead of the primary table.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation query --pk '{"userId": "u-42"}'
```

Query a GSI with a sort key filter:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation query --pk '{"status": "shipped"}' --sk '{"createdAt": "2025-01-01"}' --index statusIndex
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### get

The `get` operation retrieves a single item by its full primary key (partition key + sort key if the table has one). Requires `--pk`; use `--sk` when the table has a composite key. If no item matches, the command prints the result returned by DynamoDB.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --pk '{"userId": "u-42"}' --sk '{"orderId": "ord-99"}'
```

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Programmatic output

The `--agent` flag switches to programmatic output mode. With `--agent`, `query dynamodb` prints the operation result as a JSON object (with `ok`, `resource`, `operation`, and the operation-specific data) for programmatic consumption by scripts or AI coding agents.

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb ordersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation sample --agent
```


> **Tip:** Run `--operation schema` first on unfamiliar tables. It returns table metadata you need to choose values for `--pk` and `--sk`.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
## Examples

Quickly check if a table has data after a fresh deployment:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage dev --region us-east-1
```

Inspect the key schema and indexes before writing a query:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation schema
```

Fetch all items for a specific user:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation query --pk '{"userId": "abc-123"}' --limit 50
```

Get a single item by composite key:

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb usersTable --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --pk '{"userId": "abc-123"}' --sk '{"createdAt": "2025-03-15T10:00:00Z"}'
```

Scan for recent items (up to 10):

```bash
stacktape query dynamodb eventsTable --stage staging --region us-east-1 --operation scan --limit 10
```
