docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: Can I query a global secondary index?
docs.content:
### Can I query a global secondary index?

Yes. Pass `--index <indexName>` with the `query` operation. The `--pk` value must match the GSI's partition key, not the table's primary partition key. Run `--operation schema` first to inspect the table metadata before querying.

docs.title: query dynamodb
docs.content:
### What format does --pk expect?

The `--pk` flag takes a JSON object mapping the key attribute name to its value — for example, `'{"userId": "abc-123"}'`. The attribute name must match the partition key name in the table's schema. The same format applies to `--sk`. If the JSON is malformed, the command returns an error asking for valid JSON objects.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: What is the default limit for sample and scan?
docs.content:
### What is the default limit for sample and scan?

When `--limit` is omitted, the command uses a default limit of 100 items, for both `sample` and `scan`. Use `--limit` to request fewer or more items.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: Is this command safe to run against production tables?
docs.content:
### Is this command safe to run against production tables?

Yes. All five operations are strictly read-only — the command never writes, updates, or deletes items. Be mindful of `scan` on large tables: it consumes DynamoDB read capacity units proportional to the data scanned, which could affect performance if your table's provisioned capacity is low. Use `--limit` to keep scans bounded.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: How is this different from aws call, and can I use it on tables not managed by Stacktape?
docs.content:
### How is this different from aws call, and can I use it on tables not managed by Stacktape?

The [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call) command gives raw AWS SDK access and requires you to construct the full DynamoDB API input (including the physical table name and marshalled attribute values). `query dynamodb` instead resolves your Stacktape resource name to the underlying table and provides higher-level operations like `schema` and `sample`, so you can inspect data without knowing the physical table name or DynamoDB API shape. The trade-off: it only accepts a deployed Stacktape resource whose type is `dynamo-db-table`. For tables outside Stacktape, use [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call) with the DynamoDB SDK commands directly.

docs.title: query dynamodb
headingPath: Does this command need a bastion tunnel or VPC access?
docs.content:
### Does this command need a bastion tunnel or VPC access?

No. DynamoDB is a regional AWS service accessible over the public internet — it does not run inside a VPC. No bastion tunnel is needed, unlike VPC-only resources such as [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) or [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis).

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
# query opensearch

The `query opensearch` command runs read-only queries against a deployed [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) directly from your terminal. Use it to list indices, check document counts, inspect field mappings, retrieve individual documents, or search with Query DSL — without setting up a separate OpenSearch client or dashboard.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation indices
```

The command takes the domain's resource name as a positional argument (`query opensearch <resource-name>`) and always requires `--stage` and `--region`. The resource name must match an OpenSearch domain resource defined in your Stacktape configuration. Additional flags depend on the operation.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
## Operations

The `--operation` flag selects what kind of query to run. Five operations are available: `indices`, `mapping`, `count`, `get`, and `search`. If omitted, the command defaults to `indices`.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### indices

Lists all indices in the OpenSearch domain. This is the default operation and the best starting point when exploring an unfamiliar domain. No additional flags are needed.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation indices
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### mapping

Returns the field mapping for a specific index — useful for understanding the index schema before writing search queries. Requires `--index`.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation mapping --index users
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### count

Returns the document count. You can pass `--index` to count documents in a specific index; omit it to count across all indices.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation count --index orders
```

Count across the entire domain (no `--index`):

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation count
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### get

Retrieves a single document by ID. Requires both `--index` and `--id`.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --index users --id doc123
```

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
### search

Runs an OpenSearch Query DSL search. Requires `--query` with a valid JSON string. You can optionally scope the search to a specific index with `--index` and control result count with `--limit` (defaults to 10).

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation search --query "{\"match_all\": {}}"
```

Search within a specific index with a limited result set:

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation search --index users --query "{\"match\": {\"name\": \"alice\"}}" --limit 5
```


> **Info:** The `--query` flag accepts [OpenSearch Query DSL](https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/query-dsl/) as a JSON string. The command parses the JSON before sending it — malformed JSON is rejected with `Invalid JSON in --query` and the hint `Provide valid OpenSearch query DSL JSON`. On Windows, escape inner double quotes with backslashes. On Linux/macOS, wrap the entire value in single quotes.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content:
## Agent mode

When running with `--agent`, the command prints a structured JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `operation`, and the operation result. This makes it suitable for programmatic consumption by AI coding assistants and automation scripts.

```bash
stacktape query opensearch mySearch --agent --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation indices
```

For automation, prefer `--agent`. The global `--output-format` flag is documented in the flags reference below.

docs.title: query opensearch
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: Which flags does each operation require?
docs.content:
### Which flags does each operation require?

The `mapping` operation requires `--index`. The `get` operation requires both `--index` and `--id`. The `search` operation requires `--query`. For `indices`, no additional flags are needed. For `count`, `--index` is optional — omit it to count across all indices.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: Do I need a bastion host to query OpenSearch?
docs.content:
### Do I need a bastion host to query OpenSearch?

No. The command reads the deployed domain endpoint from the stack, connects over HTTPS, and authenticates with the stack's read-only debug role. When the stack has no such role or it cannot be assumed, the command fails instead of using your configured AWS credentials. Unlike [`query sql`](/cli/query-sql) or [`query redis`](/cli/query-redis), `query opensearch` does not accept a `--bastion-resource` flag.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: What format does the --query flag expect?
docs.content:
### What format does the --query flag expect?

The `--query` flag accepts a JSON string containing an [OpenSearch Query DSL](https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/query-dsl/) query body. The command parses the JSON before sending it. If the JSON is malformed, the command rejects it with `Invalid JSON in --query` and the hint `Provide valid OpenSearch query DSL JSON`. On Windows, escape inner double quotes with backslashes; on Linux/macOS, wrap the entire value in single quotes.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: How is query opensearch different from OpenSearch Dashboards?
docs.content:
### How is query opensearch different from OpenSearch Dashboards?

`query opensearch` is a CLI tool for quick, ad-hoc inspection from your terminal — checking an index exists, verifying document counts, or running a one-off search. OpenSearch Dashboards provides a full web UI with visualizations, saved queries, and interactive exploration. Use the CLI for fast debugging; use Dashboards for ongoing analytics and dashboard building.

docs.title: query opensearch
headingPath: What happens if the OpenSearch domain is not deployed?
docs.content:
### What happens if the OpenSearch domain is not deployed?

The command looks up the domain endpoint from the deployed stack. If the resource does not exist in the stack or the domain is not yet provisioned, the command fails with an error indicating it could not retrieve the OpenSearch endpoint. Verify the stack is deployed and the `--resource-name` matches a resource in your configuration.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
# query redis

The `query redis` command lets you inspect a deployed [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) directly from the command line. It supports five read-only operations — `keys`, `get`, `ttl`, `info`, and `type` — so you can check cached values, list keys by pattern, or view server stats without setting up a local Redis client or tunnel.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation info
```

The resource name argument must refer to a `redis` resource defined in your Stacktape configuration. The command resolves the cluster's connection details (host, port, password) from the deployed stack automatically.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Operations

The `--operation` flag selects what to do. If omitted, it defaults to `info`.

| Operation | What it does | Required flags |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| `info` | Returns Redis server information (memory, clients, stats). Optionally filter with `--section`. | — |
| `keys` | Lists keys matching a glob pattern. `--pattern` is optional and defaults to `*`. | — |
| `get` | Returns the value stored at a specific key. | `--key` |
| `ttl` | Returns the remaining time-to-live (in seconds) for a key. | `--key` |
| `type` | Returns the data type of a key (string, list, set, hash, zset, etc.). | `--key` |

All operations are read-only. You cannot write, delete, or modify data through this command.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Accessing VPC-only clusters

Redis caches deployed inside a VPC are not publicly accessible. To reach them from your local machine, pass `--bastion-resource` to tunnel through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) in your stack. When `--bastion-resource` resolves a tunnel target, the command starts an SSM port-forwarding session, uses localhost for the query, and closes the tunnel after the query.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion --operation keys --pattern "session:*"
```

If the Redis endpoint is reachable from your machine, omit `--bastion-resource`. For VPC-only clusters, pass a bastion resource name.

docs.title: query redis
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### View server info

Returns the full Redis INFO output.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation info
```

Use `--section` to pass a Redis INFO section such as `server`, `memory`, or `stats`. The command passes the section string directly to Redis.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation info --section memory
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### List keys by pattern

Lists keys matching a glob pattern. The `--pattern` flag is optional and defaults to `*` (all keys). Use `--limit` to cap the number of returned keys.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation keys --pattern "user:*" --limit 20
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Get a key's value

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --key "session:abc123"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Check a key's TTL

Returns the remaining time-to-live in seconds. A value of `-1` means the key has no expiration; `-2` means the key does not exist.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation ttl --key "session:abc123"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Check a key's type

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation type --key "user:42"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
### Query through a bastion tunnel

When your Redis cache is VPC-only, pass `--bastion-resource` to route the connection through a bastion host.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion --operation get --key "config:feature-flags"
```

docs.title: query redis
docs.content:
## Agent mode

When running inside an AI coding agent or CI pipeline, pass `--agent` to switch to agent-oriented output. In agent mode, `query redis` prints the Redis result as a JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `operation`, and the operation-specific result fields. Agent mode also disables interactive terminal UI.

```bash
stacktape query redis myRedis --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --operation get --key "session:abc123" --agent
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
# query sql

Run read-only SQL queries against a deployed [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) directly from the command line. Use `query sql` when you need to check a row, verify a migration, or inspect table structure in a deployed PostgreSQL or MySQL database without setting up a local database client.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
## Usage

Query a table in a deployed database:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

Query a database through a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host):

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SHOW TABLES" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
## What it does

The `query sql` command connects to a deployed Stacktape `relational-database` resource, executes a read-only SQL query, and prints the results. Stacktape resolves the database connection string — including host, port, username, and password — from your deployed stack's SSM parameters automatically. You don't need to look up credentials or endpoints.

The command validates that the SQL string starts with an allowed read-only prefix before sending it to the database. Accepted prefixes are `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`, and `\d` (PostgreSQL meta-commands). Any SQL that does not start with one of these prefixes is rejected.

When the deployed database exposes a `readerConnectionString` SSM parameter, `query sql` uses it. Otherwise it uses the primary `connectionString` parameter. This means read queries are automatically routed away from the writer instance when a reader endpoint is available.

The command passes SSL connection options to the database client automatically.


> **Warning:** This command is for ad-hoc inspection, not bulk data export. Results are capped by the `--limit` flag (default: 1000 rows). For persistent database access with a local client like `psql` or DataGrip, use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) instead.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `<sql>` (required)

The SQL query to execute, passed as the second positional argument. Wrap it in double quotes on the command line. The command accepts queries starting with `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`, or `\d`.

Select specific columns:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT id, email, created_at FROM users WHERE active = true LIMIT 20" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

Inspect table structure in PostgreSQL:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'users'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

List tables in MySQL:

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SHOW TABLES" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `<resource-name>` (required)

The first positional argument: the name of the relational database resource as defined in your Stacktape configuration. The resource must be a `relational-database` — other resource types are not supported by this command.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--bastion-resource`

Name of a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) resource to tunnel through. Use `--bastion-resource` when you want `query sql` to tunnel through a Stacktape bastion host to reach a VPC-only database. Stacktape opens an SSM port-forwarding session for the duration of the query and tears it down automatically afterward.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT count(*) FROM orders" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource myBastion
```

If you need a persistent tunnel (for example, to connect a local GUI client), use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) instead.

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--limit`

Maximum number of rows to return. Default: **1000**. The output indicates whether results were truncated.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM events" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --limit 50
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--timeout`

Maximum time to wait for the query to finish, in milliseconds. Default: **30000** (30 seconds). Increase this for queries against large tables or complex joins.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM large_table" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --timeout 60000
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### `--agent`

Switches output to structured JSON for programmatic consumption. In agent mode, `query sql` writes a JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `engine`, `sql`, `rows`, `fields`, `rowCount`, and `truncated`. Use this when calling `query sql` from scripts or AI coding assistants.

```bash
stacktape query sql myDatabase "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content: ## Examples

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Check if a migration ran

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT * FROM _prisma_migrations ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 5" --stage staging --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Count rows in a table

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2025-01-01'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Describe a PostgreSQL table

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'users'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Explain a slow query

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id WHERE users.email LIKE '%@example.com'" --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
### Query through a bastion host

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDb "SELECT * FROM products WHERE stock = 0" --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --bastion-resource bastion
```

docs.title: query sql
docs.content:
## Output

In interactive mode, `query sql` prints results as a formatted ASCII table with column headers. When no rows match, it prints "No rows returned."

In agent mode (`--agent`), the output is a structured JSON object containing:

- `ok` — `true` on success
- `resource` — the resource name argument
- `engine` — `postgres` or `mysql`
- `sql` — the executed query string
- `rows` — array of row objects
- `fields` — array of column name strings
- `rowCount` — number of rows returned
- `truncated` — `true` if `rowCount` hit the `--limit` cap

docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: What SQL statements does `query sql` accept?
docs.content:
### What SQL statements does `query sql` accept?

The command accepts SQL whose trimmed text starts with `SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`, or `\d` (PostgreSQL meta-commands). Any SQL that does not start with one of these prefixes is rejected before it reaches the database. This is intended for read-only inspection of deployed databases from the CLI.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: What database types does it work with?
docs.content:
### What database types does it work with?

The `query sql` command works with deployed Stacktape `relational-database` resources whose connection string uses the `postgresql://` or `mysql://` protocol. The engine is detected automatically from the connection string, and the appropriate database client driver is used.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: Do I need to know the database password?
docs.content:
### Do I need to know the database password?

No. Stacktape resolves the full connection string — including host, port, username, and password — from the deployed stack's SSM parameters at query time. You only need the resource name and stage. The connection uses SSL automatically.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: When should I use `query sql` vs `bastion tunnel`?
docs.content:
### When should I use `query sql` vs `bastion tunnel`?

Use `query sql` for quick, one-off inspections: checking a row, verifying a migration, counting records. Use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) when you need a persistent connection for a local database client (psql, DataGrip, TablePlus) or need to run write operations. The `query sql` command is read-only by design.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: Can I query a database that is only reachable inside a VPC?
docs.content:
### Can I query a database that is only reachable inside a VPC?

Yes, if your stack includes a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host). Pass `--bastion-resource` and Stacktape opens an SSM port-forwarding session for the duration of the query, then tears it down automatically afterward. Without a bastion resource in the stack, `query sql` cannot reach a VPC-only database.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: What happens if my query returns too many rows?
docs.content:
### What happens if my query returns too many rows?

Results are capped by the `--limit` flag, which defaults to 1000 rows. The output includes a `truncated` indicator when the limit is reached. Increase `--limit` if you need more rows, but keep in mind that large result sets are printed to the terminal. For bulk data exports, use [`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) with a dedicated database client.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: Does `query sql` use the reader or writer endpoint?
docs.content:
### Does `query sql` use the reader or writer endpoint?

When the deployed database exposes a `readerConnectionString` SSM parameter, `query sql` uses it. Otherwise it uses the primary `connectionString` parameter. This routes read queries away from the writer instance when a reader endpoint is available.

docs.title: query sql
headingPath: How do I get machine-readable output for scripts or AI agents?
docs.content:
### How do I get machine-readable output for scripts or AI agents?

Pass `--agent` to switch from the formatted ASCII table to a structured JSON object containing `ok`, `resource`, `engine`, `sql`, `rows`, `fields`, `rowCount`, and `truncated`. This is the format to parse when calling `query sql` from scripts or AI coding assistants.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
# rollback

The `stacktape rollback` command reverts a deployed stack to a previous release. It downloads the CloudFormation template from that release and deploys it. Every deployment that changed something is a release, including fast deployments that updated code without CloudFormation. Artifacts, such as Lambda zips and container images, are reused — no rebuild or packaging step is needed. Use it to recover from a bad deployment without redeploying from source.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## When to use

Use `rollback` when a recent deployment introduced a bug, performance regression, or broken configuration and you want to restore the previous working state. No code rebuild or workload artifact packaging occurs. Stacktape downloads the stored CloudFormation template, prepares it as a new deployment version, uploads that rollback template, and asks CloudFormation to deploy it.


> **Warning:** Rollback primarily restores the previous CloudFormation template and stored workload artifacts (Lambda zips, container images). For bucket-synced static content, Stacktape also attempts a manifest-based restore after the rollback. Application-side data changes are not undone — treat database migrations and application-written objects as separate recovery work. If your deployment included a schema migration, rolling back the code without rolling back the schema may cause errors.


If your stack is stuck in an `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` state and cannot accept new updates, use [`stack recover`](/cli/cf-rollback) instead — it uses CloudFormation's native recovery mechanism to restore the stack to a working state. A stack in `UPDATE_FAILED` can be rolled back with either command.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Usage

The only required argument is `--region`. `--stage` and `--project` are optional arguments used to identify the target stack.

Roll back one version (the default):

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production
```

Roll back to a specific version:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --target-version v000003
```

Roll back multiple steps:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --rollback-steps 3
```

List available versions before deciding:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --list-versions
```

docs.title: rollback
docs.content: ## Important flags

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--target-version`

Specifies the exact deployment version to roll back to, for example `v000003`. Versions commonly use values like `v000001`, `v000003`; when `--rollback-steps` is used, Stacktape calculates a six-digit zero-padded target. Use `--list-versions` to see which versions are available in your deployment bucket.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--rollback-steps`

Number of stored releases to step back from the current one. Defaults to `1` (the previous release). For example, if the current release is `v000008` and all older releases are still stored, `--rollback-steps 3` targets `v000005`. Releases removed by `previousVersionsToKeep` are skipped. If neither `--target-version` nor `--rollback-steps` is provided, the command rolls back one version.

Targeting the current release re-applies it. Use this when a fast deployment failed partway and left some functions or services on other code.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--list-versions`

When previous versions exist, the command prints the current version and the available rollback versions, then exits without rolling back. If no previous versions exist, it reports that none were found. Use this to inspect what's available before committing to a rollback.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### `--config`

Rollback initializes with `commandRequiresConfig: false`, so a local configuration file is not required. `--config` appears in the command's optional arguments because rollback includes common config-dependent CLI arguments.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## How rollback works

Stacktape stores CloudFormation templates and deployment artifacts for each deployment version in an S3 deployment bucket. When you run `rollback`:

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Flow
1. **Version resolution**: The target version is --target-version, or the release --rollback-steps steps back among the stored releases.
2. **Artifact verification**: Stacktape verifies that artifacts for the target version are available in the deployment bucket before proceeding.
3. **Safety check**: The command reads rollback safety metadata from the deployed stack, when present, and prints warnings for directives, TypeScript transforms, custom directives, or after:deploy hooks.
4. **Template preparation**: The old CloudFormation template is downloaded and stored as a new release. The function code and container images it uses are copied under the new release, so CloudFormation updates every function and container service to the restored code, including those a fast deployment changed.
5. **Deployment**: CloudFormation applies the rollback template. Lambda zips and container images are reused, not rebuilt. Every container service runs a rolling deployment, even one whose code did not change.
6. **Bucket content restoration**: If the stack includes static hosting with bucket-synced content, Stacktape attempts to restore the bucket contents from a version manifest.


> **Info:** Each rollback creates a new deployment version. Rolling back from `v000008` to `v000005` produces `v000009` — so you maintain a full audit trail and can roll forward again if needed.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Safety warnings

The rollback command reads rollback safety metadata from the deployed stack and warns about situations where a template-only rollback may not fully restore the previous behavior:

- **Directives that embed local or external state** — directives such as `$File` are reported by name. The rolled-back template contains values from the original deploy time, not from your current local files. This is expected behavior for a rollback.
- **TypeScript transforms** — if rollback safety metadata reports that the config uses TypeScript transforms, Stacktape warns that those transforms are not captured in the CloudFormation template.
- **`after:deploy` hooks** — when rollback safety metadata reports `after:deploy` hooks, Stacktape warns that they will not be re-executed during rollback. If the original deployment relied on post-deploy scripts (database seeding, cache warming), you may need to run them manually.
- **Custom directives** — custom directive results were baked into the template at deploy time and are not re-evaluated during rollback.

If the stack was deployed before rollback support was added, the safety metadata may be missing. The rollback still proceeds, but with a warning that results may be unpredictable if the config used `$File`, TypeScript transforms, custom directives, or `after:deploy` hooks.

Shared-layer fast deployments check that the old handler can run on the new layer before attaching it. They do not require the new handler to run on the old layer. CloudFormation restores code and layers separately during rollback: across an edit that added a used export, restoring the old layer first can briefly fail invocations until the old handler is restored. The forward deployment prints a note when it detects this incompatibility. Rollbacks across several releases can also cross incompatible chunk generations. The final restored code and layers are consistent; rollback does not guarantee uninterrupted invocations during that transition.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Version availability

Use `--list-versions` to see which versions are still available. If a target version is not found in the deployment bucket, Stacktape reports that it was not found, lists the versions that are available, and notes that old versions may have been cleaned up based on the `previousVersionsToKeep` setting.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
## Bucket-synced content

If the stack includes static hosting with bucket-synced content, Stacktape attempts to restore the bucket contents from a version manifest stored during the original deployment. If Stacktape cannot restore bucket-synced content, it warns that stacks with static websites may need to be redeployed from the original commit.

headingPath: Quick rollback after a bad deploy
docs.content:
### Quick rollback after a bad deploy

The most common use case — revert to the version that was running before the last deployment:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production
```

This is equivalent to `--rollback-steps 1`. No config file is needed.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### Inspect available versions first

Before rolling back, check which versions are available:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --list-versions
```

The output prints the current version and the available rollback versions. If the current version appears in the listed versions, Stacktape marks it as current. Pick a version and roll back to it:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --target-version v000005
```

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### Rollback in CI/CD

Use `--agent` for output optimized for programmatic consumption:

```bash
stacktape rollback --region eu-west-1 --stage production --rollback-steps 1 --agent
```

The `--agent` flag uses JSONL/NDJSON output and disables interactive terminal UI.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: rollback
headingPath: What is the difference between `rollback` and `stack recover`?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between `rollback` and `stack recover`?

The `rollback` command deploys a previously stored CloudFormation template as a new version — use it when a *successful* deployment introduced a problem in your application. The [`stack recover`](/cli/cf-rollback) command uses CloudFormation's native rollback mechanism to recover a stack stuck in `UPDATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` state. Use `rollback` for "the deploy worked but the app is broken" and `stack recover` for "the deploy itself failed."

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### Does rollback rebuild my code?

No. Rollback reuses stored deployment artifacts (Lambda zips, container images) from the original deployment. No code rebuild or packaging occurs. Stacktape still prepares and uploads a rollback CloudFormation template for the new deployment version.

docs.title: rollback
docs.content:
### Does rollback affect my database?

Rollback primarily restores the previous CloudFormation template and stored workload artifacts. For bucket-synced static content, Stacktape also attempts a manifest-based restore. Application-side data changes such as database migrations or records written by your application are not undone. If your deployment included a schema migration, you may need to manually reconcile the database state after rolling back.

docs.title: rollback
headingPath: How far back can I roll back?
docs.content:
### How far back can I roll back?

It depends on the `previousVersionsToKeep` setting — older versions may have been cleaned up after successful deployments, and once a version's artifacts are gone you can no longer roll back to it. Use `--list-versions` to see which versions still have their artifacts available in the deployment bucket.

docs.title: rollback
headingPath: Can I roll forward after a rollback?
docs.content:
### Can I roll forward after a rollback?

Yes. Each rollback creates a new deployment version (e.g., rolling back from `v000008` to `v000005` produces `v000009`). You can [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) again normally, or roll back the rollback by targeting the version you came from.

docs.title: rollback
headingPath: Will my `after:deploy` hooks run during rollback?
docs.content:
### Will my `after:deploy` hooks run during rollback?

No. When rollback safety metadata reports `after:deploy` hooks, Stacktape warns that they will not be re-executed during rollback. If your deployment relies on post-deploy scripts (database seeding, cache warming), you need to run them manually after the rollback completes.

# script run

The `script run` command executes a script defined in the `scripts` section of your Stacktape configuration. It takes the script name as a positional argument (`script run <script-name>`), requires `--stage`, accepts additional environment variables via `--env`, and can optionally assume a deployed resource's IAM role with `--assume-role-of-resource`. Use `script run` when you need to execute a named script from the `scripts` section without deploying the full stack.

docs.title: script run
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape script run myMigration --stage production
```

`script run` requires the script name and `--stage`. Pass `--region` when you do not rely on a configured default (set via [`defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure)).

docs.content:
## Examples

Add `--region` when you want to override or avoid relying on a configured default region:

```bash
stacktape script run migrate --stage staging --region eu-west-1
```

Pass extra environment variables to a seed script:

```bash
stacktape script run seed --stage dev --env SEED_FILE=./data/seed.json --env VERBOSE=true
```

Run a script while assuming the IAM role of a deployed resource (so the script operates with that resource's AWS permissions):

```bash
stacktape script run exportData --stage production --assume-role-of-resource dataProcessor
```

Use a custom config path when the configuration is not at the default location:

```bash
stacktape script run cleanup --stage dev --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```


> **Info:** If `assumeRoleOfResource` is also defined in the script's configuration properties, the CLI flag takes precedence.

docs.title: script run
docs.content:
## Errors

If the script name does not match any key in the `scripts` section of your configuration, the command throws `stpErrors.e20({ scriptName })`. The command looks up the script by key in `scripts`, so the script name must exactly match a key defined in your configuration.

docs.content:
# secret delete

The `secret delete` command deletes a specified AWS Secrets Manager secret by name in the selected AWS region. Use it to clean up secrets that are no longer referenced in your Stacktape configuration — for example, retired API keys, rotated credentials, or secrets from deleted stages.


> **Warning:** Before deleting a secret, verify that no active Stacktape configuration references it via `$Secret('secret-name')`. If a configuration still references a deleted secret, future operations that need to resolve that secret may fail.

docs.title: secret delete
docs.content:
## Usage

In non-agent mode, Stacktape prompts for the secret name regardless of other flags.

```bash
stacktape secret delete --region eu-west-1
```

In agent mode (CI pipelines or AI coding agents), pass the secret name as an argument — it becomes required.

```bash
stacktape secret delete my-api-key --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

On success, the CLI reports `Secret "my-api-key" deleted.`

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
# secret set

The `secret set` command creates or updates a secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Once stored, you can reference the secret in your Stacktape configuration using the [`$Secret('secret-name')`](/configuration/directives) directive — keeping sensitive values like API keys, database passwords, and third-party tokens out of your config files and version control.

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Usage

In interactive mode (the default), the command walks you through a guided flow — prompting for the secret name, input method, and value:

```bash
stacktape secret set --region eu-west-1
```

In agent mode (for CI/CD pipelines or AI coding assistants), provide all values as flags:

```bash
stacktape secret set my-api-key --region eu-west-1 --value sk-abc123 --agent
```

To store the contents of a file as the secret value, exactly as they are in the file:

```bash
stacktape secret set firebase-creds --region eu-west-1 --file ./firebase-service-account.json --agent
```

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Interactive vs agent mode

The command operates in two modes depending on whether `--agent` is set.

**Interactive mode** (default) prompts you for:

1. The secret name.
2. How to provide the value — either by typing it directly (masked input) or by specifying a file path.
3. If a secret with the same name already exists, confirmation before overwriting.

**Agent mode** (`--agent`) is designed for non-interactive environments. It requires the secret name and either `--value` or `--file`. If the secret already exists, the command fails unless you pass `--force-update`. Agent mode outputs structured JSONL and skips all prompts.

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Updating existing secrets

When a secret with the given name already exists in the target region:

- **Interactive mode** — you are prompted to confirm the update.
- **Agent mode** — the command fails with an error unless `--force-update` is passed.

To update an existing secret without prompts:

```bash
stacktape secret set my-api-key --region eu-west-1 --value new-value --force-update --agent
```

docs.title: secret set
docs.content:
## Important flags

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--region` | **(required)** AWS region where the secret is stored. |
| `<secret-name>` | Positional argument. Name of the secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Required in agent mode; prompted in interactive mode. |
| `--value` | The value to store. Mutually exclusive with `--file`. |
| `--file` | Path to a file whose contents are stored as the secret value. Mutually exclusive with `--value`. |
| `--force-update` | Overwrite an existing secret without confirmation. Only relevant in agent mode. |
| `--agent` | Run in non-interactive mode with JSONL output. Requires the secret name and one of `--value` or `--file`. |

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
# synth

The `stacktape synth` command compiles your Stacktape configuration into a CloudFormation template and writes it to a local file. Use it when you need the generated CloudFormation template on disk for inspection or downstream tooling. No stack is created or modified.

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

This reads your Stacktape configuration, resolves all resources, finalizes the CloudFormation template, and writes it to `compiled-template.yaml`. Both `--stage` and `--region` are required so the command can resolve a concrete stack context.

To write the template to a custom path, use `--out`.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --out ./infra/template.yaml
```


> **Info:** Unlike [`deploy`](/cli/deploy), `synth` does not create or modify any stack resources. It does not require a previously deployed stack, and it does not require a Stacktape subscription.

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --out

Controls where the synthesized template is saved. Defaults to `compiled-template.yaml`. Use this when you want the template in a specific location for CI artifacts, version control, or external tooling.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage prod --region us-east-1 --out ./output/prod-template.yaml
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --config

Points to your Stacktape configuration file when it is not in the default location. The path is relative to the current working directory.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --keep-temp-files

When set, Stacktape preserves temporary files generated during synthesis under `.stacktape/[invocation-id]`. Useful for debugging the synthesis pipeline when the final template doesn't match your expectations.

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --keep-temp-files
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
### --project

Specifies the Stacktape project name for the operation. Pass the same value you would use with [`deploy`](/cli/deploy).

```bash
stacktape synth --stage prod --region us-east-1 --project my-app
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## Examples

Synthesize a production template and save it to a specific directory:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage prod --region us-east-1 --out ./artifacts/prod.yaml
```

Synthesize with debug-level logging to troubleshoot configuration resolution:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --debug
```

Synthesize using a specific AWS profile:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage staging --region eu-west-1 --profile my-aws-profile
```

Synthesize and keep temporary files for inspection:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --keep-temp-files --out ./debug-template.yaml
```

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## synth vs validate vs diff

| Command | What it does | Writes a file? | Modifies stack? | Requires deployed stack? |
|---------|-------------|---------------|----------------|------------------------|
| [`synth`](/cli/synth) | Compiles config into a CloudFormation template | Yes (`compiled-template.yaml`) | No | No |
| [`validate`](/cli/validate) | Validates the Stacktape project without writing deployment artifacts | No | No | No |
| [`diff`](/cli/diff) | Shows what would change if you deployed | No | No | Yes |

Use `synth` when you need the template file on disk for inspection or downstream tooling. Use [`validate`](/cli/validate) for a quick pass/fail check without writing artifacts. Use [`diff`](/cli/diff) when you want to compare your current config against what is already deployed.

docs.title: synth
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`validate`](/cli/validate) — validates your Stacktape project without writing deployment artifacts. Use `--thorough` to validate workload packaging and ask AWS CloudFormation to validate the synthesized template.
- [`diff`](/cli/diff) — previews what would change in your deployed stack if you ran [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) with the current configuration.
- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) — deploys (or updates) your stack to AWS. Internally runs the same synthesis step that `synth` performs.

docs.title: synth
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: synth
headingPath: Why are --stage and --region required if nothing is deployed?
docs.content:
### Why are --stage and --region required if nothing is deployed?

Stacktape needs both values before synthesis so it can resolve a concrete stack context. Your configuration may use the stage and region in resource names, conditional logic, or directive expressions, so different stages can produce different templates. Pass the same values you would use for [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) or [`validate`](/cli/validate).

docs.title: synth
headingPath: Can I feed the synthesized template into CloudFormation linting or policy tools?
docs.content:
### Can I feed the synthesized template into CloudFormation linting or policy tools?

Yes — that is a primary use case. The output is a finalized CloudFormation YAML template, so you can pass it to any tool that accepts CloudFormation: linters, policy-as-code scanners, or your own scripts. A common CI pattern is to run `synth` and then run a scanner against the output. In non-TTY environments output is plain text automatically; pass `--output-format plain` to force it, or `--agent` for JSONL.

docs.title: synth
headingPath: When should I use synth vs validate vs diff?
docs.content:
### When should I use synth vs validate vs diff?

Use `synth` when you need the generated CloudFormation template on disk to inspect or feed to external tooling. Use [`validate`](/cli/validate) for a quick pass/fail check without writing any artifact. Use [`diff`](/cli/diff) when a stack is already deployed and you want to see what would change on the next deploy — unlike `synth`, `diff` compares against live stack state.

docs.title: synth
headingPath: The synthesized template doesn't match what I expected — how do I debug it?
docs.content:
### The synthesized template doesn't match what I expected — how do I debug it?

Run `synth` with `--keep-temp-files` to keep the intermediate files generated during synthesis under `.stacktape/[invocation-id]`, and add `--debug` to trace how your configuration is resolved. This lets you inspect the synthesis pipeline rather than only the final template.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
# upgrade

The `stacktape upgrade` command upgrades your Stacktape CLI to the latest published version. It detects how Stacktape was installed — native binary, global package, or local project dependency — and either runs the appropriate upgrade command automatically or prints it for you to run. No Stacktape API key is required.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape upgrade
```

The command compares your installed version against the latest published release using semver. If you are already on the latest version, it exits with a success message and takes no action.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## How it works

When an upgrade is available, Stacktape detects your installation type and responds accordingly:

- **Native installation**: Stacktape downloads the installer for your platform and runs it.
- **Global package install**: Stacktape runs `npm install -g stacktape@<version>`, or the pnpm or Bun equivalent.
- **Local project dependency**: Stacktape prints the appropriate update command for you to run yourself, since modifying project dependencies should be an explicit choice.
- **Unknown installation method**: Stacktape prints a command to run manually.

The installer runs as a file: through PowerShell on Windows and through `sh` on macOS and Linux. A preview version upgrades to the newest preview, or to a stable release once one is newer.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content: ## Flags

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## CLI Options: `stacktape upgrade`

| Option | Required | Type | Description | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h, --help` | no | `string` | Show Help — If provided, the command will not execute and will instead print help information. | - |
| `--log-level` | no | `string` | Log Level — The level of logs to print to the console. • `info`: Basic information about the operation. • `error`: Only errors. • `debug`: Detailed information for debugging. | `info`, `debug`, `error` |
| `--new-version (positional 1)` | no | `string` | New Version — The version of Stacktape to install. | - |
| `--quiet` | no | `boolean` | Quiet — Hide progress, banners, success messages and hints. Command output, warnings and errors are still printed. | - |


Without a version argument, Stacktape installs the latest published version.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## Examples

Upgrade to the latest Stacktape version:

```bash
stacktape upgrade
```

Install a specific version:

```bash
stacktape upgrade 4.0.1
```


> **Info:** If Stacktape is installed as a local project dependency (in `node_modules`), the command prints the appropriate update command instead of running it. Run the printed command yourself to complete the upgrade.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`version`](/cli/version) — print the currently installed Stacktape version.
- [`login`](/cli/login) — configure your API key after upgrading.
- [`help`](/cli/help) — display available commands and options.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: upgrade
headingPath: Does `stacktape upgrade` require an API key or AWS credentials?
docs.content:
### Does `stacktape upgrade` require an API key or AWS credentials?

No Stacktape API key is required. The command has no required arguments — it reads local version metadata, resolves the latest published version, and runs or prints an install command. It does not accept AWS account or region flags.

docs.title: upgrade
headingPath: What happens if I'm already on the latest version?
docs.content:
### What happens if I'm already on the latest version?

Stacktape compares your installed version against the latest published release. If they match, it prints a success message confirming you are up to date and exits without making any changes.

docs.title: upgrade
headingPath: Why does the command print a command for local installs instead of running it?
docs.content:
### Why does the command print a command for local installs instead of running it?

Stacktape classifies your install as `native`, `package-global`, `package-local`, or unknown. Native and global package installs are upgraded automatically. For a local project dependency, upgrading modifies `node_modules` and the lockfile and affects your whole project, so Stacktape prints the exact command instead — letting you review and run it in the right project context.

docs.title: upgrade
headingPath: Can I downgrade or pin a specific Stacktape version?
docs.content:
### Can I downgrade or pin a specific Stacktape version?

Pass the version as an argument, for example `stacktape upgrade 4.0.1`. Stacktape installs exactly that version, including an older one. Without it, `upgrade` installs the latest published version.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
# validate

The `stacktape validate` command loads your Stacktape configuration, resolves resources, and synthesizes the CloudFormation template in memory — without modifying AWS resources. With `--thorough`, it also packages workloads and asks CloudFormation to validate the template. Add `--out` when you want to inspect the exact successfully validated template. Use it to catch config errors before deploying.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Usage

The `validate` command requires a stage and region. It checks your configuration file, resolves all resource definitions, validates configured [guardrails](/guardrails/overview), and synthesizes the CloudFormation template in memory.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The command does not create, update, or delete any AWS resources and does not require a deployed stack.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Validation levels

The `validate` command supports three levels of thoroughness, each building on the previous one. Choose the level that matches how much confidence you need before proceeding.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
### Default — config, resources, and template

Stacktape loads the configuration, resolves all resources, validates [guardrails](/guardrails/overview), and synthesizes the CloudFormation template in memory. This is the fastest option and catches most configuration-level mistakes — broken resource references, invalid property values, and guardrail violations.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
### With packaging — add `--with-package`

The `--with-package` flag runs workload packaging as part of validation. Stacktape packages all Lambda functions and container workloads, which catches packaging errors surfaced by the normal packaging step — such as missing entry files or misconfigured build settings. Use this when you have changed packaging settings or entry file paths.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --with-package
```

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
### Thorough — add `--thorough`

The `--thorough` flag includes workload packaging and calls CloudFormation `ValidateTemplate`. CloudFormation accepts a template of up to 51,200 bytes with the request; a larger one (an ordinary web-service stack is already larger) is uploaded to a temporary object in the stack's deployment bucket, validated from there and deleted. Before the first deploy the stack has no deployment bucket, and `validate` does not create one. A larger template then gets a warning: the `--agent` result reports `checked.cloudformation: false` and lists the warning under `warnings`. The first deploy validates it. This check requires AWS credentials and does not create or modify a stack; its only write is that temporary object.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --thorough
```


> **Info:** The `--thorough` flag implies `--with-package`. You do not need to pass both.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Security findings by stage purpose

`validate` also checks the configuration for security findings, the same ones [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) reports to the Stacktape Console: a database reachable from the internet, a public bucket, an IAM statement that allows every action, a credential pasted into an environment variable, and similar. A finding never fails validation.

How severe a finding is depends on whether the stage is production. A password-protected database open to the internet is a reasonable default for a dev or preview stage, so it is `LOW` there and `HIGH` in production. Rules that only matter once real users depend on the stack, such as deletion protection, backups, termination protection and running two container instances, are not reported for other stages; `validate` lists them separately so you know what to fix before production.

| Finding | Production | Other stages |
|---------|------------|--------------|
| Database or OpenSearch domain reachable from the internet | `HIGH` | `LOW` |
| Public load balancer without a web application firewall | `MEDIUM` | `LOW` |
| Queue without a dead-letter queue | `LOW` | `INFO` |
| Database without deletion protection, data store without backups | `MEDIUM` | listed under "before production" |
| Stack without termination protection, container service with one instance | `LOW` | listed under "before production" |
| Public bucket, wide IAM statement, secret in an environment variable | same in every stage | same in every stage |

Wide IAM statements keep their severity because dev stages often share the AWS account with production, so a role that can do anything in the account reaches production too.

A stage is production when [`stackConfig.stageType`](/configuration/stages-and-environments#production-and-non-production-stages) is `production`. Without that setting, `deploy` uses the type you chose when you created the stage in the Stacktape Console; `validate` does not contact the Console, so it skips this step unless you pass `--aws-account`. Otherwise the stage name decides: `prod`, `production`, `prd` and `live`, alone, as a segment (`prod-eu`) or followed by a number (`prod2`), count as production, and names with a rehearsal marker (`pre-prod`, `prod-test`) do not. The same answer decides incident handling and the delete-production permission in the Console. Set `stageType` when your production stage has another name, so `validate` and `deploy` always agree:

```yaml
stackConfig:
  stageType: production
```

For a non-production stage, the output looks like this:

```text
Security posture: 1 low (stage `dev` is non-production by its name).
  [LOW] mainDatabase: Database reachable from the internet (HIGH in production)
Also fix before production (not reported for this stage):
  [LOW] web: Production container service runs a single instance
  [LOW] Production stack without termination protection
```

With `--agent`, the result's `security` object carries `stage` (`name`, `purpose` and `decidedBy`: `stackConfig.stageType`, `stacktape-console` or `stage-name`), `findings` with each finding's `severity` for this stage and, when production rates it higher, its `productionSeverity`, `productionOnlyFindings`, and `exposure`. `deploy` returns the same object, reports the stage's `findings` to the Console, and only counts the production-only findings in its output.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Missing secrets

A `$Secret` whose secret does not exist yet in the region is a finding, not a failure: `validate` reports it and checks the rest of the configuration, with a placeholder reference in the template. This is the normal state after [`init`](/cli/init), which keeps a generated database or Redis password in a secret it does not create.

```text
[!] Secret my-app-cache does not exist in eu-west-1 yet. It holds a generated database password: stacktape dev creates it when it starts, and stacktape deploy creates it before it deploys (in a terminal it asks first). To create it yourself, run stacktape secret set my-app-cache with a JSON value that has a `password` key.
```

Any other missing secret, such as an API key, has to be created with [`secret set`](/cli/secret-set) before `deploy` or `dev` can run; both stop until it exists. With `--agent`, the result lists them in `missingSecrets`, each with its `name`, the `jsonKeys` the configuration reads and whether Stacktape `generated` its value.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## When to use validate

The `validate` command is a fast pre-deploy check that confirms your configuration synthesizes correctly. Use it when you want a validation gate instead of a written template file.

- **Before deploying.** Run `stacktape validate` to catch configuration errors in seconds without waiting for a full CloudFormation deployment to fail.
- **In CI pipelines.** Add `validate` (or `validate --thorough`) as a CI step on pull requests. This prevents broken configs from reaching [`deploy`](/cli/deploy).
- **After config refactors.** When you reorganize resources, rename stages, or change packaging modes, `validate` confirms the config still synthesizes correctly.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Inspecting the validated template

By default, `validate` produces only a pass/fail result. Add `--out <path>` to write the template after every requested validation step succeeds. When packaging is enabled, this is the packaged template and includes generated Lambda layers and their function references.

Use [`synth`](/cli/synth) when you only need the faster, un-packaged template compilation. Use [`diff`](/cli/diff) when you need to see what a deployment would change against a live stack.

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Important flags

| Flag | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `--with-package` | Runs workload packaging as part of validation, catching packaging errors for Lambda functions and container workloads. |
| `--thorough` | Validates packaging and asks CloudFormation to validate the template. Templates over 51,200 bytes go through the stack's deployment bucket; before the first deploy they are reported as not checked. Implies `--with-package`. |
| `--out` | Writes the template only after the requested validation steps succeed. With packaging enabled, the file includes generated artifact and layer references. |
| `--stage` | Required. The stage name used for template synthesis (e.g., `dev`, `staging`, `production`). |
| `--region` | Required. The AWS region used for template synthesis. |
| `--config` | Path to your Stacktape configuration file if it is not in the default location. |
| `--agent` | Optimizes CLI output for programmatic/LLM consumption. Uses JSONL/NDJSON output and disables the interactive terminal UI. |

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Examples

Validate config for a production stage in `us-east-1`.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage production --region us-east-1
```

Validate with a specific config file path.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

Run the most thorough validation, including packaging and CloudFormation validation, before merging a pull request.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage ci --region eu-west-1 --thorough --out ./validated-template.yaml
```

Use JSONL output for CI or AI-agent consumption.

```bash
stacktape validate --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

docs.title: validate
docs.content: ## Flags reference

For a list of available regions, see the [AWS documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/rande.html). Inside a project whose config declares `region`, the flag is optional and overrides the config. | `us-east-2`, `us-east-1`, `us-west-1`, `us-west-2`, `ap-east-1`, `ap-south-1`, `ap-northeast-3`, `ap-northeast-2`, `ap-southeast-1`, `ap-southeast-2`, `ap-northeast-1`, `ca-central-1`, `eu-central-1`, `eu-west-1`, `eu-west-2`, `eu-west-3`, `eu-north-1`, `me-south-1`, `sa-east-1`, `af-south-1`, `eu-south-1` |

The command fails if that account is not connected. | - |

docs.title: validate
docs.content:
## Related commands

- [`synth`](/cli/synth) — compiles the configuration into an un-packaged CloudFormation template and writes it to a file. Use `validate --with-package --out ...` when you need the packaged template.
- [`diff`](/cli/diff) — shows a preview of changes that would be applied to a deployed stack. Requires a deployed stack, unlike `validate`.
- [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) — deploys or updates a stack. Running `validate` before `deploy` catches errors before they reach CloudFormation.
- [`package`](/cli/package) — packages workloads and writes artifacts to disk. The `--with-package` flag on `validate` runs workload packaging as part of validation, while `package` is the dedicated command for preparing packaged outputs for inspection or deployment.

docs.title: validate
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: validate
headingPath: Does validate create or modify any AWS resources?
docs.content:
### Does validate create or modify any AWS resources?

No. The `validate` command does not create, update, or delete any AWS resources and does not require a deployed stack. Initialization can read AWS identity or metadata used during synthesis. With `--thorough`, CloudFormation's read-only `ValidateTemplate` API checks the template without creating a stack. A template over 51,200 bytes is first uploaded as a temporary object to the stack's existing deployment bucket and deleted after the check; for a stack that was never deployed, there is no bucket and the check is skipped with a warning.

docs.title: validate
headingPath: How is validate different from synth?
docs.content:
### How is validate different from synth?

Both commands synthesize a CloudFormation template from your configuration. [`synth`](/cli/synth) writes an un-packaged template immediately (default `compiled-template.yaml`). `validate` runs the selected checks first and writes nothing unless `--out` is supplied; with `--with-package` or `--thorough`, that file contains the packaged template. Use `validate` for CI gates and exact validated output, or `synth` for quick template inspection.

docs.title: validate
headingPath: Do I need AWS credentials to run validate in CI?
docs.content:
### Do I need AWS credentials to run validate in CI?

Stacktape normally needs an AWS identity because the account id participates in deterministic names and synthesized ARNs. `--thorough` additionally calls CloudFormation's `ValidateTemplate` API, and for a template over 51,200 bytes writes and deletes a temporary object in the stack's deployment bucket. Use a CI profile scoped to the intended account that can read the stack and write to that bucket.

docs.title: validate
headingPath: What errors does --thorough catch that the default level misses?
docs.content:
### What errors does --thorough catch that the default level misses?

Default validation catches configuration errors and synthesis failures. `--thorough` also catches packaging errors, then asks CloudFormation to check the template. Only a template over 51,200 bytes of a stack that was never deployed skips that check; the result then has `checked.cloudformation: false` and a warning. Even an AWS-checked template can fail during provisioning; verify deployment behavior in a deployed stage.

docs.title: validate
headingPath: Can I use validate with AI agents or in scripts?
docs.content:
### Can I use validate with AI agents or in scripts?

Yes. Pass `--agent` to optimize CLI output for programmatic or LLM consumption. This flag uses JSONL/NDJSON output (one JSON object per line) and disables the interactive terminal UI. You can also use `--json` for machine-readable output without the other `--agent` behaviors.

docs.title: version
docs.content:
# version

The `stacktape version` command prints the currently installed version of Stacktape. It requires no arguments, no configuration file, and no API key. Use it to verify your installation or check whether you need to [upgrade](/cli/upgrade).

docs.title: version
docs.content:
## Usage

```bash
stacktape version
```

The command outputs the installed version number and exits. No AWS credentials, project configuration, or login are required.

`stacktape --version` and `stacktape -v` print the same output.

headingPath: Does `stacktape version` require an API key or login?
docs.content:
### Does `stacktape version` require an API key or login?

No. The `version` command runs entirely locally and does not contact the Stacktape API. You can run it before logging in or configuring any credentials.

docs.title: version
headingPath: How do I check if my Stacktape version is out of date?
docs.content:
### How do I check if my Stacktape version is out of date?

Run `stacktape version` to see what you have installed, then run [`stacktape upgrade`](/cli/upgrade) to move to the latest release (or `stacktape upgrade 4.0.1` for a specific version). Re-run `stacktape version` afterward to confirm the new version is active.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
# Configuration Files

Stacktape configuration defines your infrastructure as code in a single file. You declare resources — APIs, databases, containers, functions — and Stacktape provisions them on AWS. The configuration supports two formats: TypeScript (recommended) and YAML. Both produce identical infrastructure; the choice affects your authoring experience.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## Choosing a format

TypeScript is the recommended format for most teams. It provides full type safety, IDE autocompletion, conditional logic, loops, and the ability to split configuration across multiple files with standard imports. YAML works for straightforward projects where configuration is static and short.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | TypeScript | YAML |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type checking | yes | no |
| IDE autocompletion | Full | With VS Code extension |
| Conditional logic | Native (if/else, ternary) | Via directives only |
| Loops / dynamic resources | Native (for, map) | no |
| Code reuse | Imports, functions, modules | Variables only |
| Refactoring support | yes | no |
| Multi-file configs | yes | no |


> **Tip:** Use TypeScript when your configuration involves per-stage differences, dynamic resource creation, or shared patterns across projects. Use YAML for prototypes or small projects with a fixed set of resources.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## When to use TypeScript

Most teams should default to TypeScript. It catches configuration errors before deployment, enables per-stage branching without separate config files, and supports extracting shared patterns into reusable modules. If your project has more than a handful of resources, or if you deploy to multiple stages with different sizing, TypeScript eliminates duplication and reduces misconfiguration risk.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## When to use YAML

YAML is appropriate for very small, static projects or when your team strongly prefers declarative-only configuration. A single Lambda function with an API gateway, or a static hosting bucket with a custom domain — these are cases where YAML's simplicity is an advantage. If you keep the same resource names and properties, TypeScript can represent the same configuration shape as YAML, so you can move to TypeScript later when you outgrow YAML (needing conditionals, loops, or multi-file organization).

docs.title: Configuration Files
Configuration Files
docs.content:
### The defineConfig callback

The `defineConfig` function receives a callback whose argument provides deploy-time context. Use these values for per-stage branching without separate config files.

| Property      | Type       | Description                                                  |
| ------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `stage`       | `string`   | Current stage name (e.g. `dev`, `production`)                |
| `region`      | `string`   | AWS region for this deployment (e.g. `eu-west-1`)            |
| `projectName` | `string`   | Project name: `--project`, the settings object, or the machine-wide default |
| `command`     | `string`   | The CLI command being run (`deploy`, `delete`, `dev`, etc.)  |
| `cliArgs`     | `string[]`   | Additional CLI arguments passed after `--`                   |

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
### Project name and region

Declare the project name and region in the first argument of `defineConfig`. Commands run inside the project then need only `--stage`: `stacktape deploy --stage dev`, `stacktape logs api --stage dev`, `stacktape status --stage dev`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig({ projectName: 'my-app', region: 'eu-west-1' }, ({ stage }) => ({
  resources: { uploads: new Bucket({}) }
}));
```


Example (YAML):

```yaml
projectName: my-app
region: eu-west-1
resources:
  uploads:
    type: bucket
```


Stacktape reads these two values before it runs the config, because choosing credentials and the AWS region comes first. Write them as plain strings: a variable, an environment variable or another computed value is rejected with the supported form. Return everything else from the callback; the callback always receives the effective `projectName` and `region`.

A `--project` or `--region` flag overrides the config for one command. Without a value in the config, the region comes from `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, the machine-wide default (`stacktape defaults set region`) and then the AWS profile, in that order. Commands that do not use the config, such as `stacktape secret get`, take only the region from it and never fail because of it.

docs.title: Configuration Files
Configuration Files
Configuration Files
docs.content:
### IDE experience

With TypeScript, your editor provides autocompletion for every property, inline JSDoc documentation on hover, go-to-definition for resource types, and real-time error highlighting. Typos in property names or invalid values are caught before you deploy. The `stacktape` package ships its own type definitions — no additional `@types` package is needed.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## YAML configuration

For simpler projects, create a `stacktape.yml` file in your project root.

YAML uses a `type` + `properties` structure for each resource. The `type` corresponds to the TypeScript resource class, and `properties` correspond to the constructor argument.


> **Info:** The Stacktape VS Code extension provides autocompletion, syntax validation, and inline documentation for YAML configuration files.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
### When YAML falls short

YAML configuration cannot express conditional logic natively — you need [directives](/configuration/directives) for deploy-time interpolation. There are no loops, so you cannot generate resources dynamically. Large YAML configs tend to become repetitive because there is no import mechanism; [variables](/configuration/variables-and-reuse) provide limited reuse. If you find yourself working around these constraints, switch to TypeScript.

docs.title: Configuration Files
Configuration Files
docs.content:
## Config file detection

Stacktape auto-detects configuration files named `stacktape.ts`, `stacktape.yml`, `stacktape.yaml`, or `stacktape.js` in your project root. You can point to a different location with the `--config` option. See the [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) command reference for details.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production --config ./infrastructure/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## Directives in configuration

Both TypeScript and YAML configurations support [directives](/configuration/directives) — built-in functions that resolve values at deploy time. In TypeScript, directives are imported as functions from the `stacktape` package. In YAML, all directives use a `$DirectiveName()` string syntax.

Common built-in directives available as TypeScript functions from the `stacktape` package:

| Directive              | Purpose                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `$Secret()`            | Reference a Stacktape secret                                 |
| `$ResourceParam()`     | Reference a deployed resource's parameter                    |
| `$Stage()`             | Returns the current stage name                               |
| `$Region()`            | Returns the current AWS region                               |
| `$Format()`            | String interpolation with deploy-time values                 |
| `$Var()`               | Reference a value from the `variables` section               |
| `$File()`              | Include contents of a file at deploy time                    |

In TypeScript configs, you can often use normal constants instead of `$Var()`, standard `import`/`readFileSync` instead of `$File()`, and template literals instead of `$Format()`. The directive functions are available when you need deploy-time resolution behavior that cannot be replaced by build-time TypeScript evaluation.

See [Directives](/configuration/directives) for the full list of available directives and detailed usage.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.content:
## How TypeScript maps to YAML

YAML resources use a `type` plus `properties` shape. In TypeScript, the equivalent resource is represented by a resource class whose constructor receives the corresponding property shape. Nested objects in YAML (packaging modes, engines, integrations) also use `type` + `properties`; in TypeScript, these correspond to nested class constructors.

The table below shows the mapping between TypeScript classes and YAML types. This is not exhaustive — see individual resource pages for the full set of options.

| TypeScript class                       | YAML type                       |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `LambdaFunction`                       | `function`                      |
| `EdgeLambdaFunction`                   | `edge-lambda-function`          |
| `WebService`                           | `web-service`                   |
| `PrivateService`                       | `private-service`               |
| `WorkerService`                        | `worker-service`                |
| `MultiContainerWorkload`               | `multi-container-workload`      |
| `BatchJob`                             | `batch-job`                     |
| `NextjsWeb`                            | `nextjs-web`                    |
| `RelationalDatabase`                   | `relational-database`           |
| `DynamoDbTable`                        | `dynamo-db-table`               |
| `Redis`                                | `redis`                         |
| `MongoDbAtlasCluster`                  | `mongo-db-atlas-cluster`        |
| `UpstashRedis`                         | `upstash-redis`                 |
