If your config matches the deployed stack exactly, the output shows `NO CHANGES DETECTED`. If CloudFormation reports internal changes that don't affect any user-facing Stacktape resource, the output shows `NO MEANINGFUL STACKTAPE RESOURCE CHANGES` — this means the infrastructure is effectively unchanged from your perspective.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
## Agent mode output

When agent mode is active (via the `--agent` flag), the command switches from colorized interactive output to a compact, machine-readable format suitable for programmatic consumption by CI scripts, coding assistants, and automation tools.

The terminal JSONL result includes `data.result.changePlan`, a self-versioned `stacktape.change-plan.v1` object. It contains target and baseline identifiers, semantic template and workload-build digests, a short plan ID, Stacktape resource-change counts, protected-resource risks, and `aws-change-set` as the change-evidence source. It does not contain the generated template, resolved property values, credentials, or local paths.

The output follows three paths depending on what CloudFormation reports:

- **No changes at all** — when both raw CloudFormation changes and Stacktape resource changes are empty, the command prints `NO CHANGES DETECTED`.
- **Raw changes but no meaningful resource changes** — when CloudFormation reports internal or dependency-only changes that don't map to Stacktape resources, the command prints a `SUMMARY` line followed by `NO MEANINGFUL STACKTAPE RESOURCE CHANGES`.
- **Meaningful resource changes** — the command prints a `SUMMARY` line (e.g. `SUMMARY: 2 new, 0 removed, 0 replaced, 1 updated`) followed by per-resource detail.

The per-resource output includes:

- One line per changed resource with the action symbol, resource name, resource type, and action label
- Up to three highlights per resource
- Replacement warnings (`Will replace` / `May replace` lines) per resource

See [Agent mode in dev](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev) for broader context on using Stacktape with AI coding assistants.

Without `--agent`, the output is colorized and formatted for interactive terminal use.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
## Using preview in CI/CD

Running `diff` in a CI pipeline before deploying is a reliable safety net for production stages. Capture the output and post it as a PR comment or Slack message so the team reviews infrastructure changes alongside code changes.

A typical CI workflow:

1. Run `stacktape diff` with `--stage production` on the PR branch. Use `--agent` for simpler text output that's easier to parse in CI.
2. Review the output for `Will replace` and `May replace` lines — treat these as a review signal before deploying.
3. After merge, run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy).

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
### Example: GitHub Actions preview step

Use `--agent` for output that's easier to parse in scripts:

```bash
stacktape diff --stage production --region eu-west-1 --agent
```

For a full CI/CD integration, see [custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd) or [GitOps with the Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
## Preview vs synth

Stacktape offers two ways to inspect what a deployment would produce:

| | `diff` | [`synth`](/cli/synth) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Requires deployed stack** | Yes | No |
| **Shows resource-level diff** | Yes — create, update, replace, delete | No — shows the raw template only |
| **Detects replacements** | Yes — via CloudFormation change set | No |
| **Packages workloads** | Yes | Yes |
| **Modifies stack resources** | No | No |
| **Best for** | Pre-deploy safety check | Inspecting the generated CloudFormation template (see the [CLI reference](/cli/synth) for exact behavior) |

Use `diff` when you want to know *what will change*. Use `synth` when you want to see the full generated CloudFormation template without needing a deployed stack — useful for auditing or debugging template generation.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
### "Stack does not exist" error

The `diff` command requires an already-deployed stack to compare against (the command initializes with `commandRequiresDeployedStack: true`). If the stage has never been deployed, deploy it first with [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy). You cannot preview changes for a stage that doesn't exist yet.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
headingPath: Preview shows changes you didn't make
docs.content:
### Preview shows changes you didn't make

Stacktape normalizes the template diff to filter out internal-only changes, but some edge cases can still surface unexpected diffs. The human-readable output describes these as "internal runtime churn or dependency re-evaluation." Common causes include:

- **Dependency re-evaluation** — CloudFormation may report changes to resources that depend on a resource you modified, even if the dependent resource itself is unchanged. The normalized preview filters these when no meaningful Stacktape resource changes are present, but they can still appear alongside real changes.
- **Container image digest changes** — if a container image is rebuilt and produces a different digest (even without source changes), the change set may report the associated resources as updated.
- **Changed secret or SSM parameter values** — if a referenced secret or SSM parameter value changed since the last deploy, resources that reference it may appear as updated in the change set.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
### Preview takes a long time

The preview command packages all workloads (Lambda bundles, container images) before generating the change set. If packaging is slow, the bottleneck is usually container image builds. Stacktape enables caching for this step (`commandCanUseCache: true`) — if you're seeing slow builds, check that your Docker layer cache is working. See [container packaging](/packaging/overview#container-packaging) for details on optimizing build times.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
### Does diff cost anything?

CloudFormation change sets are free. The only costs are S3 storage for the uploaded template (negligible — a few KB) and any container image builds that happen during packaging. The command enables packaging cache, but container builds can still dominate runtime.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
headingPath: How is this different from CloudFormation drift detection?
docs.content:
### How is this different from CloudFormation drift detection?

Drift detection checks whether someone changed your AWS resources outside of CloudFormation (e.g., via the AWS Console or AWS CLI). Preview-changes checks what would happen if you deployed your *current Stacktape config* to an existing stack. They answer different questions: drift detection asks "has my infrastructure drifted from what was last deployed?", while preview asks "what would change if I deployed this new config?".

docs.title: Previewing Changes
headingPath: What's the difference between "will replace" and "may replace"?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between "will replace" and "may replace"?

"Will replace" means CloudFormation has already determined the resource must be replaced — a replacement physical resource is created and the old one retired, which can cause downtime or data loss on stateful resources. "May replace" means CloudFormation cannot decide at change-set time; the outcome depends on the specific property values and the AWS service's behavior during the actual update. Treat "may replace" on stateful resources like [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) and [DynamoDB tables](/resources/databases/dynamodb) as if it were "will replace" — back up your data before deploying.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
headingPath: What's the difference between diff and Terraform plan?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between diff and Terraform plan?

Both show what an apply/deploy would change before doing it. Stacktape's `diff` uses CloudFormation change sets under the hood, which means AWS itself evaluates the diff. CloudFormation evaluates replacements and Stacktape surfaces both definite `Will replace` and conditional `May replace` warnings — without maintaining local state files. The trade-off is that `diff` requires a deployed stack to compare against, whereas `terraform plan` works against a local state file and can preview a first-time apply.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
docs.content:
### Does diff validate my configuration?

Yes. The command runs the same validation and guardrail checks as [`deploy`](/cli/deploy) before creating the change set. If your configuration has errors, they'll surface during the preview rather than during a real deployment. The generated template is also validated against CloudFormation before the change set is created.

docs.title: Previewing Changes
headingPath: When should I use diff vs just deploying?
docs.content:
### When should I use diff vs just deploying?

Use `diff` for production stages, stages with stateful resources (databases, queues, tables), or any stage where an accidental replacement would cause real damage. For development stages where you're iterating quickly and can tolerate failed deploys, deploying directly is faster and usually safe enough. The preview adds the overhead of packaging and change-set creation, so treat it as a safety measure for high-risk deploys rather than a step in every iteration cycle.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
# Rollbacks

Stacktape provides two rollback commands for recovering from bad deployments. [`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback) re-deploys a previous good version using stored deployment artifacts. [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/cf-rollback) triggers Stacktape's CloudFormation rollback flow when a deployment leaves the stack in a failed state. Neither command requires your local source code or config file — version rollback works from stored deployment artifacts and CloudFormation state rather than rebuilding from your current working tree.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: When to use each rollback type
docs.content:
## When to use each rollback type

Stacktape's two rollback commands serve different failure scenarios. Choosing the wrong one wastes time or leaves the stack in a worse state.

| Scenario | Command | What it does |
|----------|---------|--------------|
| Last deploy succeeded but introduced a bug | `stacktape rollback` | Re-deploys a previous version's CloudFormation template as a new deployment |
| Deploy failed and you want to continue from the failure | `stacktape deploy` | Fixes and continues a stack left in `CREATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_FAILED`, keeping what the failed deploy created |
| Update failed and you want to undo it instead | `stacktape stack recover` | Triggers Stacktape's CloudFormation rollback flow and cleans up rolled-back deployment artifacts |
| First deploy failed and you want to remove it | `stacktape delete` | Deletes the stack and everything the failed deploy created |
| You want to undo multiple deploys back | `stacktape rollback --rollback-steps 3` | Targets an older version by stepping back N versions |

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
## Version rollback

The [`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback) command re-deploys a previously working CloudFormation template and reuses the original deployment artifacts from that version. It creates a **new** deployment version — it does not rewrite history. This is the command you want when your stack is healthy (last deploy succeeded) but the application is broken due to a code or config change you need to undo.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
### How it works

Every successful Stacktape deployment stores a versioned snapshot of the CloudFormation template and all packaged artifacts in the deployment bucket. Versions follow the format `v000001`, `v000002`, etc.

When you run `stacktape rollback`, Stacktape:

1. **Resolves the target version** — determines which version to roll back to, either by an explicit `--target-version` flag or by stepping back N versions (default: 1).
2. **Verifies artifacts for the target version** — confirms the CloudFormation template and all referenced deployment artifacts still exist.
3. **Checks rollback safety** — inspects the current stack's rollback safety metadata and warns if the config uses features that may not replay cleanly (e.g., `$File` directive, `after:deploy` hooks, TypeScript transforms, custom directives).
4. **Deploys the old template** — downloads the old CloudFormation template, patches the version output, uploads it, and triggers a CloudFormation stack update.
5. **Restores bucket-synced content** — Stacktape attempts to restore bucket-synced content from the target version's manifest. If that restore fails, Stacktape warns that static websites may need redeployment from the original commit.

The rolled-back template is deployed as a new version number. Rolling back from `v000005` to `v000003` creates `v000006` containing the `v000003` template. After a successful rollback, the stack has a new deployment version, so the next normal deploy continues from that version.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
### Basic usage

Roll back one version (the most common case — undoes the most recent deploy):

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

Roll back to a specific version:

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1 --target-version v000003
```

Roll back multiple steps:

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1 --rollback-steps 3
```

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
### Listing available versions

Before rolling back, check which versions are available:

```bash
stacktape rollback --stage production --region eu-west-1 --list-versions
```

This prints the current version and versions found in Stacktape's previous-version list. Stacktape still verifies the selected version's artifacts before performing the rollback. Versions are numbered sequentially, so you can correlate them with your deployment history. Old versions may be cleaned up based on `previousVersionsToKeep`; if a target version is no longer available, Stacktape cannot roll back to it.

docs.title: Rollbacks
Rollbacks
docs.content:
### Rollback safety warnings

Not all deployments can be rolled back cleanly. After Stacktape verifies the target version artifacts, rollback safety checks print warnings without blocking the rollback. The safety checks cover:

- **State-embedding directives (`$File` and similar)** — the rolled-back template contains values that were baked in at the original deploy time. If the referenced file has changed since then, the rollback uses the old content.
- **TypeScript transforms** — Stacktape warns when the deployment used TypeScript transforms, because those transforms are not captured in the CloudFormation template and may require manual review after rollback.
- **`after:deploy` hooks** — Stacktape warns when the config has `after:deploy` [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) (database migrations, cache warming, etc.); those hooks are not re-executed during rollback.
- **Custom directives** — results from custom directives were captured at original deploy time.

When rollback safety metadata is present, Stacktape prints warnings only for the safety fields that are set. The command does not block the rollback. Older deployments without rollback safety metadata still produce a cautionary warning. In all cases, the rollback is still a CloudFormation stack update and can fail for normal CloudFormation reasons. For configs that use these features, review the warnings and decide whether manual follow-up is needed after the rollback completes.


> **Info:** When rollback safety metadata is not found — typically because the deployment predates rollback support — Stacktape proceeds with the rollback but warns that results may be unpredictable if the config used any of the features above.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
## CloudFormation rollback

The [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/cf-rollback) command triggers Stacktape's CloudFormation rollback flow for the target stack and then cleans up any deployment artifacts that were uploaded during the failed deployment. Use this when a deployment failed and left your stack in a broken state — it does not target a specific previous version like `stacktape rollback` does.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
### When to use stack recover

A failed deployment keeps what it created and leaves the stack in `CREATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_FAILED` unless [automatic rollback](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#automatic-rollback) is on. Deploying again continues from the failure. Use `stacktape stack recover` when you want to undo a failed update instead. For a failed first deployment there is no earlier state to return to: CloudFormation deletes its resources and leaves an empty `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` stack, which you then delete, so run `stacktape delete` directly. The command triggers Stacktape's CloudFormation rollback flow and then deletes the artifacts uploaded during the failed deployment. Note that CloudFormation rollback itself can still fail in some cases — if the stack cannot be restored, manual recovery through the AWS Console or AWS CLI may be required.

You do NOT need this command when:

- The stack is healthy and you want to go back to an earlier version — use `stacktape rollback` instead
- The deploy failed but the stack already rolled back on its own — the stack is already recovered

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
### Basic usage

```bash
stacktape stack recover --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

After a successful `stack recover`, Stacktape automatically cleans up any deployment artifacts that were uploaded during the failed deployment.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: What's the difference between `stacktape rollback` and `stacktape stack recover`?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between `stacktape rollback` and `stacktape stack recover`?

`stacktape rollback` is a version-targeted operation — it picks a specific previous deployment version, verifies its artifacts still exist, and re-deploys its CloudFormation template as a new version. Use it when your stack is healthy but the latest code or config is wrong. `stacktape stack recover` is a recovery operation — it triggers Stacktape's CloudFormation rollback flow to unstick a stack left in a failed state, then cleans up artifacts from the failed deployment. Use it when the stack itself is broken, not just the application.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: What happens to my database during a rollback?
docs.content:
### What happens to my database during a rollback?

`stacktape rollback` does not run reverse database migrations; it deploys the old CloudFormation template. If your schema changed between versions (for example, you added a column via a [deployment script](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deployment-scripts-and-hooks)), you need to review and handle any schema or data changes separately before and after the rollback.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: How do I know which version to roll back to?
docs.content:
### How do I know which version to roll back to?

Run `stacktape rollback --list-versions` to see all available versions with their version numbers. Versions are numbered sequentially (`v000001`, `v000002`, etc.), so you can correlate them with your deployment history. For most incidents, rolling back one step (the default) is correct — you're undoing the most recent change.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: Can I roll forward after a rollback?
docs.content:
### Can I roll forward after a rollback?

Yes. A version rollback creates a new deployment version (e.g., rolling back from `v000005` to `v000003` creates `v000006`). After a successful version rollback, Stacktape reports the new deployment version. You can then deploy normally with [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) or run another rollback to any retained version.

docs.title: Rollbacks
headingPath: Why can't I roll back to an old version?
docs.content:
### Why can't I roll back to an old version?

Each version stays a valid rollback target only while its deployment artifacts are retained. Once a version's artifacts are cleaned up, `stacktape rollback` can no longer restore it — even though it may still appear in your deployment history. Retention is controlled by `deploymentConfig.previousVersionsToKeep`; raise it if you need a longer rollback window, at the cost of keeping more artifacts in storage.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.content:
### Does CloudFormation rollback always succeed?

Not always. AWS CloudFormation rollback can fail if a resource can't be restored to its previous state — for example, if someone manually deleted a resource outside of CloudFormation, or if a resource's previous configuration is no longer valid (a deleted AMI, a deregistered domain). When this happens, the stack ends up in a state that requires manual recovery through the AWS Console or AWS CLI before further Stacktape deployments can proceed.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
# CI/CD

Stacktape offers two paths to automated deployments: **GitOps via the Stacktape Console** (recommended) and **custom CI pipelines** using the CLI. GitOps gives you push-to-deploy and PR preview environments without writing a GitHub Actions workflow file for the deploy path. Custom CI gives full control when you already have an established workflow.


> **Info:** Already have CI/CD running? Skip ahead to [Going to production](/getting-started/going-to-production).

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
## GitOps via the Stacktape Console

GitOps is the recommended path for most teams. You connect your repository once, then Stacktape manages the deployment trigger — every push to the configured branch deploys automatically.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### CLI prompt after first deploy

After a successful CLI deploy that creates a new stack, Stacktape runs a CI/CD setup prompt when invoked from an interactive terminal. If you skip the prompt, you can configure GitOps at any time in the Stacktape Console.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### What you can configure

Each GitOps configuration maps a git event to a deployment action. In the Console, you set:

- **Deployment trigger** — push to a branch, or pull request opened against a branch
- **Source branch** — the branch that triggers the deployment
- **Target stage** — the stage name to deploy (e.g. `production`, `staging`, or `pr-{#number}` for PR previews)
- **AWS region** — where the stack deploys
- **AWS account** — which connected account to use
- **Auto-delete on PR close** — when enabled (`deleteStackAfterPrClose`), Stacktape deletes the PR stack when the PR is merged or closed

You can create multiple GitOps configurations per project — for example, one that deploys `main` to `production` and another that creates preview environments for every PR.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### PR preview environments

When you configure a pull-request trigger, Stacktape creates an isolated stage for each PR (named `pr-{#number}` by default). The PR stage deploys when the PR is opened, redeploys on every new commit pushed to the PR branch, and deletes automatically when the PR is merged or closed (if auto-delete is enabled). This gives reviewers a live URL to test against without touching your production or staging stage.

For the full reference on branch patterns and advanced configuration, see [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### Connecting your repository

GitOps uses the GitHub App integration to react to git events. Connect your repository in the Stacktape Console before creating your first GitOps configuration.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
## Custom CI/CD integration

If you prefer managing your own pipeline — or need pre-deploy steps like tests and lint — use the Stacktape CLI directly. Any CI system that can run shell commands works: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, and others.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### Required environment variables

| Variable | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` | Authenticates the CLI against the Stacktape API. Create one in the Console under [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys). |

Store this key in your CI provider's secret store and expose it to the CLI as an environment variable. The CLI deploys into the AWS account you connected to your Stacktape organization.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### GitHub Actions example

Create `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` in your repository:

```yaml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
      - name: Deploy to production
        env:
          STACKTAPE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.STACKTAPE_API_KEY }}
        run: |
          npx stacktape deploy --project my-project --stage production --region us-east-1 --yes
```

Replace `my-project` with your Stacktape project name. Store `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` in your repository's secrets settings. The `--yes` flag skips the interactive confirmation prompt that would block CI.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### GitLab CI example

Add to `.gitlab-ci.yml`:

```yaml
deploy:
  image: node:20
  stage: deploy
  only:
    - main
  script:
    - npx stacktape deploy --project my-project --stage production --region us-east-1 --yes
  variables:
    STACKTAPE_API_KEY: $STACKTAPE_API_KEY
```

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
### PR previews in custom CI

Use dynamic stage names based on the PR number to create isolated preview environments.

Deploy when the PR opens or updates:

```bash
npx stacktape deploy --project my-project --stage "pr-${PR_NUMBER}" --region us-east-1 --yes
```

Clean up when the PR closes:

```bash
npx stacktape delete --project my-project --stage "pr-${PR_NUMBER}" --region us-east-1 --yes
```

For more detail on custom pipelines, see [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
## Which path to choose

Use this comparison to decide between Console-managed GitOps and a self-managed CI pipeline.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | GitOps (Console) | Custom CI/CD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup effort | Minutes, no files | Write workflow file |
| Pipeline maintenance | Stacktape manages the deploy trigger | You own it |
| PR previews | Built-in with auto-delete | Manual setup with dynamic stage names |
| Custom steps (tests, lint, gates) | Not supported | Full control |
| Repository source | Connected git repository | Any CI system |


**Recommendation:** Start with GitOps. It takes minutes to set up and handles PR previews automatically. If you need custom test steps, approval gates, or multi-stage pipelines that run before or after the deploy, switch to custom CI or combine both — use GitOps for staging and custom CI for branches that need extra validation before deploying to production.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.content:
## Next step

Your deployments are now automated. The final step covers production hardening — alarms, budgets, custom domains, and guardrails.

docs.title: Configure Your Stack
docs.content:
# Configure Your Stack

A `stacktape.ts` file defines your AWS infrastructure — APIs, functions, databases, containers — using typed TypeScript classes. Stacktape reads this file when you deploy, run dev mode, or manage resources, and creates the corresponding AWS resources in your account. Create one from scratch, bootstrap from a starter, or let `stacktape init` analyze your repository.


> **Info:** Already have a `stacktape.ts`? Skip to [using dev mode](/getting-started/use-the-dev-mode) or [deploying your first stage](/getting-started/deploy-your-first-stage).


> **Tip:** **Recommended starting path:** Run `stacktape init` in your repository. It reads the code and proposes the infrastructure, or starts a new project from a starter template. Either way, understanding the config format below will help you customize what you get.

docs.title: Configure Your Stack
docs.content:
## Install the package

```bash
npm install stacktape --save-dev
```

Install the `stacktape` package for typed resource classes and directives such as [`$Secret`](/configuration/directives) and [`$ResourceParam`](/configuration/directives). You get full IDE autocompletion and type checking as you write your config.

docs.title: Configure Your Stack
Configure Your Stack
Configure Your Stack
docs.content:
### Context properties

The context object passed to the `defineConfig` callback includes:

| Property      | Type                                             | Description                                                |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `stage`       | `string`                                         | Current stage name (e.g., `dev`, `production`)             |
| `region`      | `string`                                         | AWS region (e.g., `us-east-1`, `eu-west-1`)                |
| `projectName` | `string`                                         | Project name, always set when the config declares it ([project settings](/configuration/configuration-files#project-name-and-region)) |
| `command`     | `string`                                         | CLI command being run (`deploy`, `delete`, `dev`, etc.)     |
| `cliArgs`     | `Record<string, string \| number \| boolean>`    | Key-value arguments passed via the `--arg` CLI flag        |

See [configuration files](/configuration/configuration-files) for the complete config reference.

docs.title: Configure Your Stack
docs.content:
## Quick-start with stacktape init

[`stacktape init`](/cli/init) reads an existing repository and writes a config for it, after you review the
proposed infrastructure in its wizard. In an empty directory, it starts a new project from a starter template:

```bash
npx stacktape@latest init
```

This is the fastest path from zero to a working project. Keep the config it writes in version control, so
infrastructure changes are reviewed with code changes.

docs.title: Configure Your Stack
docs.content:
## Beyond resources

The `resources` section is the only required part of a Stacktape config, but several optional sections are available as your project grows: [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) for running scripts automatically before or after deploy, delete, dev, or bucket sync operations; [scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) for runnable tasks like database migrations (three types: `local-script`, `local-script-with-bastion-tunneling`, and `bastion-script`); [variables](/configuration/variables-and-reuse) for reusable values; [directives](/configuration/directives) for custom deploy-time logic; and [deployment settings](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks) for rollback behavior and termination protection. See [configuration files](/configuration/configuration-files) for the complete reference.

docs.title: Configure Your Stack
docs.content:
## Next step

You have a config that defines what to deploy. Next, use dev mode to iterate locally — edit your code and see changes without waiting for full deployments.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
# Deploy Your First Stage

Deploying a Stacktape stage takes your `stacktape.ts` configuration and provisions real AWS infrastructure — a CloudFormation stack containing every resource you declared. This page walks you through authentication, AWS account connection, and running your first deploy command.


> **Info:** Already deployed before? Skip to [CI/CD](/getting-started/ci-cd) or [Going to production](/getting-started/going-to-production).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Prerequisites

Before deploying, you need:

- A `stacktape.ts` configuration file (created in [Configure your stack](/getting-started/configure-your-stack))
- A Stacktape account (free — created during login)
- An AWS account to deploy into

If you followed [Use the dev mode](/getting-started/use-the-dev-mode), your config is already tested locally and ready for a real deployment.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Step 1: Log in to Stacktape

The [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) command authenticates your CLI with the Stacktape platform. The command verifies your credentials, saves the API key locally, and shows the authenticated user and organization.

```bash
stacktape login
```

The CLI opens an interactive auth flow. You can authenticate with Google, sign up with email, or enter an existing API key. After successful authentication, the CLI stores your credentials locally and displays your user and organization name.

For CI environments or headless servers where a browser is not available, pass an API key directly.

```bash
stacktape login --api-key YOUR_API_KEY
```

You can create API keys in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/api-keys).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Step 2: Connect your AWS account

Stacktape deploys resources into your own AWS account. Before your first deploy, you need to connect an AWS account to your Stacktape organization. This creates a cross-account IAM role that Stacktape assumes to perform deployments, read logs, and manage resources on your behalf.

Open the connected AWS accounts page in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) and click **Connect AWS account**. Enter an **Account name** (an arbitrary name like `dev-account`), then click **Connect account in AWS console**. This opens a CloudFormation Quick Create link in your AWS console. After the stack finishes creating, the connection activates automatically and the account status changes to `ACTIVE` in the Console.


> **Tip:** Connecting an AWS account is free. AWS resources created by your stacks are billed by AWS in your AWS account.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### What the connection creates

The connection CloudFormation stack must be created in the `eu-west-1` region and creates an IAM role with cross-account trust. Stacktape assumes this role to deploy and manage resources in your account. Your actual project stacks can deploy to any AWS region — the connection stack location does not restrict where your infrastructure runs.

You can revoke access at any time by deleting the connection in the Console or deleting the CloudFormation stack directly in AWS. For details on the exact permissions granted, see [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Step 3: Deploy

With authentication and AWS connection in place, deploy your stack with the [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) command.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

Stages let you run multiple independent copies of your infrastructure — `dev`, `staging`, `production` — from the same configuration. See the [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) CLI reference for the full list of flags and their accepted values.

If your configuration file is not named `stacktape.ts` or is in a different directory, point the CLI at it explicitly.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --region eu-west-1 --config ./infra/stacktape.ts
```

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### What happens during deploy

Stacktape processes your configuration in four phases:

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Flow
1. **Build & Package**: Bundles your application code (Lambda zips, container images), resolves resource configuration, evaluates directives and secrets, and generates the CloudFormation template.
2. **Upload**: Packaged artifacts are uploaded to an S3 deployment bucket in your AWS account.
3. **Deploy**: A CloudFormation stack is created (first deploy) or updated with the generated template. CloudFormation provisions, updates, or removes AWS resources as needed.
4. **Post-deploy**: For stacks that include hosting buckets or CDNs, Stacktape syncs static files and invalidates CDN caches. Then it prepares deployed stack information and resource links.


On the first deploy, CloudFormation creates the stack and all resources from scratch. On subsequent deploys, Stacktape prepares the CloudFormation template, computes a diff, uploads artifacts, and submits the template to CloudFormation to update the stack. When only code changed, Stacktape updates the changed Lambda functions or container services directly instead of running a CloudFormation stack update.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### Deploy output

After a successful CLI deploy, Stacktape includes resource links and a Console URL in the completion output. The Console URL follows the pattern:

```
https://console.stacktape.com/projects/{project}/{stage}/overview
```

The Console URL includes the project name. The project name is set via `--project`, a configured default (see [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure)), or an interactive prompt on your first deploy. See the [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) CLI reference for the full list of flags. Open this URL to manage the deployed stack in the Console.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## What gets created in AWS

A standard Stacktape deploy creates or updates a CloudFormation stack in the connected AWS account. When only code changed, Stacktape updates Lambda function code or container services directly without a CloudFormation stack update. The CloudFormation stack is the unit Stacktape manages for the stage. Inside the stack, CloudFormation provisions whatever your configuration declares:

| What | Example |
|---|---|
| Your declared resources | Lambda functions, container services, databases, buckets, queues — everything in your `stacktape.ts` |
| Deployment artifacts | Uploaded before the stack is deployed; Stacktape passes the CloudFormation template URL to CloudFormation |
| IAM roles and policies | Resource access configured through [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources); see [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for details |
| Log groups | CloudWatch log groups for each compute resource that produces logs |

Because Stacktape deploys through CloudFormation, the resulting AWS resources also appear in the AWS console for direct inspection.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Verifying the deploy

After the deploy completes, verify your stack is running.

Open the resource URL printed by the CLI. For a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) or [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) with an HTTP trigger, this is a live HTTPS endpoint you can hit immediately.

The deploy output also includes a Console URL for the deployed stack. See [Manage your app in the Console](/getting-started/using-console-ui) for what you can do there.

To view logs from the CLI, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs).

```bash
stacktape logs
```

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Redeploying after changes

After making code or configuration changes, run the same deploy command again.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

Stacktape prepares the CloudFormation template, computes a diff, uploads artifacts, and submits the template to CloudFormation to update the stack.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### Code-only changes deploy in seconds

When a deployment changes only the code of functions or container services, Stacktape updates them directly instead of through CloudFormation. You don't need a flag for this. Changes to infrastructure or configuration always go through CloudFormation, and `--full` forces it. See [Fast deployments](/cli/deploy#fast-deployments).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
## Deploying multiple stages

Stages are independent copies of your infrastructure. Deploy a staging environment alongside dev by choosing a different stage name.

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage staging --region eu-west-1
```

Each stage is deployed as its own CloudFormation stack with its own resources and URLs. Use different stage names to run separate copies of the resources declared by your configuration. This lets you test changes in staging without affecting production users. For automated stage-per-branch workflows, see [Stacks per git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### "No connected AWS accounts"

You need to connect an AWS account before deploying. Open the connected AWS accounts page in the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) and follow the connection flow described in Step 2.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: "belongs to AWS account …, which is not connected"
docs.content:
### "belongs to AWS account …, which is not connected"

`--profile`, `AWS_PROFILE` or AWS keys in your environment point to an AWS account that is not connected to your organization. Stacktape deploys to the account your local AWS credentials belong to. Unset them, pass `--aws-account <name>`, or connect that account. See [Choosing the account for a CLI command](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account#choosing-the-account-for-a-cli-command).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### Deploy takes longer than expected

First deploys take longer because every resource must be created from scratch. Databases and container services take longer to provision than Lambda functions. Subsequent deploys that only change code take seconds, because Stacktape updates the code directly.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### A resource fails to create

If a resource fails to create, the resources that were already created stay, and the stack is left in `CREATE_FAILED`. Fix the error and deploy again to continue from there, or run `stacktape delete` to remove everything. The CLI displays the specific error. Common causes include IAM permission issues, resource limit quotas, or invalid configuration values. For rollback options, see [`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback) for version-based rollback and [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/cf-rollback) for CloudFormation-level rollback.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content:
### Deploy fails during dev mode

You cannot deploy to a stage that currently has an active [dev mode](/getting-started/use-the-dev-mode) session. Stop dev mode first with [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop), or deploy to a different stage name.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: How long does a first deploy take?
docs.content:
### How long does a first deploy take?

First deploys depend on the resources being provisioned. Lambda-only stacks are the fastest. Stacks with databases, container services, or custom domains take longer because AWS provisions those resources sequentially. Subsequent deploys that only change application code are faster since CloudFormation only updates the diff — and code-only changes skip CloudFormation entirely.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: Does Stacktape cost money to use with AWS?
docs.content:
### Does Stacktape cost money to use with AWS?

Connecting an AWS account is free. AWS resources created by your stacks are billed by AWS in your AWS account. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for Stacktape plan details.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: Can I deploy to any AWS region?
docs.content:
### Can I deploy to any AWS region?

Yes. The AWS account connection stack is created in `eu-west-1`, but your project stacks can deploy to any AWS region. Specify the region with `--region` on each deploy command, or set a default with [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure).

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: Is the connection between Stacktape and my AWS account secure?
docs.content:
### Is the connection between Stacktape and my AWS account secure?

The connection uses a CloudFormation stack that grants Stacktape cross-account AssumeRole access — the standard AWS approach for third-party integrations. You can revoke access instantly by deleting the connection stack in AWS or removing the account from the Console.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: What happens if I lose internet during a deploy?
docs.content:
### What happens if I lose internet during a deploy?

CloudFormation continues the deployment on AWS's side regardless of your local connection. If the CLI disconnects, check the stack status with [`stacktape status`](/cli/info-stack) before running another deploy.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: What's the difference between stages and AWS accounts?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between stages and AWS accounts?

Stages are logical environments (dev, staging, production) within a single AWS account — each stage gets its own CloudFormation stack with fully isolated resources. You can also connect multiple AWS accounts in the Console and deploy different stages to different accounts (e.g., production in a separate account). See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for details.

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: Can I preview what a deploy will change before running it?
docs.content:
### Can I preview what a deploy will change before running it?

Yes. Use [`stacktape diff`](/cli/diff) to see the CloudFormation change set without actually deploying. This shows which resources would be created, updated, replaced, or deleted.

---

docs.title: Deploy Your First Stage
headingPath: What does the CLI send to Stacktape?
docs.content:
### What does the CLI send to Stacktape?

The CLI sends usage statistics and reports of its own crashes, so we can see which commands fail and fix them. Set `STP_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` to turn both off.

- **After every command:** the command name, the names of the options you used (not their values), how long it took, whether it succeeded, the error code if it failed, your operating system, locale, time zone and the CLI version.
- **When the CLI crashes:** the error type, message and stack trace, the command, your operating system, CPU architecture and whether it ran in CI. The CLI prints an error ID you can give our support. Errors in your configuration, code or AWS account are not reported this way; only failures of the CLI itself are.
- **Identity:** a random ID of your machine. After `stacktape login`, events are linked to your Stacktape user and organization, and your account's email and name are attached to your user.

Before a crash report leaves your machine, the CLI masks tokens and other credentials, email and IP addresses, AWS account IDs and the user name in home-directory paths. Error messages can still contain other text, such as file or resource names. The CLI never sends configuration values, source code, environment variables or AWS credentials. Stacktape processes this data in [PostHog](https://posthog.com) in the EU.

docs.title: Going to Production
docs.content:
# Going to Production

Your stack is deployed and CI/CD pushes changes automatically. Before real users hit it, harden the deployment with alarms, budgets, custom domains, gradual rollouts, and policy guardrails. Each topic below covers what to configure, why it matters, and links to its dedicated deep-dive.


> **Info:** Already hardened? Skip ahead to [Resources](/configuration/resources) to configure individual resource types, [Observability](/observability/overview) for monitoring, or [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview) for spend control.

docs.title: Going to Production
Going to Production
docs.content:
## Budgets

Budget alerts prevent surprise AWS bills. Configure them in the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/using-console-ui) with a dollar threshold and percentage-based triggers (e.g., alert at 50%, 80%, 100%). Budgets can scope to your entire organization or to individual stacks — filter by project and stage to set different limits for production versus development.

You can also enable forecast-based alerts that fire when projected spend is on track to exceed the threshold, even if actual spend hasn't reached it yet. When creating a budget, attach one or more [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) — Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, email, or webhooks — so notifications reach your team automatically. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) for setup details.


> **Tip:** Set a budget alert for every production stack. Even a generous threshold catches misconfigurations (e.g., a runaway Lambda loop or an oversized database instance) before they become expensive. Alert at 80% and 100% of expected monthly spend as a starting point.

docs.title: Going to Production
Going to Production
docs.content:
## Gradual deployments

Instead of switching all traffic to a new version instantly, gradual deployments shift traffic incrementally — catching regressions before they affect all users. Stacktape supports canary and linear strategies for [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and [web services](/resources/compute/web-service) (and other container workloads — see [Gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments) for the full list).

**Lambda functions** support nine deployment strategies. Canary strategies (`Canary10Percent5Minutes`, `Canary10Percent10Minutes`, `Canary10Percent15Minutes`, `Canary10Percent30Minutes`) send 10% of traffic to the new version first, then shift the rest after the specified wait period. Linear strategies (`Linear10PercentEvery1Minute`, `Linear10PercentEvery2Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery10Minutes`) shift 10% of traffic at regular intervals until complete. `AllAtOnce` provides an instant switch with no gradual rollout.

Lambda deployments also support optional `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` and `afterTrafficShiftFunction` hooks — references to Lambda functions in your config that run smoke tests before traffic begins shifting and validation after all traffic has moved. If the `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` hook signals failure, the deployment rolls back.

**Web services** and other container workloads expose gradual deployments through the `deployment` property, which requires `application-load-balancer` load balancing. Container workloads support five strategies: `Canary10Percent5Minutes`, `Canary10Percent15Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery1Minutes`, `Linear10PercentEvery3Minutes`, and `AllAtOnce`. Container deployments also support `beforeAllowTrafficFunction` and `afterTrafficShiftFunction` hooks. See [Gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments) for rollback behavior and hook configuration.

docs.title: Going to Production
Going to Production
Going to Production
docs.content:
## Multi-region deployments

Deploy the same stack to multiple AWS regions for lower latency or regional compliance. Each region gets its own independent stage — deploy with `--region eu-west-1` and `--region us-east-1` as separate commands or CI pipelines. Stacktape does not automatically replicate data between regions; you handle cross-region data strategy (DynamoDB global tables, Aurora Global Database, or application-level replication).

Multi-region adds operational complexity and cost — you manage separate deployments, cross-region data consistency, and region-specific monitoring. Use it when you have users on multiple continents and latency matters, or when regulations require data residency in specific regions. For most apps, a single region with a [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) provides good global performance at lower cost. See [Multi-region deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/multi-region-deployments) for patterns and tradeoffs.

docs.title: Going to Production
docs.content:
## Guardrails

Guardrails define organization-wide policy rules that restrict what deployments can do — which stages and regions are allowed, what resource types and sizes are permitted, and which security settings are required. They prevent teams from deploying configurations that violate your standards.

Available guardrail types cover four categories:

| Category | Guardrail types |
|----------|----------------|
| **Deployment** | Stage restriction, region restriction, command restriction, resource type restriction, resource count limit |
| **Security** | Require VPC-only databases, require WAF on application load balancers, require custom domains on web services and hosting buckets |
| **Data protection** | Require deletion protection on relational databases, require dead-letter queues on SQS queues |
| **Resource limits** | Function memory limit, function timeout limit, container CPU/memory limit, database engine restriction, database instance size restriction |

Guardrails are most valuable once your team has more than one person deploying, or when you run both production and development stages and want to enforce stricter rules on production. For solo developers or early-stage projects, you can skip guardrails and revisit when your team or compliance requirements grow. See [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) for configuration details and per-type documentation.

docs.title: Going to Production
docs.content:
## Verify before go-live

Before sending real traffic, run through these concrete checks:

1. **Confirm alarms notify correctly.** Trigger a test error in your function or service and verify the notification reaches your on-call channel. An alarm without `notificationChannels` fires silently in CloudWatch — check that every production alarm has at least one target configured. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to confirm CloudWatch is receiving log data.

2. **Set a budget threshold.** Open the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/using-console-ui) Budgets page and create a budget alert matching your expected monthly spend. Set alerts at 80% and 100%. Enable forecast-based alerts so you catch spend trends before they hit the threshold.

3. **Verify your custom domain resolves.** Open your custom domain in a browser and confirm the TLS certificate is valid (lock icon, no warnings). If you registered the domain with [`stacktape domain add`](/cli/domain-add), the DNS records are managed automatically. If you manage DNS externally, verify the CNAME or alias record points to the correct AWS endpoint.

4. **Test a gradual deployment.** Push a small change and monitor the deployment in the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/using-console-ui). Confirm that traffic shifts gradually according to your chosen strategy. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to verify the new version is handling requests correctly.

5. **Review guardrails.** Confirm deletion protection is required for production databases, VPC-only access is enforced where needed, and resource limits match your team's standards. See [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) for the full list of policy rules.

## What's next

You've completed the Getting Started guide. Your stack is deployed, monitored, automated, and hardened. From here:

- [Resources](/configuration/resources) — the full resource catalogue with configuration guides
- [Observability](/observability/overview) — logs, metrics, alarms, and alerting in depth
- [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview) — dashboards, budgets, and optimization
- [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) — deployment, security, and resource-limit policies
- [Deploying & Lifecycle](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks) — deploys, previews, rollbacks, and multi-region patterns

docs.title: Starter Projects
docs.content:
# Starter Projects

Starter projects are complete, production-ready stacks you can deploy in minutes. Each one ships with
application code, a `stacktape.yml` config and all the infrastructure it needs — pick the one closest to
what you're building, deploy it to your own AWS account, and start iterating.

There are two ways to use a starter:

- **Deploy in Console** — open the project in the [Stacktape Console](https://console.stacktape.com) and
  deploy it to your AWS account with a guided flow.
- **Scaffold locally with the CLI** — bootstrap the project into your working directory and deploy it
  yourself:

```bash
stacktape init --starter-id <starter-id>
```


> **Info:** The `<starter-id>` matches the project's GitHub repository slug shown on each card (for example
`hono-api` or `nextjs-saas`).


Browse the current starter projects at https://docs.stacktape.com/getting-started/starter-projects or scaffold one with `stacktape init --starter-id <starter-id>`.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
# Upgrading from v3

Stacktape v4 makes deliberate breaking changes. v4 does not accept the old names, so update your configuration before deploying with v4. This page covers packaging, removed resource parameters and what the first v4 deployment changes in an existing stack.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Deployed stacks

Deploying a v4 configuration over a stack created by v3 is an ordinary stack update. Databases, buckets, DynamoDB tables, Redis caches, EFS file systems, user pools, Kinesis streams and SQS queues keep their CloudFormation logical IDs and physical names, so they are neither replaced nor deleted. Default domains keep their names as well. Stacktape checks this before every deployment: the change plan printed by `stacktape deploy` lists every resource it would replace or delete, and it stops for confirmation when one of them holds data.

The first v4 deployment adds a log subscription filter to every function and container log group for issue detection. On stacks without databases, load balancers or private service discovery, it also deletes Stacktape's internal tagging schedule (an EventBridge rule and its Lambda permission), which had nothing to tag.

On stacks with a CDN, it deletes Stacktape's origin-response Lambda@Edge function unless a bucket sets custom metadata headers, the only case that uses it. It also deletes the origin-request Lambda@Edge function unless a bucket cache behaviour uses URL normalization or SPA routing without a custom origin-request handler. API Gateway, load balancer, Lambda URL and custom HTTP origins do not use that helper. When no edge function remains, its internal artifact bucket is removed too. CloudFormation updates distributions before deleting a helper they previously referenced. AWS may retain detached Lambda@Edge replicas for a few hours; this does not fail the update. After AWS releases the replicas, delete any retained function in `us-east-1` with `aws lambda delete-function --profile <profile> --region us-east-1 --function-name <name>`.

Batch jobs now run on Amazon Linux 2023 instances, because AWS Batch stopped creating compute environments with its Amazon Linux 2 images on 30 June 2026. A compute environment last deployed by v3.0.10 or later keeps Amazon Linux 2: changing the image would make CloudFormation replace the environment and could interrupt jobs running on it. AWS keeps such environments running but no longer patches their image. An older environment, or one that a later change replaces anyway (such as a change to the stack's `tags`), moves to Amazon Linux 2023. CloudFormation then deletes the old environment, which can interrupt jobs still running on it, so deploy such a change when no jobs run; the change plan lists the compute environment as replaced. Amazon Linux 2023 requires IMDSv2 and uses cgroup v2; see [compute resources](/resources/compute/batch-job#compute-resources). The first v4 deployment also gives each batch job an execution role with `AmazonECSTaskExecutionRolePolicy`, which the ECS agent uses to pull the job's image from ECR, write its logs and read its secrets. The job's own role is unchanged.

Existing organization-wide Console alarm rules remain as legacy rules. The Console no longer creates or edits alarm rules; use `stacktape alarm export` to [move them into stack configuration](/observability/alarms#migrating-legacy-console-alarm-rules).

Container services without gradual deployments shut down more gracefully in v4. The default container `stopTimeout` is 30 seconds instead of 2, and a load balancer gives an old container 30 seconds instead of 5 to finish its requests. The first v4 deployment therefore registers a new task definition and replaces the running containers, as a code change would. Set `stopTimeout: 2` on a container to keep the v3 shutdown window.

A container service whose `minInstances` equals `maxInstances` (the default is 1 and 1) no longer gets CPU and memory scaling policies, because they could never change its instance count. Services whose `overrides` change the scalable target or a scaling policy keep both policies. The first v4 deployment deletes both policies and their CloudWatch alarms. The service keeps its scalable target and its instance count.

Code-only deployments of web services behind the default HTTP API finish once the new tasks are `RUNNING` and API Gateway can discover them, plus a 4-second routing allowance. Old tasks drain in the background. No health check is added by default, so this does not confirm that the new application works. Add an `internalHealthCheck` for application failure detection and automatic rollback. HTTP API tasks also gain a managed drain container, which waits 35 seconds before ECS signals the application so cached routes can expire. This uses one of ECS's 10 container slots and has a 16 MiB memory limit. The protection applies once those task definitions are running; the first rollout still retires the previous unprotected tasks. Keep an application shutdown delay or use a maintenance window for that transition. Services with an `internalHealthCheck`, and ALB/NLB services, keep their existing health-based completion checks. Code-only deploy timing stays the same. Full CloudFormation deployments, scale-in and deletion take about 36 seconds longer per task stop; tasks can stop in parallel. The 35-second delay can be raised through task definition overrides, with a matching increase to the helper’s stop timeout. The helper is non-essential and pulls a digest-pinned image from the stack’s private ECR; the CLI copies both amd64 and arm64 images there once without Docker. The privileged Console connection role already covers this copy. Restricted deployer roles need `ecr:BatchGetImage`, `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`, `ecr:InitiateLayerUpload`, `ecr:UploadLayerPart`, `ecr:CompleteLayerUpload` and `ecr:PutImage` on the stack’s deployment repository, even when all application images are prebuilt. Upgrade every team and Console runner CLI before adopting the helper: older CLIs can delete its cached images during retention. See [web-service health checks](/resources/compute/web-service#health-checks).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## CLI command and flag names

v4 commands and flags use standard spelling: words separated by spaces, and lowercase flags with dashes. For example, `stacktape secret set my-key --region eu-west-1` replaces `stacktape secret:set --region eu-west-1 --secretName my-key`. The old spellings, such as colon commands (`info:stack`) and camelCase flags (`--projectName`), still work, so existing scripts and CI jobs keep running. Run `stacktape help <command>` to see the current names.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Error tracking names

Use `error list`, `error ignore`, `error resolve`, and `error reopen` in place of the `issues:*` CLI commands. The `issues:*` commands still work, so existing scripts, automation and MCP command requests keep running. Replace `deploymentConfig.issues` with `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` in YAML and TypeScript configs; the old config name is rejected. Issue IDs and status values are unchanged. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) for capture settings and triage commands.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Failed deployments keep what they created
docs.content:
## Failed deployments keep what they created

v3 rolled a failed deployment back: a failed update returned the stack to its previous state, and a failed first deployment deleted the stack, including a database that had already taken minutes to create. In v4, a failed deployment keeps every resource it created or updated, unless it replaced existing resources: CloudFormation can only replace resources in a deployment it may roll back. The stack stays in `CREATE_FAILED` or `UPDATE_FAILED`, and the next `stacktape deploy` continues from the failure. To undo a failed update, run `stacktape stack recover`; to remove a failed first deployment, run `stacktape delete`. See [when a deployment fails](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deploying-stacks#when-a-deployment-fails).

- Replace `deploymentConfig.disableAutoRollback: true` by deleting it; this is now the default. The old name is rejected.
- To keep the v3 behaviour, set `deploymentConfig.autoRollback: true`, or pass `--auto-rollback` to one deployment. Stacks with `triggerRollbackOnAlarms` or `monitoringTimeAfterDeploymentInMinutes` keep rolling back automatically without a change.
- Remove `--no-auto-rollback` (`--disableAutoRollback`, `--dar`) from scripts and CI jobs. The flag no longer exists.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Security findings in agent output

In the `--agent` result of `validate` and `deploy`, one `security` object replaces the `securityFindings` and `securityExposure` fields that `4.0.0-preview.10` returned: read `security.findings` and `security.exposure` instead. See [security findings by stage purpose](/cli/validate#security-findings-by-stage-purpose).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Target AWS account

v3 stack commands ignored `--profile` and `AWS_PROFILE` for accounts connected with Stacktape-managed access. They deployed to `--aws-account`, the saved default, or the organization's only connected account. In v4, when `--aws-account` is not set, `--profile`, `AWS_PROFILE` or AWS keys in the environment choose the connected account they belong to. If they belong to an account that is not connected, the command stops before changing anything.

Check scripts and CI jobs that set an AWS profile or AWS keys for a different account than the one they deploy to. Pass `--aws-account <name>` in them, or remove the AWS settings. See [Choosing the account for a CLI command](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account#choosing-the-account-for-a-cli-command).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Redis caches

`type: redis-cluster` is now `type: redis`, and the node settings (`instanceSize`, replicas, sharding, `port`, `logging`) moved under `engine.properties`. To keep a deployed cache unchanged, use `engine.type: redis` and set `version` to the version it runs: the former `engineVersion`, or `6.2` if it was not set. The CLI rejects `redis-cluster` and prints this replacement for your settings. TypeScript configs replace `RedisCluster` with `Redis`.

The cache keeps its endpoint and data. New caches use Valkey (`engine.type: valkey` or `valkey-serverless`); to move an existing cache to Valkey, change `engine.type` to `valkey`. See [Redis](/resources/databases/redis#migrating-from-redis-cluster).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Removed resource parameters

The `MultiContainerWorkload` class no longer has a `logGroupArn` property, and `$ResourceParam('<workload>', 'logGroupArn')` is rejected. Stacktape never published this parameter, so a v3 configuration using it could not deploy.

A multi-container workload has one log group per container. To reference one, use [`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives) with the log group's CloudFormation logical ID: the workload name and the container name in PascalCase, followed by `LogGroup`. For the `app` container of a workload named `orders`, use `$CfResourceParam('OrdersAppLogGroup', 'Arn')`. A container with `logging.disabled` has no log group. Run [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) to check the logical IDs in the generated template.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## User auth pool token lifetimes

v3 sent `accessTokenValiditySeconds` and `idTokenValiditySeconds` to Cognito without a unit, so Cognito read them in hours and accepted only 1 to 24. v4 sends them in seconds. A value from 1 to 24 keeps its meaning in hours, and the CLI warns you to write it in seconds: replace `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 1` with `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 3600`. Unset lifetimes stay at 1 hour, and deploying updates the user pool client in place. See [token lifetimes](/resources/security/user-auth-pool#token-lifetimes).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
## Packaging

v4 replaces the v3 packaging types with a smaller set:

| v3 type | v4 type | v4 class |
|---|---|---|
| `stacktape-lambda-buildpack`, JavaScript or TypeScript entry file | `js-bundle` | `JsBundleLambdaPackaging` |
| `stacktape-lambda-buildpack`, Python, Java, Go, Ruby or .NET entry file | `buildpack` | `BuildpackLambdaPackaging` |
| `stacktape-image-buildpack`, JavaScript or TypeScript entry file | `js-bundle` | `JsBundleImagePackaging` |
| `stacktape-image-buildpack`, other languages | `buildpack` | `BuildpackImagePackaging` |
| `nixpacks` | `buildpack` | `BuildpackImagePackaging` |
| `external-buildpack` | `buildpack` or `dockerfile` | `BuildpackImagePackaging` or `DockerfilePackaging` |
| `custom-dockerfile` | `dockerfile` | `DockerfilePackaging` |
| `custom-artifact` | `custom-artifact` (unchanged) | `CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging` |
| `prebuilt-image` | `prebuilt-image` (unchanged) | `PrebuiltImagePackaging` |

In TypeScript configurations, rename the classes in both the `new ...Packaging(...)` calls and the `import` list.

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### JavaScript and TypeScript Lambda functions

Rename the type to `js-bundle` and move the options from `languageSpecificConfig` up one level.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/api.ts
          languageSpecificConfig:
            nodeVersion: 22
            outputModuleFormat: esm
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/api.ts
          nodeVersion: 22
          outputModuleFormat: esm
```

See [JS Bundle for Lambda](/packaging/function/js-bundle).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Python, Java, Go, Ruby and .NET Lambda functions
docs.content:
### Python, Java, Go, Ruby and .NET Lambda functions

Rename the type to `buildpack`. Rename `languageSpecificConfig` to `python`, `java` or `dotnet`, depending on the language. Delete the version fields and set the function's `runtime` instead. Go and Ruby have no options, so delete their `languageSpecificConfig`.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  processor:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-lambda-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/process.py
          languageSpecificConfig:
            pythonVersion: 3.12
            packageManagerFile: ./pyproject.toml
            minify: false
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  processor:
    type: function
    properties:
      runtime: python3.12
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/process.py
          python:
            packageManagerFile: ./pyproject.toml
```

v3 ignored the runtime when it built a function: without a version field, it built for Python 3.12, Java 11, Ruby 3.3 or .NET 8. v4 builds for the function's runtime. A function without `runtime` keeps `python3.13` or `dotnet10`, as in v3. Java moves from `java21` to `java25` and Ruby from `ruby3.3` to `ruby4.0`; set `runtime` to keep the v3 one.

See [Buildpack for Lambda](/packaging/function/buildpack).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Rust Lambda functions

v3 had no Rust support, so Rust functions used `custom-artifact` with a hook that ran cargo-lambda. In v4, delete the hook and use `buildpack`.

Before:

```yaml
hooks:
  beforeDeploy:
    - scriptName: buildRust
scripts:
  buildRust:
    type: local-script
    properties:
      executeCommand: cargo lambda build --release --output-format zip
resources:
  resizer:
    type: function
    properties:
      runtime: provided.al2023
      packaging:
        type: custom-artifact
        properties:
          packagePath: ./target/lambda/resizer/bootstrap.zip
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  resizer:
    type: function
    properties:
      runtime: provided.al2023
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/main.rs
```

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### JavaScript and TypeScript container services

Rename the type to `js-bundle` and move the options from `languageSpecificConfig` up one level. `requiresGlibcBinaries` and `customDockerBuildCommands` stay where they are.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/server.ts
          requiresGlibcBinaries: true
          languageSpecificConfig:
            emitTsDecoratorMetadata: true
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/server.ts
          requiresGlibcBinaries: true
          emitTsDecoratorMetadata: true
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

The v4 image installs nothing beside the runtime by default. v3 images ran `tini` and shipped `curl` and `openssl`:

- ECS and AWS Batch now start the init process (`initProcessEnabled`), so stop signals still reach your server.
- `curl` is installed only when the container's `internalHealthCheck` command calls it. If a script in the image calls `curl`, or your code runs the `openssl` command, add it with `customDockerBuildCommands`, for example `apk add --no-cache curl`.
- The OpenSSL libraries that Prisma loads are still in the image. When your code, or a package installed beside the bundle, uses Prisma, the Alpine image also gets the `openssl` command, which Prisma 5 needs to choose its query engine.

See [JS Bundle for Containers](/packaging/containers/js-bundle).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
headingPath: Python and other non-JavaScript container services
docs.content:
### Python and other non-JavaScript container services

Rename the type to `buildpack`. The container `buildpack` builds the whole project directory, so replace `entryfilePath` with `sourceDirectoryPath`. Replace `runAppAs` with a `startCommand` that starts the server on `$PORT`, and add the server (for example `uvicorn` or `gunicorn`) to the project's dependencies.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: stacktape-image-buildpack
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./app/main.py:app
          languageSpecificConfig:
            runAppAs: ASGI
            packageManagerFile: ./pyproject.toml
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  api:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: .
          startCommand: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

For a WSGI app, use gunicorn, for example `gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT app.main:app`. When a FastAPI, Flask or Django project uses the conventional module layout, the start command is detected and `startCommand` can be omitted.

The v4 images are Debian-based and larger than the v3 Alpine images. See [Buildpack for Containers](/packaging/containers/buildpack).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Nixpacks

Rename the type to `buildpack` and `startCmd` to `startCommand`. Nixpacks phases have no direct equivalent: move install and build commands to `installCommand` and `buildCommand`, and use `railpackConfig` for anything else.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: nixpacks
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
          startCmd: node dist/server.js
          phases:
            - name: build
              cmds:
                - npm run build
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
          startCommand: node dist/server.js
          buildCommand: npm run build
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### External buildpacks

Cloud Native Buildpacks and the pack CLI are no longer supported. Try `buildpack`, which detects most projects without configuration. If you depended on a specific builder or buildpack, write a Dockerfile and use `dockerfile`.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: external-buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
          builder: paketobuildpacks/builder-jammy-base
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  web:
    type: web-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: buildpack
        properties:
          sourceDirectoryPath: ./web
      resources:
        cpu: 0.25
        memory: 512
```

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Custom Dockerfiles

Rename the type to `dockerfile`. The properties are unchanged.

Before:

```yaml
resources:
  worker:
    type: worker-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: custom-dockerfile
        properties:
          buildContextPath: ./worker
          dockerfilePath: Dockerfile.prod
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

After:

```yaml
resources:
  worker:
    type: worker-service
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: dockerfile
        properties:
          buildContextPath: ./worker
          dockerfilePath: Dockerfile.prod
      resources:
        cpu: 0.5
        memory: 1024
```

See [Dockerfile](/packaging/containers/dockerfile).

docs.title: Upgrading from v3
docs.content:
### Removed packaging properties

- `languageSpecificConfig`: its options are direct properties of `js-bundle`, or `python`, `java` and `dotnet` on the Lambda `buildpack`.
- `pythonVersion`, `javaVersion`, `rubyVersion` and `dotnetVersion` on Lambda functions: set the function's `runtime`.
- `packageManager`, `minify` and `runAppAs` for Python Lambda functions.
- `entryfilePath`, `runAppAs`, `languageSpecificConfig`, `requiresGlibcBinaries` and `customDockerBuildCommands` for non-JavaScript container services. Use `sourceDirectoryPath`, `startCommand`, `aptPackages` or a Dockerfile.
