In a region far from you, every first connection takes noticeably longer (several hundred milliseconds per round trip), and a client with a short connect timeout can fail. Node.js, for example, gives up on each address after 250 ms by default; raise it with `NODE_OPTIONS=--network-family-autoselection-attempt-timeout=2000`, or run dev mode in a region close to you.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content:
## Rebuilding workloads

The dev mode terminal accepts commands while running. Type a command and press Enter:

| Command | Action |
|---|---|
| `rs` | Rebuild all workloads |
| `rs <name>` | Rebuild a specific workload by name |
| `c` or `clear` | Clear the log output |
| `q` or `quit` | Stop dev mode and exit |

When running with `--watch`, workloads rebuild automatically on file changes. Without `--watch`, use `rs` after editing code to see changes. Use `rs <name>` to rebuild a single workload without restarting others — useful when iterating on one service in a multi-resource config.

A workload whose rebuild fails, for example because of a syntax error, shows the error and stays failed until a rebuild succeeds. A Lambda function keeps its previous code until then. A rebuild deploys code only: after a change to the configuration file, stop dev mode and start it again.

That start updates the dev stack only when the change reaches it. Changing how a local container is built or started (its `packaging`, including `startCommand`), a frontend's `dev` settings or a local script restarts only what runs on your machine. When the dev stack is updated, functions whose code did not change keep their deployed code.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content:
### Local EFS storage

Configured EFS mounts are not mounted or emulated on local containers. Use explicit local test storage and verify the deployed [EFS configuration](/resources/compute/web-service#efs-storage) in a deployed stage.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content:
## Lifecycle hooks

Dev mode registers configured `beforeDev` script hooks and displays them in the dev TUI. See [Hooks and scripts](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) for configuration details, hook types, and the full execution model.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content:
## Dev stack isolation

Dev mode creates a dedicated dev stack and refuses to reuse any stack it did not create, regardless of name or status. Use a separate stage name such as `dev`, `dev-local`, or `dev-jane`. To connect selected databases or Redis resources to deployed AWS resources, keep the dedicated dev stage and pass `--remote-resources`.


> **Warning:** Dev mode only updates a stack that `stacktape dev` created. It marks every dev stack with the stack tag `stp:dev-stack`, and refuses any other stack on the stage, whatever its name or status: use a different stage name, or delete that stack with `stacktape delete --stage <stage>` yourself. Dev mode never deletes a stack.

If the first start of a stage fails or is interrupted, CloudFormation rolls the dev stack back. The next `stacktape dev` recognizes the stack by its tag and updates it again. Only a dev stack whose very first create failed (status `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`) can't be updated; dev mode then asks you to delete it with `stacktape delete --stage <stage>`.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content:
## Agent mode

When started with `--agent`, Stacktape spawns a detached daemon process. The daemon starts the agent server, writes a lock file with process and connection details, and reports readiness back to the parent command, which then exits. See [Agent mode in dev](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev) for the full guide.

Start dev mode as an agent:

```bash
stacktape dev --stage dev --region us-east-1 --resources all --agent
```

When `--agent-port` is omitted, Stacktape starts at port 7331 and searches ports 7331–7430 if the default is in use. Use `--agent-port` to request a specific port. The agent listens on `127.0.0.1` only, and every request must carry the session token stored in `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token` (see [Authentication](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#authentication)). If Stacktape finds an already running dev agent, the command returns that agent's connection details instead of starting another one. A Lambda build or deploy failure can leave the session running with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES` and `ready: false`; fix the code and rebuild. A failure that aborts startup is reported separately. Inspect the returned session and status before starting another agent.

While the agent starts, the command prints its progress as JSONL `event` lines: the agent's port first, then the dev network, the dev box, the dev stack deployment with CloudFormation resource counts, and each workload and database. A first start that creates the dev network and the dev stack takes several minutes, and a heartbeat line every 20 seconds names the step it waits for.

Stop the agent of the current project with [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop) (`--stage` chooses between several stages, `--cwd` names another project directory):

```bash
stacktape dev stop --stage dev
```

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content:
## Command reference

For the complete list of flags and options, see the [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) CLI reference. For stopping agents, see [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop).

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--stage` | Stage name for the dev stack |
| `--region` | AWS region |
| `--resources` | Resources to run (`all` or comma-separated names) |
| `--skip-resources` | Resources to exclude from the run |
| `--watch` | Auto-rebuild on file changes |
| `--remote-resources` | Emulatable databases to connect to AWS instead of local emulation |
| `--fresh-db` | Start local databases from a fresh state |
| `--no-tunnel` | Skip the tunnels from deployed Lambda functions to local databases |
| `--agent` | Run as a background daemon with HTTP server |
| `--agent-port` | Port for the agent HTTP server (default: 7331) |

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
headingPath: Do I need Docker installed for dev mode?
docs.content:
### Do I need Docker installed for dev mode?

Yes. Dev mode uses Docker to run container workloads and emulated databases locally. You need Docker Desktop or a compatible Docker runtime installed and running before starting dev mode. Hosting buckets and SSR frontends run through their framework dev servers rather than Docker, and Lambda functions deploy directly to AWS — but most dev mode workflows involve at least one container or database.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
headingPath: Which resource types does dev mode support, and what isn't emulated locally?
docs.content:
### Which resource types does dev mode support, and what isn't emulated locally?

Dev mode supports container workloads ([web-service](/resources/compute/web-service), [worker-service](/resources/compute/worker-service), [private-service](/resources/compute/private-service), [multi-container-workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload)), [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [hosting buckets](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) (with `dev` config), and all SSR frontends (Next.js, Astro, Nuxt, SvelteKit, SolidStart, TanStack Start, Remix). Local emulation covers relational databases, Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch. Other resource types such as [SQS queues](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue), [SNS topics](/resources/messaging/sns-topic), [S3 buckets](/resources/storage/s3-bucket), and [state machines](/resources/orchestration/state-machine) run in the dev stack according to the dev deployment policy, rather than only when selected workloads need them. Batch jobs also run in AWS; restart dev mode to rebuild their images.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
headingPath: How do Lambda functions connect to local databases in dev mode?
docs.content:
### How do Lambda functions connect to local databases in dev mode?

Through the dev box of your account's dev network. Functions connect to the box's private address, and the box forwards each connection to your machine over an encrypted AWS Systems Manager session that your machine opens. Nothing is published on the internet. Bulk transfers are limited to about 0.7 MB/s. See [Connecting to local databases](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases).

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
headingPath: How do I reset my local database data?
docs.content:
### How do I reset my local database data?

Use the `--fresh-db` flag: `stacktape dev --stage dev --region us-east-1 --fresh-db`. This resets databases prepared during startup, including relay dependencies that may be unselected; DynamoDB Local tables share storage. See [reset scope](/local-development/local-databases#resetting-local-data). Without this flag, local database data persists between dev mode sessions under `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/`, which is usually what you want during iterative development.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
headingPath: What is the difference between dev mode and deploying to a dev stage?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between dev mode and deploying to a dev stage?

Dev mode (`stacktape dev`) runs workloads on your local machine with Docker and deploys a dev stack to your AWS account when one does not already exist. [Deploying](/cli/deploy) to a dev stage (`stacktape deploy --stage dev`) provisions the full AWS infrastructure for your config and runs everything in the cloud. Use dev mode for rapid daily iteration; use a deployed dev stage for integration testing against real AWS infrastructure.

docs.title: Dev Mode Overview
headingPath: Does dev mode cost anything on AWS?
docs.content:
### Does dev mode cost anything on AWS?

Dev mode creates a minimal dev stack in AWS, so AWS charges can come from the AWS resources in that dev stack, Lambda invocations, and any deployed resources you choose to use through `--remote-resources`. The dev box costs about $0.01 per hour while a dev session runs; it stops itself 30 minutes after the last session and then costs about $0.75 per month for its disk and the SSM parameter that holds its relay. Container workloads and locally emulated databases run on your machine and don't generate AWS charges. Small development workloads may fall within AWS Lambda free-tier usage, depending on account eligibility and invocation volume.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
# Local Databases

Stacktape [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) runs supported databases locally in Docker, avoiding the corresponding AWS database service. Dev-stack resources and the [dev network](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#the-dev-network) can still incur AWS charges. Data persists between sessions and workloads receive connection settings automatically. Use `dev.remote: true` to connect to the deployed database instead.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
## When to use local databases

Local databases are the default for day-to-day development and isolate each developer's data. Local clients connect on your machine. Lambda and Batch clients in AWS reach them through the dev network and incur a cloud-to-machine round trip. Use local databases for application logic, migrations and prototypes; test cloud-specific behavior against deployed resources.

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: When NOT to use local databases
docs.content:
## When NOT to use local databases

Switch to [remote (deployed) databases](#using-remote-databases) when your work depends on behavior that local emulation cannot replicate — Aurora multi-AZ failover, DynamoDB Streams, OpenSearch security plugins, or engine-specific query plan differences. Also prefer remote databases when you need to test against a realistic data volume or share state across a team. Set `dev.remote: true` on the resource to connect to the deployed AWS resource instead.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
## Supported databases

Dev mode can run the following database resource types locally. Each runs as a Docker container, with data persisted to a host directory mounted into the container.

| Resource type | Local emulation |
|---|---|
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB) | Docker container |
| RDS Aurora (PostgreSQL, MySQL — including Serverless v1/v2) | Mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL container |
| RDS Oracle, RDS SQL Server | Not supported — set `dev.remote: true` |
| [Redis](/resources/databases/redis) | Docker container |
| [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) | `amazon/dynamodb-local` container |
| [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) | Docker container |
| [MongoDB Atlas](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) | Not supported — third-party managed service |
| [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) | Not supported — third-party managed service |

For [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), local containers use the literal credentials from your config. Locally, `credentials.masterUserName` defaults to `postgres` for PostgreSQL and `root` for MySQL/MariaDB. Local databases never use the deployed database's secret: when `credentials.masterUserPassword` is not set or reads a value with a directive such as `$Secret('db.password')`, dev mode generates a random password for each local database and stores it in `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/<resourceName>/password`, readable only by your user. Every worktree or copy of the project on your machine gives new local data the same password for a stage, so moving the stage between worktrees does not have to update the dev stack. A Redis `defaultUserPassword` read from a directive gets a generated password the same way, and Redis without a password runs without authentication. The container, deployed dev functions and local workloads all receive the same password through the injected connection information. Properties like `instanceSize` only apply to the deployed AWS resource and are ignored locally.

Aurora engine types — Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL, Aurora Serverless v1, and Aurora Serverless v2 — are mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL containers locally. Aurora-specific features (multi-AZ replication, serverless ACU scaling, reader endpoints) are not available in the local emulation. For most application-level SQL access, the local container provides the same kind of SQL endpoint and connection-string shape. Test Aurora-specific behavior against a deployed stage.


> **Info:** Dev mode needs Docker to start local database containers. If Docker is not running, dev mode cannot proceed with local databases.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
## How it works

When you run [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev), Stacktape identifies database resources in your config and starts Docker containers for each one.

1. **Container naming** — each container is named after the project, stage, resource and a short hash of the project directory, so multiple stages, projects and Git worktrees of one project can run in parallel without sharing or stopping each other's containers.
2. **Port allocation** — dev mode finds an available host port for each container, avoiding conflicts when several sessions run in parallel. The port is published on `127.0.0.1` only, so other machines on your network cannot reach the database. The selected port is reflected in the injected connection information.
3. **Data persistence** — dev mode mounts a local data directory into the container, so data survives dev mode restarts.
4. **Readiness checks** — Stacktape polls the container until it responds, then marks the resource ready for your workloads.
5. **Connection information** — referenceable parameters (host, port, connectionString, etc.) are resolved locally so they can be used via `$ResourceParam()`. Workloads that list the database in their `connectTo` receive the documented environment variables following the `STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]` pattern described in [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources).

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content: ## Relational databases

docs.title: Local Databases
Local Databases
Local Databases
docs.content:
### Aurora engines

All Aurora engine types — Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL, Aurora Serverless v1, Aurora Serverless v2 — are mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL containers locally. The mapping is:

| Aurora engine type | Local container |
|---|---|
| `aurora-postgresql`, `aurora-postgresql-serverless`, `aurora-postgresql-serverless-v2` | PostgreSQL |
| `aurora-mysql`, `aurora-mysql-serverless`, `aurora-mysql-serverless-v2` | MySQL |

This is a pragmatic tradeoff: the SQL interface, schema behavior, and connection string format match the deployed database, which is sufficient for application development. Aurora-specific behavior — ACU scaling, multi-AZ replication, reader endpoints, pause-after-inactivity — is only available on the deployed AWS resource. Test these features against a deployed stage using `dev.remote: true`.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
### Oracle and SQL Server

RDS Oracle (`oracle-ee`, `oracle-se2`) and SQL Server (`sqlserver-ee`, `sqlserver-se`, `sqlserver-ex`, `sqlserver-web`) engines do not have local emulation. If your config includes an Oracle or SQL Server database, use `dev.remote: true` to connect to the deployed AWS resource during development.

docs.title: Local Databases
Local Databases
Local Databases
docs.content:
## OpenSearch

In dev mode, Stacktape runs a local OpenSearch container as a single-node cluster. Cluster-level features (sharding across nodes, dedicated master nodes) are not available locally.

Referenceable parameters available for the local domain include `domainEndpoint` and `arn`.

docs.title: Local Databases
Local Databases
docs.content:
### When to use remote databases

- **Testing against real data** — when you need to reproduce a production issue with actual records.
- **Aurora-specific behavior** — to test failover, reader endpoints, or serverless ACU scaling.
- **DynamoDB advanced features** — Streams, Global Tables, TTL, and backups are only available on the deployed resource.
- **Shared development database** — when multiple developers need to see the same state.

Local emulation avoids AWS database service charges and isolates test data. Deployed clients still use the dev network, with its network latency and AWS costs.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
## Resetting local data

Data persists across sessions in host directories mounted into the containers. Use `--fresh-db` to reset databases that startup prepares:

```bash
stacktape dev --fresh-db
```

`--fresh-db` deletes data, schema and local password/identity files when startup prepares a database. This includes selected databases and databases prepared for deployed-workload relay connections, which can include unselected resources. Databases never prepared are untouched; this is not a stage-wide wipe. The stage password can be reused, so it does not promise a new password.

Relational databases, Redis and OpenSearch store data under `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/<resourceName>/data/`. Stop dev mode before manually removing one of these data directories.

All DynamoDB Local tables share `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/dynamodb-local/data/`. Preparing any local DynamoDB table with `--fresh-db` removes every persisted table in that storage, even tables not selected this time. For a table-specific item reset that preserves schema, use the [local reset endpoint](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#reset-and-seed-local-databases) or MCP `reset_db` with the table's `resource` name and `confirm: true`.


> **Tip:** Add `.stacktape/` to your `.gitignore` to avoid committing local database data to version control.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content:
## Databases without local emulation

Not all Stacktape database resources support local emulation:

| Resource | Local support | Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| RDS Oracle / SQL Server | No | Set `dev.remote: true` to use the deployed RDS instance |
| [MongoDB Atlas](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) | No | Stacktape dev mode does not provide local emulation for MongoDB Atlas. Use a deployed cluster during development. |
| [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) | No | Stacktape dev mode does not provide local emulation for Upstash Redis. Use a deployed Upstash instance during development. |

Oracle and SQL Server engines are not mapped to a local container type. MongoDB Atlas and Upstash Redis are third-party managed services without local emulation in dev mode.

docs.title: Local Databases
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: Does local database data persist when I restart dev mode?
docs.content:
### Does local database data persist when I restart dev mode?

Yes. Local data survives restarts. `--fresh-db` resets databases prepared during startup, including relay dependencies, and removes their local credential/identity files. DynamoDB Local tables share storage, so resetting it removes every persisted table there. See [reset scope](#resetting-local-data).

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: Can I run multiple stages locally at the same time?
docs.content:
### Can I run multiple stages locally at the same time?

Yes. Each stage gets its own container name and its own non-conflicting port assignment, so two developers or two stages on the same machine do not collide. You can run `stacktape dev --stage dev-alice` and `stacktape dev --stage dev-bob` in parallel. Two Git worktrees of the same project can also run the same stage in parallel: each worktree has its own data directory, containers and ports. When the stage's deployed Lambda functions use local databases, only one session can receive their connections, so the second session refuses to start unless you pass [`--take-over`](/cli/dev#--take-over).

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: Why does dev mode warn that my database keeps the password `localdevpassword`?
docs.content:
### Why does dev mode warn that my database keeps the password `localdevpassword`?

Earlier Stacktape versions gave every local database without a configured password the fixed password `localdevpassword`, and a database with a `$Secret` password got the directive text itself as its password. A database stores its password in its data, so a data directory created then keeps working with that password, and dev mode warns about it. To switch to a generated password, start dev mode once with `--fresh-db`. This deletes the database's local data.

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: How do I connect to the local database with a GUI tool?
docs.content:
### How do I connect to the local database with a GUI tool?

Use the host `localhost` and the port from the injected connection string or referenceable parameters. For PostgreSQL, the local username defaults to `postgres`; for MySQL/MariaDB it defaults to `root`. If your config sets no literal password, read the generated one from `.stacktape/dev-data/<stage>/<resourceName>/password`. For Redis, use the injected connection string. DynamoDB Local and OpenSearch use HTTP endpoints.

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: Does local DynamoDB support Streams and Global Tables?
docs.content:
### Does local DynamoDB support Streams and Global Tables?

No. The `amazon/dynamodb-local` image used by dev mode does not include Streams, Global Tables, Time to Live (TTL), or on-demand backups. If your application depends on these features, set `dev.remote: true` on the [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) resource to connect to the deployed AWS resource.

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: How does Stacktape handle Aurora Serverless locally?
docs.content:
### How does Stacktape handle Aurora Serverless locally?

Aurora Serverless v1 and v2 engine types are mapped to standard PostgreSQL or MySQL containers locally. Serverless scaling (ACU-based), pause-after-inactivity, and automatic failover are AWS-only features. For most application-level SQL access, the local container provides the same kind of SQL endpoint and connection-string shape. Test Aurora-specific behavior against a deployed stage.

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: Can I use the local database for running migrations?
docs.content:
### Can I use the local database for running migrations?

Yes. Workloads that list the database in `connectTo` receive the connection string as an environment variable, so migration tools that read the connection string from the environment work without changes. Run migrations from your application startup code, a local migration command (e.g. `npx prisma migrate dev`), or manually via a database client connected to `localhost:<port>`. Schema changes persist across dev sessions because the data directory is mounted from the host.

docs.title: Local Databases
headingPath: Where can I find the actual port a local database is using?
docs.content:
### Where can I find the actual port a local database is using?

Dev mode finds an available host port for each container, so the actual port may differ from the database's default. The assigned port is reflected in the referenceable parameters and in the connection information provided to workloads via `connectTo`, so your application code does not need to handle port differences.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
# Budgets

Stacktape budget alerts notify you before AWS spending exceeds a threshold you define. Created and managed in the Stacktape Console, budget alerts track actual and forecasted spend at the whole-organization scope in the selected AWS account, or filtered by project and stage for per-stack budgets. When costs cross a percentage of your configured threshold, alerts are delivered through your configured [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels). AWS infrastructure costs are billed directly to your AWS account; the Stacktape subscription fee is separate. Budgets help you catch runaway AWS spend before it becomes a surprise invoice.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Creating a budget alert

Budget alerts are created in the Stacktape Console on the Budgets page. The list shows name, scope, threshold, alert percentages, project/stage filters, and created date. Click the Show details icon on any row to open a detail modal that additionally shows the Include forecast setting and attached alert channels. Budget alerts in the Console include these properties:

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **Name** | A descriptive label for the budget (e.g. "Production spend limit"). |
| **Scope** | **Whole organization** (monitors the entire AWS account) or **Per stack** (filtered by specific projects and stages). |
| **Threshold** | The dollar amount and currency that defines your spending threshold. |
| **Alert at percentages** | One or more percentage values. An alert fires when actual (or forecasted) spend crosses each percentage of the threshold. |
| **Include forecast** | When enabled, also alerts when AWS predicts spend will exceed the threshold. |
| **For projects** | When scope is Per stack, which projects to monitor — individual project names or all projects. |
| **For stages** | When scope is Per stack, which stages to monitor — individual stage names or all stages. |
| **Alert channels** | Where alerts are delivered, using channels configured on the [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) page. |


> Screenshot: Stacktape Console Budgets page showing a list of budget alerts with columns for name, scope, threshold, alert percentages, projects, stages, and created date Caption: The Budgets page lists all budget alerts with their scope, threshold, and alert configuration.


> **Info:** Organization-wide budget alerts are created in the selected AWS account when you save them. Stack-scoped budget alerts depend on Stacktape deployment metadata — deploy matching stacks after creating or changing a stack-scoped alert so the Console can track their spend.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Scoping

Stacktape budget alerts support two scope levels. Choosing the right scope depends on whether you need a single cost ceiling or per-team accountability.

| Scope | Monitors | Project/stage filters | Best for |
|-------|----------|----------------------|----------|
| **Whole organization** | Total AWS account spend | Not applicable — covers everything | A single safety net across all stacks |
| **Per stack** | Spend attributed to matching stacks | Filter by specific projects and/or stages, or select all | Separate budgets for production vs. development, or per-team cost tracking |

**Whole organization** is the simpler option. It catches any spike regardless of which project caused it. Start here if you want a single ceiling for your AWS account.

**Per stack** gives you granular control. Select individual project names or all projects, and individual stage names or all stages. For example, you can create one budget for your production stage across all projects and a separate, lower budget for development stages. When scope is "Whole organization", the project and stage filter columns display "Whole organization" and are not configurable.


> **Tip:** Most teams benefit from having both: one Whole organization budget as a safety net, plus Per stack budgets for production stacks where cost accountability matters.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Forecast alerts

When "Include forecast" is enabled on a budget alert, Stacktape delivers an additional alert when AWS predicts spend will exceed your threshold — even if actual spend is still below it. This gives you lead time to investigate and react before costs actually cross the limit.

Enable forecast alerts on production budgets where early warning matters. For development or short-lived stages, threshold-exceeded alerts on actual spend are usually sufficient.

AWS Budgets forecasts are produced by AWS based on historical usage patterns. For newly created accounts or recently deployed stacks, there may not be enough usage history for AWS to generate a meaningful forecast. As usage data accumulates over time, forecast predictions become available and more accurate. If your forecast alert isn't firing on a new stack, this is the most likely reason.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Managing budgets

The Budgets page in the Console shows all budget alerts in a table. Use the Show details icon on any row to inspect a budget's full configuration. Each row also includes a delete button to remove the budget alert.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## Budget history

Budget history in the Console is a log of budget alert events, including threshold-exceeded and forecasted-overspend events. Check budget history to see when budget alerts were triggered.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## When to use

Set up at least one budget alert before going to production. AWS spend can increase quickly when traffic spikes, a runaway process loops, or someone deploys a resource larger than intended. Budgets are the fastest way to detect cost anomalies early.

- **Start with a Whole organization budget** at 80% and 100% of your expected AWS bill. This catches any stack that misbehaves.
- **Add Per stack budgets** for production stacks where you need tighter accountability per team or project.
- **Enable forecast alerts** on production budgets so you get advance warning before overruns.
- **Connect alert channels** such as Slack, email, or a webhook so budget alerts reach the tools your team already monitors. In a channel of the connected Slack workspace, a budget card shows the spending pace, answers **Show drivers** with the stacks behind the spend, and can be snoozed until the end of the month (`org:manage-budgets` permission); the budget's details in the Console show the snooze and can resume the alerts.

Budgets complement other cost management tools in the Console:

| Tool | Purpose | When to use |
|------|---------|-------------|
| [Dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) | View spending trends over time | Understanding what you're spending |
| **Budget alerts** (this page) | Get notified when spend crosses a threshold | Controlling and reacting to spend |
| [Per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) | Attribute costs to individual resources | Identifying which resources drive costs |
| [Optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) | Reduce baseline spend | Lowering costs proactively |

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content:
## When NOT to use

Budget alerts notify you — they do not stop spend. AWS Budgets cannot automatically scale down or terminate resources when a threshold is crossed. If you need preventive cost controls that block expensive deployments, use [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) to restrict resource sizes, instance types, and regions.

Budget alerts are also not a substitute for right-sizing resources. If baseline spend is already higher than it should be, the [per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) helps identify which specific resources are driving costs, and [optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) offers concrete ways to reduce spend directly.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Do budget alerts stop AWS from charging me?
docs.content:
### Do budget alerts stop AWS from charging me?

No. AWS Budgets is an alerting mechanism, not a spending cap. When a threshold is crossed, you receive a notification — AWS does not automatically shut down or throttle resources. You need to respond to the alert by scaling down, removing unused resources, or adjusting your configuration. For preventive cost controls, combine budgets with [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) that restrict what can be deployed.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Can I set a budget alert for a single resource like one database?
docs.content:
### Can I set a budget alert for a single resource like one database?

Stacktape budget alerts scope to projects and stages (stacks), not individual resources within a stack. For per-resource cost visibility, use the [per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) in the Console.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: How much do AWS Budgets cost?
docs.content:
### How much do AWS Budgets cost?

AWS may charge for AWS Budgets depending on your account and usage — check the [AWS Budgets pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/aws-cost-management/aws-budgets/pricing/) for current rates.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Why isn't my forecast alert firing?
docs.content:
### Why isn't my forecast alert firing?

AWS Budgets forecasts rely on historical usage data. For newly created AWS accounts or recently deployed stacks, there may not be enough usage history for AWS to generate a meaningful forecast yet. As usage data accumulates over time, forecast-based alerts become available and more accurate. Verify that "Include forecast" is enabled on the budget alert in question, and that the budget's scope matches the stacks generating spend.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Should I use budgets, guardrails, or both for cost control?
docs.content:
### Should I use budgets, guardrails, or both for cost control?

Use both — they serve different purposes. Budget alerts are reactive: they notify you when spend crosses a threshold so you can investigate. [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) are preventive: they block deployments that violate your rules (e.g. oversized instances, unauthorized regions, restricted resource types). Start with budget alerts for cost visibility, then layer in guardrails once you know which constraints protect your team from common mistakes.

docs.title: Budgets
headingPath: Why isn't my stack-scoped budget tracking any spend?
docs.content:
### Why isn't my stack-scoped budget tracking any spend?

Stack-scoped budget alerts depend on Stacktape deployment metadata to attribute spend to matching stacks. If you create or change a stack-scoped alert but haven't deployed matching stacks since, the Console has nothing to track. Deploy (or redeploy) the stacks whose projects and stages match the budget's filters, and confirm the filters actually match your project and stage names.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
# Cost Dashboards

The Stacktape Console provides two cost views: a high-level overview with KPI cards and charts on the organization dashboard, and a detailed per-stack cost breakdown on the dedicated Costs per stack page. Both views use AWS cost report data, which is generated daily.


> **Info:** AWS bills infrastructure costs directly to your AWS account. Stacktape's subscription fee is separate and does not appear in these dashboards. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for subscription details.


This page covers **viewing** your AWS costs. For setting up spend alerts, see [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets). For understanding which individual resources cost the most, see [Per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown). For reducing costs, see [Optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips).

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
## Organization overview

The organization overview dashboard includes cost-related KPI cards and charts alongside deployment and operational metrics. Cost data on the overview always reflects the **current calendar month** — the time range selector (7d, 14d, 30d, 90d, 6m, 1y) controls deployment statistics only, not cost views. The cost widgets give you a quick read on total spend, spend distribution, and budget status without navigating to the dedicated costs page.


> Screenshot: Organization overview dashboard showing the AWS Costs KPI card with current-month total, month-over-month trend percentage, and a sparkline of recent monthly spend Caption: The AWS Costs KPI on the organization overview shows current-month spend with a trend indicator.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
### AWS Costs KPI

The AWS Costs KPI card displays your total spend for the current month with a month-over-month trend indicator. The trend compares current spend against the previous month's total and displays one of these labels:

| Trend label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `+X%` or `-X%` | Percentage increase or decrease vs the previous month |
| `Flat` | 0.1% change or less in either direction |
| `New spend` | Spend this month with a previous-month total of zero |
| `No spend` | Zero spend in both the current and previous month |

A sparkline below the card shows a recent monthly cost trend, giving you a quick visual of whether spend is rising or falling. The subtitle reads "This month" and includes the trend label for context.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
### AWS Costs by Project

A horizontal bar chart titled "AWS Costs by Project" displays up to 10 items sorted by current-month spend. If more than 10 items have costs, the remainder is grouped under "Other." Hover over any bar to see the exact amount and name. This chart helps you identify which applications drive the largest share of your bill at a glance.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
### AWS Costs by Resource

A separate horizontal bar chart titled "AWS Costs by Resource" breaks down current-month spend by AWS resource type. This view is useful for identifying which resource types drive your bill, independent of which project uses them. If a particular resource type suddenly spikes, you know where to start investigating — even before checking which project is responsible.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
### Budget Alerts

The Budget Alerts panel shows all configured [budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets) with their name, scope (organization-wide or per stack), threshold amount, and the percentage levels that trigger notifications. Clicking a budget row navigates to the Console budgets page. When no budgets are configured, the panel displays "No budget alerts configured."

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
## Costs per stack

The dedicated Costs per stack page provides a month-by-month table of AWS spend attributed to each deployed stack. You select an active connected AWS account and a month, and the table shows every stack with its project name, stage, region, and total attributed cost for that period.


> Screenshot: Costs per stack page showing a table with columns for project name, stage, region, and month-to-date costs, with AWS account and month filters at the top Caption: The Costs per stack page shows attributed AWS spend by project, stage, and region.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
### Filters

Two filters at the top of the page control the displayed data:

- **AWS account** — select from your active [connected AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account). Switch between accounts to compare spend across different AWS environments.
- **Time range** — select a month. The selector includes each month so far in the current year plus all 12 months of the previous year — between 13 and 24 selectable months depending on when in the year you view it.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content:
### Cost table

The table shows one row per stack with the following columns:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| Project name | The Stacktape project the stack belongs to |
| Stage | The stage name (e.g., `production`, `staging`) |
| Region | The AWS region the stack is deployed in |
| Month-to-date costs | Total attributed spend for the selected month |

The table sorts by cost descending by default and paginates at 10 rows per page. Clicking a row opens a per-resource cost breakdown for that stage — see [Per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) for a walkthrough of that view and [Optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) for guidance on acting on the findings.


> **Warning:** Cost reports are generated daily and may not be available immediately after a new deployment.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
headingPath: How often is cost data updated?
docs.content:
### How often is cost data updated?

Cost reports are generated daily and may not be available immediately after a new deployment. Reloading the page fetches the latest available report data.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
headingPath: Does Stacktape add any markup to AWS costs?
docs.content:
### Does Stacktape add any markup to AWS costs?

No. AWS infrastructure costs are billed directly to your AWS account, and the dashboards show those charges as-is. Stacktape's subscription fee is separate and does not appear in these dashboards. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for subscription details.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
headingPath: How is this different from the AWS Billing console?
docs.content:
### How is this different from the AWS Billing console?

The AWS Billing console shows account-wide cost data. The Stacktape Console attributes costs to your specific projects, stages, and regions, so you can see per-stack spend directly without slicing through raw billing data.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
headingPath: Can I set up alerts when costs exceed a threshold?
docs.content:
### Can I set up alerts when costs exceed a threshold?

Yes. Stacktape supports budget alerts that notify you when spend reaches specified percentage thresholds. You can scope budgets to the entire organization or to individual stacks. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) for setup details.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
headingPath: How far back can I view cost history?
docs.content:
### How far back can I view cost history?

The time range selector on the Costs per stack page includes each month so far in the current year plus all 12 months of the previous year. This gives you between 13 and 24 selectable months depending on when in the year you view it.

docs.title: Cost Dashboards
headingPath: Can I compare costs across multiple AWS accounts?
docs.content:
### Can I compare costs across multiple AWS accounts?

Yes. If you have multiple active [connected AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), use the AWS account dropdown on the Costs per stack page to switch between them. Each account's cost data is displayed independently — select a different account to compare spend across environments.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
# Cost Optimization Tips

AWS bills go directly to your AWS account — Stacktape's subscription fee is separate. Many deployed AWS resources can incur cost, and always-on resources compound over time. This page covers the highest-impact levers for reducing what you pay without sacrificing reliability.


> **Info:** Use the [cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) and [per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) in the Stacktape Console to identify where your spend is concentrated before optimizing. Set up [budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets) so you catch cost spikes early.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Choose the right compute model

The biggest cost lever is choosing the right compute model for your workload. [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), container services, and [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) have fundamentally different pricing structures — picking the wrong one can cost you 5–10x more than necessary.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
### Lambda functions: pay-per-invocation

[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) cost nothing when idle — you pay only for the compute time consumed during each invocation. This makes them the cheapest option for low-traffic or bursty workloads. Beyond sustained high traffic, a container service running 24/7 is usually cheaper per-request because you avoid per-invocation overhead.

Provisioned concurrency can reduce cold starts, but it adds idle compute cost — each provisioned instance bills continuously. Use it only when latency requirements justify the tradeoff. For most internal or background endpoints, occasional cold starts are an acceptable tradeoff for zero idle cost.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
### Container services: always-on cost

A Stacktape [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is a container running 24/7 with a public HTTPS URL, so treat it as always-on compute that bills continuously. [Private services](/resources/compute/private-service) and [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service) are also container-based resources — see their resource pages for runtime and scaling behavior. Before deploying a container service, confirm your workload genuinely needs an always-on process. If traffic is sporadic, a Lambda function with an [HTTP trigger](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) is usually cheaper.

Right-size the `resources` block. For Fargate-backed container workloads, AWS pricing is tied to requested CPU and memory, so right-sizing is the first optimization. Start at the smallest combination that keeps your application responsive and scale up only when metrics show resource pressure.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: Batch jobs: pay only for runtime
docs.content:
### Batch jobs: pay only for runtime

[Batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) run containerized tasks to completion — you pay only for the compute time used. Use batch jobs for data processing, ML training, image encoding, or any task that runs to completion rather than serving ongoing traffic. Set `timeout` on jobs with a known upper bound so an overrun attempt is killed; if `retryConfig` is set, Stacktape retries the job after failure, timeout, or Spot interruption.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Lambda function | Web service | Batch job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing model | Per-invocation | Per-hour (24/7) | Per-job runtime |
| Best for traffic pattern | Bursty / low | Steady / high | Periodic tasks |

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Use ARM/Graviton architecture

AWS Graviton (`arm64`) instances are typically priced below comparable x86 (`x86_64`) instances across Lambda and Fargate. Where your application code supports it, choosing ARM reduces compute cost without changing behavior.

ARM works with most application code without changes — Node.js, Python, Go, Java, and .NET all run natively on `arm64`. The main exception is native compiled binaries or Lambda layers built specifically for x86. Native binaries and prebuilt artifacts need to match the target architecture.

Prefer ARM unless you have native binary compatibility constraints. See the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), [private service](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service), and [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) pages for how to configure architecture on each resource type.


> **Tip:** Start every new project on ARM where supported. Only fall back to x86 if you hit a specific compatibility issue — that's rare for modern application stacks.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: Use spot instances for batch jobs

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Pick the right load balancing

For [web services](/resources/compute/web-service), the load balancing type directly affects monthly cost. The `loadBalancing` property accepts three types:

**`http-api-gateway` (default)** charges ~$1 per million requests with no base cost. At low traffic, this is the cheapest option. At high sustained traffic (above ~500k requests/day), the per-request charges add up and a flat-rate load balancer becomes more cost-effective.

**`application-load-balancer`** has a flat base cost of ~$18/month plus usage-based charges. It becomes more cost-effective than API Gateway at higher traffic volumes. It's required for [gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments), top-level [firewalls](/resources/security/web-application-firewall), and WebSocket support.

**`network-load-balancer`** is for non-HTTP traffic (TCP/TLS) like MQTT, game servers, or custom protocols — use it only when you need raw TCP. It does not support CDN, top-level firewall, or gradual deployments.


> **Tip:** Most teams should start with the default `http-api-gateway`. Switch to `application-load-balancer` only when you need its specific features (gradual deployments, WebSockets, firewall) or when your request volume makes the flat monthly cost cheaper than per-request pricing.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Right-size Lambda memory

Lambda CPU scales proportionally with memory. More memory means more CPU, which often means faster execution and lower total cost — a function that takes 3 seconds at 256 MB might finish in 800 ms at 1,024 MB, costing less overall despite the higher per-millisecond rate.

Profile your functions with real-world payloads. Increase memory in steps (512 → 1,024 → 2,048) and compare total billed duration × memory. The sweet spot is where additional memory stops reducing execution time.

Set `timeout` to the lowest value your function needs. Timeouts don't affect cost directly, but they limit how long a stuck invocation runs before being killed — preventing wasted spend from runaway functions.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Choose the right database engine

[Relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) are often the largest line item in an AWS bill. The engine choice determines both the pricing model and how well it adapts to your traffic pattern.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: Aurora Serverless v2 for variable workloads
docs.content:
### Aurora Serverless v2 for variable workloads

Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity automatically based on demand. You pay only for the capacity you consume at any moment. Set a low `minCapacity` for dev/staging environments to minimize idle cost, and cap `maxCapacity` to control the upper bound of your bill.

Aurora Serverless v2 is the recommended engine for most new projects where traffic is variable or unpredictable. It handles traffic spikes automatically without manual instance resizing and avoids paying for idle capacity during off-hours.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
### Standard RDS for predictable workloads

Standard RDS uses fixed instance sizes with hourly billing. If your traffic is steady and predictable, a right-sized RDS instance can be cheaper than Aurora Serverless v2 because you avoid the per-ACU premium. Use burstable `t` family instances for databases with occasional spikes, and switch to memory-optimized `r` family only for steady, memory-intensive workloads.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
### Avoid over-provisioning high availability

Enabling `multiAz` on a standard RDS instance creates a synchronous standby replica, which roughly doubles the instance cost. Skip it for development and staging stages. For production, enable it only when your uptime requirements justify the extra cost. Aurora clusters replicate across 3 AZs automatically, so multi-AZ resilience is built in without the explicit flag.


> **Tip:** For dev/staging stages, use Aurora Serverless v2 with a low `minCapacity`. This gives you a real database that costs very little when idle. For production, evaluate whether your traffic is stable enough for standard RDS (cheaper per-hour when fully utilized) or variable enough to benefit from Aurora Serverless v2 (cheaper at low or fluctuating utilization).

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Use serverless databases where possible

For key-value and document workloads, [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb) in on-demand mode costs nothing at zero traffic. You pay per read and write operation with no idle cost. This makes it ideal for applications with unpredictable or spiky access patterns. Switch to provisioned throughput only when your traffic is steady and predictable enough to forecast capacity needs.

For Redis use cases that don't require sub-millisecond latency from a dedicated cluster, consider [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) — a serverless, pay-per-request Redis with no idle cost. [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis) bill per-hour for always-on instances regardless of utilization, so they're only cost-effective when you need consistent low-latency access under sustained load.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: Add a CDN for cacheable traffic
docs.content:
## Add a CDN for cacheable traffic

A [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) (CloudFront) caches responses at edge locations for cacheable content and can reduce origin traffic. CloudFront pricing is per request and data transfer rather than a monthly base fee.

Enable a CDN on your [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) when it returns cacheable content (static assets, public API responses, server-rendered pages). The `network-load-balancer` load balancing option is designed for non-HTTP TCP/TLS traffic and does not support CDN, top-level firewall, or gradual deployments — use `http-api-gateway` or `application-load-balancer` for HTTP workloads where CDN caching is part of the design. Skip the CDN for APIs where every response is unique and user-specific — caching won't help, and the extra hop adds slight latency.

You can restrict the CDN price class to reduce per-request cost in premium regions. Lower price classes limit which edge regions serve your content, which reduces cost but increases latency for users outside the covered regions.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Delete unused stages

Every deployed [stage](/configuration/stages-and-environments) consumes AWS resources. Old feature-branch stages, abandoned test stacks, and forgotten staging environments accumulate idle cost — especially for always-on resources like container services, databases, and Redis caches.

Review your stacks regularly in the Stacktape Console or with [`stacktape stack list`](/cli/info-stacks). Delete any stage that's no longer needed:

```bash
stacktape delete --stage old-feature
```

For PR-preview workflows, see the [stacks-per-git-branch pattern](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) and make cleanup part of the workflow so old stages are deleted after branches are merged.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Avoid unnecessary NAT Gateways

A NAT Gateway is one of the most expensive networking components in AWS — it bills a flat hourly rate plus per-GB data processing fees. Avoid NAT Gateways unless you have a concrete networking requirement, such as static outbound IP allowlisting, private subnet egress for a workload that needs it, or internet access for Lambda functions inside the VPC. Most workloads don't need one. When you do need NAT, `stackConfig.nat: ec2` or `ha-ec2` runs small Stacktape-managed instances instead of gateways (about $7 instead of $32 per month per zone, no per-GB fee) at the cost of about a minute of failed outbound calls when an instance dies; see [VPC and networking](/configuration/connecting-resources#vpc-and-networking).

For details on VPC networking and private subnet configuration, see the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), and [multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) resource pages.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Use dev mode during development

Running [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) lets you iterate locally without redeploying for every code change. Use it to shorten the feedback loop during development — see the [dev mode overview](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) for exact local/cloud runtime behavior.

For databases that support running locally during development, see [local databases in dev mode](/local-development/local-databases) — running a local instance avoids the cost of a deployed database while you iterate.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Set up budget alerts

AWS costs can spike unexpectedly — a misconfigured auto-scaling policy, a traffic surge, or a forgotten stack. [Budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets) notify you when spending exceeds a threshold, giving you time to react before the bill grows.

Start with two thresholds: 80% (early warning) and 100% (immediate action). Set up budget alerts for the spend you want to monitor.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content:
## Cost optimization checklist

Use this checklist when reviewing a stack's cost profile:

- [ ] Use ARM/Graviton architecture where supported
- [ ] Lambda memory is profiled and right-sized (not left at default)
- [ ] Container CPU/memory matches actual utilization (check metrics)
- [ ] Auto-scaling is configured for container services with variable traffic
- [ ] Load balancing type matches traffic volume (API Gateway vs ALB)
- [ ] Database engine matches workload pattern (serverless vs fixed instance)
- [ ] Database `multiAz` is disabled for non-production stages
- [ ] Log retention is reduced for development/staging stages
- [ ] Unused stages are deleted
- [ ] Budget alerts are configured
- [ ] CDN is enabled for services with cacheable responses
- [ ] Batch jobs use spot instances where safe
- [ ] Batch jobs have `timeout` set to prevent runaway costs
- [ ] No unnecessary NAT Gateways (private subnet with NAT disabled unless needed)

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: How do I see what each resource costs?
docs.content:
### How do I see what each resource costs?

The Stacktape Console provides [per-resource cost breakdowns](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) that attribute AWS charges to individual resources, stages, and projects. You can also view overall AWS spend across your organization using the [cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards). AWS bills your AWS account directly — these tools help you understand the bill, but they don't add charges.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: Does Stacktape add cost on top of AWS?
docs.content:
### Does Stacktape add cost on top of AWS?

Stacktape's subscription fee is separate from your AWS bill. AWS resources are billed directly by AWS to your connected AWS account. See [billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for plan details.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: Can a Stacktape web service scale to zero?
docs.content:
### Can a Stacktape web service scale to zero?

No. A [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is a container running 24/7 with a public HTTPS URL, so treat it as always-on compute rather than a scale-to-zero endpoint. If your workload has periods of zero traffic, a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) is cheaper — it costs nothing when idle.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: When should I use Aurora Serverless v2 vs standard RDS?
docs.content:
### When should I use Aurora Serverless v2 vs standard RDS?

Use Aurora Serverless v2 when your database traffic is variable, unpredictable, or has significant idle periods — it scales capacity automatically and you pay only for what you use. Use standard RDS when traffic is steady and predictable — a fixed-size instance avoids the per-ACU premium. For dev/staging, Aurora Serverless v2 at a low `minCapacity` is almost always cheaper since it scales down when unused.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: How do I reduce Lambda cold start costs without provisioned concurrency?
docs.content:
### How do I reduce Lambda cold start costs without provisioned concurrency?

Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts but adds idle compute cost, since each provisioned instance bills continuously. To avoid that idle cost, right-size memory instead — more memory means more CPU, which speeds up initialization (see [Right-size Lambda memory](#right-size-lambda-memory)). For most internal or background endpoints, occasional cold starts are an acceptable tradeoff for zero idle cost.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: How does DynamoDB on-demand pricing compare to provisioned?
docs.content:
### How does DynamoDB on-demand pricing compare to provisioned?

DynamoDB on-demand mode charges per read and write operation with no idle cost. Provisioned mode lets you reserve a fixed throughput (reads/writes per second) at a lower per-unit price but bills continuously even at zero traffic. On-demand is cheaper for variable or low-traffic tables. Provisioned with auto-scaling is cheaper when you have sustained, predictable throughput and can accurately forecast capacity.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Tips
headingPath: How do I prevent unexpected cost spikes?
docs.content:
### How do I prevent unexpected cost spikes?

Set up [budget alerts](/managing-costs/budgets) with thresholds at 80% and 100% of your expected monthly spend. Cap auto-scaling with `maxInstances` on container services and `maxCapacity` on Aurora Serverless v2 databases. Set `timeout` on batch jobs so stuck jobs are killed. Review the [per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) weekly to catch anomalies early. Delete old [stages](/configuration/stages-and-environments) you're no longer using.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content:
# Managing Costs Overview

AWS infrastructure costs are billed directly to your AWS account, separate from Stacktape's subscription fee. The Stacktape Console provides cost dashboards, cost attribution by project and stage, and budget alerts to help you understand and control your AWS spend. This section also covers optimization strategies to reduce costs.

Managing costs involves three activities, each covered in a dedicated page:

| Activity | Question it answers | Details |
|----------|---------------------|---------|
| **Viewing costs** | What am I spending and where? | [Dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards), [Per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) |
| **Controlling costs** | How do I prevent overspend? | [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) |
| **Reducing costs** | How do I spend less? | [Optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) |


> **Tip:** If you are new to cost management, start by checking the overview dashboard for your current month-to-date spend, then set up an organization-wide budget alert as a safety net. Those two steps cover most teams.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content:
## Stacktape charges vs. AWS charges

Stacktape costs and AWS costs are independent charges on separate invoices. AWS infrastructure costs are charges in your connected AWS account. Stacktape subscription and billing are managed separately.

| Charge | Billed by | What it covers |
|--------|-----------|----------------|
| AWS infrastructure costs | AWS (to your AWS account) | Compute, storage, networking, databases — everything your resources use |
| Stacktape subscription | Stacktape (to your organization) | [Stacktape platform subscription and plan features](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) |

AWS bills your account directly — the Stacktape Console displays AWS cost report data for connected AWS accounts but does not process AWS charges. Subscription plans and billing are managed on the [Billing page](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content:
## Viewing costs

The Stacktape Console shows AWS cost data in two places: the organization overview dashboard and the dedicated costs per stack page.

The **overview dashboard** displays a month-to-date AWS costs KPI with a trend comparison against the previous month and a cost trend sparkline, an AWS Costs by Project chart (top 10 projects, with the remainder grouped as "Other" when there are more than 10), and an AWS Costs by Resource chart. These give you a quick spending snapshot without navigating away from the main dashboard. Budget alert status also appears on the overview dashboard, showing each configured budget with its name, scope, alert percentages, and threshold.

The **costs per stack page** lets you select a connected AWS account and a time range (month), then shows a table of every attributed stack with its project name, stage, region, and month-to-date costs — sortable by cost and paginated at 10 rows per page. Clicking a row navigates to the per-stage cost detail view. This is where you go to compare spend across stages or find your most expensive stack for a given month.


> **Info:** New stacks may take up to a day to appear in cost data after their first deployment.


For the full walkthrough of these views, see [Dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards). The overview dashboard includes an AWS Costs by Resource chart — see [Per-resource breakdown](/managing-costs/per-resource-breakdown) for the dedicated cost-breakdown page.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content:
### Cost attribution

The costs-per-stack view shows AWS costs broken down by project and stage, generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports. Stack attribution is based on Stacktape deployment metadata attached during deploy operations.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content:
## Controlling costs with budgets

Budget alerts let you set spending thresholds and get alerted before your AWS costs exceed them. Stacktape supports two scopes:

- **Organization-wide budgets** — applied across your organization and created in the selected AWS account when saved.
- **Stack-scoped budgets** — scoped to specific projects. Stack-scoped budget status depends on Stacktape deployment metadata, so deploy matching stacks after creating or changing stack-scoped alerts.

The overview budget panel displays each budget's name, scope, alert percentages, and threshold. Budget history records threshold-exceeded and forecasted-overspend events. Budget alerts can be scoped to specific projects or applied across the organization.

Organization-wide budgets are the simpler option. Organization-wide budget alerts are created in the selected AWS account when saved. Most teams start with an organization-wide budget and add stack-scoped budgets for production stages as they grow.


> **Tip:** Start with a single organization-wide budget at a comfortable monthly cap. Add stack-scoped budgets later for production stages that you want to monitor individually.


For setup details, see [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content:
## Reducing costs

The largest cost-reduction levers in a typical Stacktape deployment are:

1. **Right-sizing compute** — matching memory, CPU, and instance types to actual workload needs rather than over-provisioning. Right-size [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) memory so functions do not pay for capacity they do not use. The same principle applies to container-based workloads — match CPU and memory to observed usage, not worst-case estimates.
2. **Using Lambda functions for intermittent traffic** — Lambda's pay-per-invocation model is often cheaper than always-on containers for bursty or idle-heavy workloads.
3. **Choosing the right database tier** — using serverless database engines for variable workloads and provisioned instances only when sustained throughput justifies the cost. See [relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) for engine options and their tradeoffs.
4. **CDN caching** — offloading repetitive responses to [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) edge locations to reduce origin compute. If your API returns the same response for the same request, caching it at the edge avoids hitting your backend entirely.
5. **Cleaning up unused stages** — [deleting](/deployment-and-lifecycle/destroying-stacks) preview and dev stages that are no longer needed. Every running stage incurs costs for its databases, containers, and other always-on resources, even if no traffic is hitting them.

For concrete, actionable guidance on each of these, see [Optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips).

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
headingPath: How long does it take for cost data to appear, and how often does it refresh?
docs.content:
### How long does it take for cost data to appear, and how often does it refresh?

Cost reports are generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports, and new stacks may take up to a day to appear after their first deployment. There is no sub-daily spend monitoring through the Stacktape Console cost views.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
headingPath: Are AWS costs billed through Stacktape?
docs.content:
### Are AWS costs billed through Stacktape?

No. AWS bills your AWS account directly — the Stacktape Console displays AWS cost report data for connected AWS accounts but does not process AWS charges. Stacktape's own subscription is a separate charge billed by Stacktape to your organization. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription) for subscription details.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
headingPath: What's the difference between organization-wide and stack-scoped budgets?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between organization-wide and stack-scoped budgets?

You define a spending threshold and one or more percentage triggers for either scope. Organization-wide budgets apply across the whole organization and are created in the selected AWS account when saved — the simpler option for a single safety net. Stack-scoped budgets target specific projects, and their status depends on Stacktape deployment metadata, so you must deploy matching stacks after creating or changing them. There is no separate per-stage budget scope; use the costs-per-stack view for per-stage cost visibility. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) for setup steps.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
headingPath: What AWS services typically cost the most in Stacktape deployments?
docs.content:
### What AWS services typically cost the most in Stacktape deployments?

For most deployments the largest cost drivers are compute (Lambda invocations and always-on containers), databases, and networking. The exact breakdown depends on your architecture. The overview dashboard includes an AWS Costs by Resource chart that shows your actual cost distribution across AWS service categories, and [Optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) covers how to bring each of these down.

docs.title: Managing Costs Overview
headingPath: What's the difference between the overview dashboard and the costs per stack page?
docs.content:
### What's the difference between the overview dashboard and the costs per stack page?

The overview dashboard shows a spending summary — month-to-date total with a trend comparison against the previous month, a cost trend sparkline, AWS Costs by Project (top 10), and AWS Costs by Resource. The dedicated costs per stack page shows attributed stacks in a table, paginated at 10 rows per page and initially sorted by month-to-date costs, with AWS account and time range selectors and navigation to per-stage detail views. See [Dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) for a walkthrough of both.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
# Per-Resource Cost Breakdown

Stacktape Console breaks down your AWS spend by project, stage, and individual resource. You can identify which Lambda function, database, or container workload is driving costs in each stack. All costs shown are billed by AWS directly to your AWS account — the Stacktape subscription fee is separate and does not appear in these reports.


> **Info:** Cost reports are generated daily. After deploying a new stack, it can take a while before cost data appears in the Console.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
## Costs per stack

The **Costs per stack** page in the Stacktape Console displays month-to-date costs for every attributed stack in a connected AWS account. Each row shows the project name, stage, AWS region, and total cost for that stack. The table is sorted by cost (highest first) by default, so the most expensive stacks appear at the top.

Two filters narrow the view:

- **AWS account** — if your organization has multiple [connected AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), select which one to inspect. Only active accounts appear in the dropdown.
- **Month** — choose the current month, an earlier month in the current year, or any month from the previous calendar year. Costs are aggregated per calendar month.

Each row has an action that opens the per-resource cost breakdown for that stack. When no cost data is available for the selected account and month, the Console shows a message explaining that cost reports are generated daily and may not yet be available.

The costs-per-stack table formats amounts using the currency code returned by the cost report, falling back to USD when no currency code is present.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
## Per-resource breakdown

When you open a specific stack's costs, the Console shows a per-resource cost table. Each row displays the Stacktape resource name, the AWS resource type, and the cost for that resource in the selected month. A total of all resource costs is displayed above the table.

The per-resource table defaults to sorting by the Costs column. Individual resource costs are rounded to four decimal places, so even low-cost resources like infrequent Lambda invocations show meaningful data. The total is rounded to two decimal places.

The month selector works the same way as the costs-per-stack page — you can view any month in the current year or the previous calendar year.

This view helps answer questions like:

- Which resource in this stage is the most expensive?
- Is the database or the compute driving costs?
- Did a recent change cause a cost spike for a specific resource?

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
## Viewing costs vs. controlling costs

The per-resource breakdown is a **viewing** tool — it tells you what you're spending and where. Stacktape offers separate tools for the other two cost-management activities:

- **Controlling costs**: Set up [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) to receive alerts before spend exceeds a threshold. Use the breakdown data to set realistic budget limits based on actual usage.
- **Reducing costs**: Visit [optimization tips](/managing-costs/optimization-tips) for actionable strategies once you've identified the expensive resources.

The [cost overview dashboard](/managing-costs/dashboards) provides a higher-level view of spend trends across your organization.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
## Using cost data effectively

The Stacktape per-resource cost breakdown gives you the data to prioritize optimization work. Sort by cost to find the biggest line items, compare stages to catch oversized non-production resources, and track month-over-month trends to correlate cost changes with deployments. The strategies below turn raw cost numbers into concrete next steps.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
### Identify expensive resources

The per-resource table defaults to the Costs column, making it easy to spot which resources dominate your bill. In many AWS stacks, a small number of resources account for the majority of spend — commonly an always-on relational database or a high-traffic container workload. Focus optimization efforts on those top line items first.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content:
### Compare stages

Check the costs-per-stack view to compare your `production` and `staging` stages. If staging costs are close to production, open the per-resource breakdown for each stage and compare the individual resource rows — this shows which specific resources are similarly sized across stages and where non-production spend could be investigated further.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
headingPath: Track cost trends month over month
docs.content:
### Track cost trends month over month

Select different months to see how costs change over time. A sudden increase in a specific resource's cost often correlates with a recent deployment or a traffic spike. Compare the affected month's per-resource breakdown with a prior month to narrow down which resource changed.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
headingPath: Set budget alerts based on real data
docs.content:
### Set budget alerts based on real data

The per-resource breakdown shows you what you're actually spending, which makes it easier to set meaningful [budget](/managing-costs/budgets) thresholds. A budget based on observed spend (with a reasonable margin) is far more useful than an arbitrary round number.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
headingPath: Why is no cost data showing for my stack?
docs.content:
### Why is no cost data showing for my stack?

Cost reports are generated daily and may not be available immediately after deploying a new stack. If you deployed recently, it can take a while before the first report appears. Also confirm you've selected the correct AWS account and month in the filters.

docs.title: Per-Resource Cost Breakdown
headingPath: How far back can I view cost data?
docs.content:
### How far back can I view cost data?
