- **`accessKey`** — an authentication credential sent in the `X-Amz-Firehose-Access-Key` HTTP header. Store it as a [`$Secret()`](/configuration/secrets) to avoid exposing credentials in your config file.
- **`gzipEncodingEnabled`** — compress the request body with GZIP before delivery. Defaults to `false`. Enable this to reduce transfer volume, but only when your endpoint documents support for GZIP-encoded request bodies.
- **`retryDuration`** — total time in seconds that Firehose retries failed deliveries before routing logs to the backup S3 bucket. Defaults to `300` (5 minutes). Lower values reduce how long logs stay in limbo during outages; higher values give transient failures more time to recover.
- **`parameters`** — key-value pairs sent as metadata in the `X-Amz-Firehose-Common-Attributes` header. Use them only if your destination documents support for Firehose common attributes — for example, routing logs to different indexes based on a header value.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: Forwarding to a custom HTTP endpoint
docs.content:
### When to use each property

Most setups need only `endpointUrl` and `accessKey`. Add `gzipEncodingEnabled: true` when you forward high-volume logs (tens of GB/month) to reduce transfer costs. Add `parameters` only when your ingestion endpoint documents support for Firehose common attributes and uses header metadata for routing. Reduce `retryDuration` below 300 when you prefer faster failover to S3 backup over longer retry windows.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content:
## How it works

Stacktape uses AWS Kinesis Data Firehose to forward resource logs to your configured destination. The delivery flow works as follows:

1. **Kinesis Data Firehose delivers logs to your destination** — Stacktape configures a Firehose delivery stream that delivers log records over HTTPS to your configured endpoint.
2. **Failed deliveries go to a backup S3 bucket** — if the destination endpoint is unreachable or returns errors after retries are exhausted, Firehose writes the failed log batches to a backup S3 bucket.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content:
### Failure handling

When Firehose cannot deliver logs to your endpoint (network errors, 4xx/5xx responses), it retries for the configured `retryDuration`. For the custom HTTP endpoint type, this defaults to 300 seconds. After retries are exhausted, failed log batches are written to the backup S3 bucket.


> **Tip:** Failed deliveries are routed to a backup S3 bucket after retries are exhausted. Check your destination's ingestion logs and the backup S3 bucket when delivery fails.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content:
### Built-in log viewing

Log forwarding sends logs to the configured external destination through Kinesis Data Firehose. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) or the Stacktape Console for Stacktape's built-in log viewing.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content:
## Choosing a destination

| Criteria | Datadog | Highlight.io | Custom HTTP endpoint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Setup complexity | Minimal — just an API key | Minimal — just a project ID | Moderate — endpoint URL, optional auth, optional GZIP |
| Best for | Teams already using Datadog APM/infrastructure monitoring | Teams using Highlight for session replay + error tracking | Grafana Cloud, Splunk, New Relic, self-hosted solutions |
| Configurable retry | No (Firehose-managed) | No (Firehose-managed) | Yes — `retryDuration` property |
| GZIP compression | Not configurable | Not configurable | Opt-in via `gzipEncodingEnabled` |
| Custom metadata | Not supported | Not supported | Yes — `parameters` property |

Use the dedicated `datadog` or `highlight` type when you target those services — each exposes only the service-specific required property and a default endpoint URL, reducing configuration. For everything else, use `http-endpoint`.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: What happens if my endpoint is down?
docs.content:
### What happens if my endpoint is down?

Firehose retries delivery for the configured retry duration (defaults to 300 seconds for the HTTP endpoint type). After retries are exhausted, failed log batches are written to a backup S3 bucket. Check your destination's ingestion logs and that backup bucket to diagnose delivery failures.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: Can I use a custom HTTP endpoint for Grafana Cloud Logs?
docs.content:
### Can I use a custom HTTP endpoint for Grafana Cloud Logs?

Use `http-endpoint` only if Grafana Cloud Logs provides an HTTPS Firehose-compatible intake endpoint. Set `endpointUrl` to that intake URL. Use `accessKey` only if the endpoint expects the `X-Amz-Firehose-Access-Key` header — verify the authentication method in Grafana's documentation. Enable `gzipEncodingEnabled: true` only if the endpoint documents GZIP support.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: How much does Kinesis Data Firehose cost?
docs.content:
### How much does Kinesis Data Firehose cost?

AWS Kinesis Data Firehose charges ~$0.03/GB of data ingested (varies by region). Firehose cost primarily scales with forwarded GB; failed deliveries are also written to a backup S3 bucket. See [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview) for optimization guidance.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: Should I use the Datadog type or HTTP endpoint type for Datadog?
docs.content:
### Should I use the Datadog type or HTTP endpoint type for Datadog?

Use the `datadog` type. It requires only `apiKey` and uses the default Datadog endpoint unless you override `endpointUrl`. Using the `http-endpoint` type for Datadog would require you to manually set `endpointUrl` — the dedicated `datadog` type reduces configuration to a single required property.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: Does log forwarding support filtering which logs are sent?
docs.content:
### Does log forwarding support filtering which logs are sent?

The `logForwarding` configuration does not include a filter option — every log record from the resource is forwarded. If you need filtering, handle it in the destination or ingestion pipeline — for example, Datadog Log Pipelines or Grafana Cloud log processing rules.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
headingPath: Can I forward logs from any resource type?
docs.content:
### Can I forward logs from any resource type?

The `logForwarding` property accepts `http-endpoint`, `highlight`, or `datadog` destinations, but not every resource type exposes `logForwarding` in its logging configuration. Check the API reference for your specific resource type to confirm it is supported.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content: ## API reference

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.content:
### Definition: `LogForwardingBase`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/log-forwarding` with definition name `LogForwardingBase`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `logClass` | no | `string: "infrequent-access" \| "standard"` | `standard` |
| `logForwarding` | no | `http-endpoint \| highlight \| datadog` | - |

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
# Logs

Stacktape gives you two built-in surfaces for viewing application logs: the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview) and the [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) CLI command. Both read from AWS CloudWatch Logs — the log data AWS captures from your compute resources such as [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), container workloads ([web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [private services](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service), [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload)), and [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job).

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## How logging works

AWS services underlying Stacktape compute resources — Lambda functions, container workloads, and batch jobs — automatically capture everything your application writes to stdout and stderr in CloudWatch Logs. Each compute resource maps to a CloudWatch Logs log group. The CLI resolves the log group for a given `--resource-name` and optional `--container` flag; the Console log viewer receives a CloudWatch log group name and fetches events for that log group. Non-compute resources (databases, queues, buckets, etc.) may produce logs through separate AWS-native mechanisms outside this workflow.

Both surfaces fetch from CloudWatch Logs. The CLI takes `--resource-name` (and `--container` for [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload)) and resolves the matching log group; the Console log viewer receives the log group name for the selected resource and queries events from it. Application logs are whatever your code writes to stdout and stderr — the underlying AWS service streams that into CloudWatch Logs.

For cost implications of CloudWatch Logs ingestion and storage, see [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview).

docs.title: Logs
headingPath: Lower-cost ingestion for infrequently inspected logs
docs.content:
## Lower-cost ingestion for infrequently inspected logs

New log groups can opt into CloudWatch Logs Infrequent Access from the resource's existing logging block:

```yaml
resources:
  archiveWorker:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/archive.ts
      logging:
        logClass: infrequent-access
```

This lowers CloudWatch **ingestion** cost; storage and Logs Insights query pricing are unchanged. Standard remains the default because Infrequent Access does not support live tail, filter and subscription filters, embedded metrics, or Stacktape Issues and log forwarding. AWS fixes the class when a log group is created, so Stacktape blocks attempts to change an existing group and explains that the setting is for a new resource or stage.

The simple viewing workflow remains available. `stacktape logs` and the Console detect Infrequent Access and use a bounded Logs Insights snapshot automatically. The CLI's `--filter` flag uses an incompatible CloudWatch filter language, so use `--query` for filtered IA reads; the Console's IA viewer offers a literal **Message contains** filter.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## Viewing logs in the Console

The [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview) provides a paginated log viewer for resources that have a resolved CloudWatch log group. The viewer displays returned events with timestamps, and each log line is expandable to show its full content via the `ExpandableLogLine` component.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Time range filtering

The Console log viewer offers two modes for selecting the time window, accessible via tabs above the log output:

- **Relative time filter** — choose from 14 preset windows relative to the current time: 1 minute, 5 minutes, 15 minutes, 30 minutes (default), 1 hour, 2 hours, 4 hours, 6 hours, 12 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, or 30 days. This is the fastest way to get recent logs and covers most debugging sessions.
- **Time range filter** — pick an exact start and end date/time using the date-time range picker. Use this when investigating a known incident window where you need precise time boundaries.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Filter patterns

For Standard log groups, enter a CloudWatch filter pattern in the **Filter pattern** input to narrow results to matching log events. The filter uses [CloudWatch filter pattern syntax](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html). For Infrequent Access groups, the field is labeled **Message contains** and Stacktape uses a Logs Insights snapshot. The input is debounced — results refresh automatically after you stop typing, so there is no need to press a submit button.

Filter patterns are useful for isolating error messages, matching JSON field values, or excluding noisy log lines. For example, entering `ERROR` shows only lines containing that keyword, while `{ $.level = "error" }` matches structured JSON logs with a specific field value.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Pagination and display

The log viewer fetches up to 200 events per page and renders them in a virtualized, scrollable list. Each log line is expandable — click a line to see its full content. If more events are available beyond the current page, click **Show more** at the bottom to load the next batch.

The virtualized list keeps the viewer responsive even with hundreds of log entries loaded.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## Viewing logs with the CLI

The [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) command fetches logs from your terminal. It supports two modes: standard log fetching and [CloudWatch Logs Insights](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AnalyzingLogData.html) queries via the `--query` flag.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Basic usage

Fetch the most recent logs for a resource:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

This returns up to 100 log events from the last hour. Without `--raw` or agent mode, log events are passed to a formatted printer that adds timestamps and level-based coloring. Pass `--raw` for structured JSON output instead.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Time ranges

Control the time window with `--since` and `--until`.

Last 30 minutes:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since 30m
```

Last 3 hours:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since 3h
```

Last 2 days:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since 2d
```

Specific time window (used with Logs Insights queries):

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --since "2025-05-14T08:00:00Z" --until "2025-05-14T09:00:00Z" \
  --query "fields @timestamp, @message | sort @timestamp desc | limit 50"
```

The `--since` flag accepts two formats:

| Format | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Relative shorthand | `1h`, `30m`, `2d`, `10s` | Hours, minutes, days, or seconds before `--until` |
| Absolute date | `2025-05-14T08:00:00Z` | Any value accepted by the JavaScript `Date` constructor |

If `--since` is omitted, it defaults to 1 hour before `--until`. If `--until` is omitted, it defaults to the current time.

**How `--until` works:** The `--until` flag serves as the anchor point when computing relative `--since` values — for example, `--since 1h` means 1 hour before `--until`. For Logs Insights queries (when using `--query`), both `--since` and `--until` define the query's time window. For standard log fetching (without `--query`), `--until` is used only to compute relative `--since` values; the CloudWatch fetch call receives `startTime` but not an end-time bound.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Limiting results

Use `--limit` to control how many log events are returned. For example, to fetch the last 500 events:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --limit 500
```

The default limit is 100 events. The CLI applies the limit by slicing the fetched events to the first N entries (`events.slice(0, limit)`). If you are looking at a high-traffic resource, increase the limit to capture more context around an incident.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Filter patterns

Use `--filter` to apply a CloudWatch filter pattern, returning only events that match.

Filter to only errors:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --filter "ERROR"
```

Filter JSON structured logs by field value:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --filter '{ $.level = "error" }'
```

Filter patterns follow [CloudWatch filter pattern syntax](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html). Common patterns:

- `"ERROR"` — match any event containing the word ERROR
- `"ERROR" - "DeprecationWarning"` — match ERROR but exclude DeprecationWarning
- `{ $.level = "error" }` — match JSON logs where the `level` field equals `"error"`
- `{ $.statusCode >= 500 }` — match JSON logs with status code 500 or above

Filter patterns are applied server-side by CloudWatch before events are returned, so they reduce both network transfer and the number of events you need to scan. For more complex analysis, use Logs Insights queries instead.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### CloudWatch Logs Insights queries

For complex analysis — aggregations, top-N queries, statistical breakdowns — use `--query` to run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query.

Find the 20 most recent errors with timestamps:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --query "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20"
```

Count errors per hour over the last 24 hours:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --since 24h \
  --query "filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(1h)"
```

Find slowest Lambda invocations:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --query "filter @type = 'REPORT' | stats max(@duration) as maxDuration, avg(@duration) as avgDuration by bin(5m)"
```

When `--query` is provided, the command uses the CloudWatch Logs Insights engine instead of the standard log-fetching path. Both `--since` and `--until` define the query's time window. In non-agent mode, the CLI prints the result count and each row's timestamp and message. In agent mode, results are returned as structured JSON.


> **Tip:** CloudWatch Logs Insights is well suited for ad-hoc investigation and aggregate queries across large volumes of logs. Use it when simple filter patterns are not expressive enough — for example, when you need to count occurrences, compute averages, or group by a field.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Container-specific logs

For [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload), use `--container` to specify which container's logs to fetch:

```bash
stacktape logs myWorkload --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --container nginx
```

The `--container` flag is used when resolving the log group for the resource. For single-container resources ([web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [private services](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service)), the log group is resolved automatically and `--container` is not needed.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
### Raw JSON output

Use `--raw` to get structured JSON output instead of formatted text:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --raw
```

This outputs a JSON object containing the log group name and an array of events, each with `timestamp`, `message`, and `logStream` fields. Raw output is useful for piping into `jq`, storing for later analysis, or consuming in scripts.

The `logGroup` value is the resolved CloudWatch Logs log group name for your Stacktape resource.

```json
{
  "logGroup": "<resolved CloudWatch log group name>",
  "events": [
    {
      "timestamp": "2025-05-14T08:32:01.000Z",
      "message": "{\"level\":\"info\",\"message\":\"Request processed\",\"duration\":42}",
      "logStream": "2025/05/14/[$LATEST]abc123"
    }
  ]
}
```


> **Info:** When the CLI runs in agent mode (used by AI coding assistants via the [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup)), it automatically outputs structured JSON regardless of the `--raw` flag.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## CLI vs Console comparison

Both surfaces access the same underlying CloudWatch Logs data. Choose based on your workflow:

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | CLI (logs) | Console |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Historical log search | yes | yes |
| Filter patterns | yes | yes |
| CloudWatch Logs Insights queries | yes | Filter patterns only |
| Structured JSON output | yes | no |
| Time range controls | Relative shorthand + absolute | 14 presets + date-time range picker |
| Formatted output | Timestamps + level-based coloring | Expandable log lines with timestamps |
| Scriptable / CI-friendly | yes | no |


Use the Console for quick visual inspection of stored log events with its 14 preset time windows, date-range picker, and expandable log lines. Use the CLI for Logs Insights queries, JSON export, scripted analysis, and terminal-based workflows. The [`logs`](/cli/logs) command targets a single `--resource-name` per invocation; the Console log viewer operates on one log group at a time.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## Structured logging

While Stacktape captures any stdout/stderr output, writing logs as structured JSON makes them far more useful for filtering and querying. Both the CLI's `--filter` flag and Logs Insights queries can match on individual JSON fields, which is not possible with plain-text logs.

A minimal structured log entry looks like:

```json
{ "level": "error", "message": "Payment failed", "userId": "u-123", "statusCode": 502 }
```

With this format, you can run targeted queries.

Filter to errors for a specific user:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --filter '{ $.userId = "u-123" && $.level = "error" }'
```

Aggregate error counts by status code over the last 6 hours:

```bash
stacktape logs myApi --stage prod --region eu-west-1 \
  --since 6h \
  --query "filter level = 'error' | stats count(*) by statusCode"
```

Most logging libraries (Winston, Pino, Python's `structlog`, Go's `slog`) support JSON output with minimal setup. If you are starting a new project, default to structured JSON logs — the investment pays off immediately once you need to debug a production issue.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content:
## Log forwarding

For external log shipping, see [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding). That page covers the supported destinations and configuration.

docs.title: Logs
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Logs
headingPath: How much does CloudWatch Logs cost?
docs.content:
### How much does CloudWatch Logs cost?

AWS CloudWatch Logs charges for ingestion, storage, and Logs Insights queries. Pricing is billed directly to your AWS account and varies by region — check the [AWS CloudWatch pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/pricing/) for current rates. For Stacktape cost management, see [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview).

docs.title: Logs
headingPath: Can I search logs across multiple resources at once?
docs.content:
### Can I search logs across multiple resources at once?

The CLI's [`logs`](/cli/logs) command targets a single `--resource-name` per invocation, and the Console log viewer operates on one log group at a time. To search across multiple resources, run separate `stacktape logs` commands for each. For cross-resource log analysis, consider forwarding logs to a centralized platform using [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding).

docs.title: Logs
headingPath: What is the difference between filter patterns and Logs Insights queries?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between filter patterns and Logs Insights queries?

Filter patterns are simple text or JSON-field matchers applied at fetch time — they return matching log lines. CloudWatch Logs Insights is a full query language that supports aggregation (`stats count(*)`), grouping (`by bin(1h)`), sorting, and field extraction. Use filter patterns for quick keyword searches; use Insights for analytical queries like "how many errors per hour" or "what are the slowest requests." The CLI supports both filter patterns (`--filter`) and Logs Insights queries (`--query`). The Console log viewer supports CloudWatch filter patterns.

docs.title: Logs
headingPath: When should I use CloudWatch Logs vs an external logging service?
docs.content:
### When should I use CloudWatch Logs vs an external logging service?

CloudWatch Logs requires no additional setup for Stacktape resources and integrates with both the CLI and the Console, so it handles most debugging and monitoring needs. Reach for an external service when you need cross-service correlation, advanced alerting on log patterns, or a unified dashboard spanning AWS and non-AWS systems. Use [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) to ship logs to those destinations.

docs.title: Logs
headingPath: How do I set up alerts based on log patterns?
docs.content:
### How do I set up alerts based on log patterns?

Stacktape [alarms](/observability/alarms) trigger notifications based on CloudWatch metrics but do not include a built-in log-pattern alerting workflow. For log-based alerting, you can use AWS CloudWatch metric filters — an AWS-native mechanism outside the Stacktape logs workflow — to derive custom metrics from log data, then create alarms against those metrics. For alert delivery, see [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) and [notifications](/observability/notifications).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
# Metrics

Stacktape surfaces AWS CloudWatch metrics through the Stacktape Console and the [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics) CLI command. The Console metrics grid can render charts for nine metric types — Lambda, ECS, RDS, API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, and Redis — when those metric entries are present for the stage. The CLI provides targeted metric queries for four resource types directly in your terminal. No instrumentation or SDK setup is required.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
## Console metrics dashboard

The Stacktape Console metrics grid can render chart components for nine metric types: Lambda, ECS (container workloads), RDS (relational databases), API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito (user auth pools), Redis, and CloudFront, when those metric entries are present for the stage. Changing the selected time range preset recalculates each chart's start time, end time, and aggregation period.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Time range presets

The Console metrics toolbar provides selectable time range presets. The default preset is **7d**. Each preset determines the chart time window and the aggregation period used for datapoints.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Filtering by resource

The Console metrics component can be rendered with a `showOnlyForResource` prop. When a parent view passes this prop, the grid renders only charts matching the selected resource name — for example, when viewing metrics from a specific resource's detail page.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
## CLI: stacktape metrics

The [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics) command fetches a single CloudWatch metric for a specific resource and renders it as a sparkline chart in your terminal. Use it for quick spot-checks without leaving your editor.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Basic usage

The command validates that `--resource-name` (the resource name from your Stacktape config) and `--metric` (the CloudWatch metric name) are provided. The command runs against the target stack identified by `--stage` and `--region`.

```bash
stacktape metrics api Invocations --stage prod --region eu-west-1
```

If the specified metric is not valid for the resource type, Stacktape raises an error whose guidance lists the available metrics.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Supported resource types

The CLI currently supports four resource types. Each resource type has a fixed set of valid `--metric` values:

| Resource type | Deployed `resourceType` | Available `--metric` values |
|--------------|-------------|----------------------------|
| [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | `function` | `Invocations`, `Errors`, `Duration`, `Throttles`, `ConcurrentExecutions` |
| [Multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) | `multi-container-workload` | `CPUUtilization`, `MemoryUtilization` |
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | `relational-database` | `CPUUtilization`, `DatabaseConnections`, `FreeStorageSpace`, `ReadLatency`, `WriteLatency` |
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | `http-api-gateway` | `Count`, `4XXError`, `5XXError`, `Latency`, `IntegrationLatency` |

The CLI resolves metrics based on the deployed resource's `resourceType`. Resources whose deployed `resourceType` is `multi-container-workload` use the ECS metrics listed above. For DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, and Redis metrics, use the Console dashboard; the `metrics` CLI does not support those resource types.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Time range

By default, the CLI fetches the last 1 hour of data. Use `--since` to set the start of the time window and `--until` to set the end.

`--since` accepts either a relative duration or an absolute ISO 8601 timestamp. Relative durations use a number followed by a unit: `s` (seconds), `m` (minutes), `h` (hours), or `d` (days).

Fetch the last 30 minutes of CPU data for an ECS workload:

```bash
stacktape metrics backend CPUUtilization --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since 30m
```

Fetch metrics from a specific absolute time window:

```bash
stacktape metrics api Errors --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --since "2025-05-16T08:00:00Z" --until "2025-05-16T12:00:00Z"
```

When `--until` is omitted, the command uses the current time.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Aggregation and statistics

The `--period` flag controls the aggregation window in seconds. The default is **300** (5 minutes). Smaller periods produce more datapoints but require the data to exist at that granularity in CloudWatch.

The `--stat` flag selects the CloudWatch statistic and defaults to **Average**. The value is passed directly to the CloudWatch API, so any valid CloudWatch statistic string works — common choices include `Sum`, `Average`, `Maximum`, `Minimum`, and percentiles like `p99`.

Fetch maximum Lambda duration with 60-second granularity over the last hour:

```bash
stacktape metrics api Duration --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat Maximum --period 60 --since 1h
```


> **Tip:** Use `Sum` for count-based metrics (Invocations, Errors, Throttles) and `Average` or `Maximum` for utilization and latency metrics. `p99` is useful for latency when you care about tail performance rather than averages.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Output formats

Outside agent mode, the command renders the metric as a terminal chart. When agent mode is enabled (via the `--agent` flag), the command writes structured JSON containing `resource`, `metric`, `period`, `stat`, `unit` (populated from the CloudWatch result label), and timestamped `datapoints`.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
## Console vs CLI

The Console and CLI serve different workflows. Use the Console for broad monitoring across all supported metric categories in a stage. Use the CLI for targeted, scriptable queries on specific metrics.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Console dashboard | CLI metrics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interaction | Visual charts | Terminal sparkline or JSON |
| Scope | All supported metric categories at once | One resource, one metric per invocation |
| Resource categories | 9 (Lambda, ECS, RDS, API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, Redis) | 4 (Lambda, ECS, RDS, API Gateway) |
| Time range | Presets (default: 7d) | Custom (relative or absolute start/end) |
| Custom statistic | no | Any CloudWatch statistic (default: Average) |
| Scriptable output | no | JSON in agent mode |
| Best for | Daily monitoring, team visibility | Debugging, CI scripts, quick checks |

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
## Understanding key metrics

Different resource types expose different CloudWatch metrics. Knowing which metrics to watch — and what the values mean — helps you respond to issues before they affect users.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Lambda function metrics

[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) expose five metrics through the CLI. `Invocations` and `Errors` tell you how much traffic your function handles and how often it fails. `Duration` tracks execution time in milliseconds — rising duration often signals a performance regression or a slow downstream dependency. `Throttles` counts invocations rejected due to concurrency limits, which indicates you need to request a higher reserved concurrency quota or optimize function duration. `ConcurrentExecutions` shows how many function instances run simultaneously.

Check for throttled invocations over the last 24 hours:

```bash
stacktape metrics api Throttles --stage prod --region eu-west-1 --stat Sum --since 24h
```

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Container workload metrics

Resources whose deployed `resourceType` is `multi-container-workload` run on AWS ECS and expose `CPUUtilization` and `MemoryUtilization` through the CLI. Both are percentages of the allocated resources. Sustained CPU above 80% suggests the workload needs more CPU or additional containers. Memory hitting 100% causes OOM kills and container restarts — check [logs](/observability/logs) for restart events if you suspect this.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### Database metrics

[Relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database) expose five metrics through the CLI. `CPUUtilization` tracks database engine CPU usage. `DatabaseConnections` counts active connections — a sudden spike often indicates a connection leak in application code. `FreeStorageSpace` tracks remaining disk in bytes; running out halts writes. `ReadLatency` and `WriteLatency` (in seconds) track I/O performance — sustained increases suggest you need a larger instance class or need to optimize query patterns.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
### API Gateway metrics

[HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) metrics track request volume and error rates at the gateway layer. `Count` is total requests. `5XXError` and `4XXError` count server-side and client-side errors respectively. `Latency` measures end-to-end request time including backend processing, while `IntegrationLatency` measures only the time calling the backend. If `Latency` is much higher than `IntegrationLatency`, compare gateway-level configuration, authorization, mapping, and client/network effects before focusing on backend execution.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content:
## Using metrics with alarms

Metrics become actionable when paired with [alarms](/observability/alarms). An alarm watches a specific CloudWatch metric and triggers when it crosses a threshold — for example, notifying your team when Lambda error count exceeds 10 in a 5-minute window or when database CPU stays above 90% for 15 minutes. Configure [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) (Slack, email, Discord, Teams, webhook) to receive notifications when alarms fire.

For cost-related metrics and optimization, see [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Metrics
headingPath: How much do CloudWatch metrics cost?
docs.content:
### How much do CloudWatch metrics cost?

AWS CloudWatch includes basic monitoring metrics at no additional charge for most services. Detailed monitoring and custom metrics incur per-metric charges. For cost optimization guidance, see [Managing Costs](/managing-costs/overview).

docs.title: Metrics
headingPath: Why does the Console support more resource types than the CLI?
docs.content:
### Why does the Console support more resource types than the CLI?

The Console metrics grid can render charts for nine metric types — Lambda, ECS, RDS, API Gateway, DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, and Redis — when those metric entries are present for the stage. The CLI [`metrics`](/cli/metrics) command currently supports four (Lambda, ECS, RDS, API Gateway). The Console is the better choice for daily monitoring across all supported metric categories. The CLI is designed for targeted, scriptable queries on the most common compute and database resources.

docs.title: Metrics
headingPath: What is the difference between Latency and IntegrationLatency for API Gateway?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between Latency and IntegrationLatency for API Gateway?

`Latency` measures the total time from when API Gateway receives a request to when it returns a response. `IntegrationLatency` measures only the time spent calling the backend (your Lambda function or container). The difference is API Gateway overhead — routing, authorization, response mapping. If `Latency` is high but `IntegrationLatency` is low, investigate the gateway configuration. If both are high, focus on optimizing your backend code.

docs.title: Metrics
headingPath: How far back can I view metrics?
docs.content:
### How far back can I view metrics?

AWS CloudWatch retains metric data at varying resolutions: 1-minute datapoints for 15 days, 5-minute datapoints for 63 days, and 1-hour datapoints for 455 days (approximately 15 months). The Console uses time range presets (default: 7d). The CLI accepts relative durations (e.g. `--since 60d`) and absolute ISO 8601 timestamps, so you can query older data — CloudWatch determines which retained datapoints are available for the requested range.

docs.title: Metrics
headingPath: Can I create custom application metrics?
docs.content:
### Can I create custom application metrics?

The `metrics` CLI supports only the predefined AWS service metrics listed in the table above (invocations, CPU, memory, latency, etc.). To publish custom application metrics, use the AWS CloudWatch SDK in your application code to call `PutMetricData`. The Console metrics grid renders the built-in metric entry types present for the stage. See [alarms](/observability/alarms) for alarm configuration details.

docs.title: Metrics
headingPath: When should I use metrics vs logs for debugging?
docs.content:
### When should I use metrics vs logs for debugging?

Metrics tell you *what* is happening — error rates are up, latency is increasing, memory is growing. [Logs](/observability/logs) tell you *why* — the stack trace, the failing request, the slow query. Start with metrics to identify which resource has a problem and what time window to investigate, then switch to [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) for the relevant resource and time window to find the root cause.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
# Notification Rules

Notification rules decide which Stacktape events an [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels) receives, such as a failed deployment, an opened incident or a changed secret. Each rule belongs to one channel, lists one or more event types and can be limited to specific projects and stages. Rules are managed on the channel's page in the Console.


> **Info:** Notifications cover **events recorded by Stacktape**: deployments, deletions, rollbacks, Git deployments, script runs, secret and SSM parameter changes, incidents and new security findings. For **metric-based alerts** on running resources (CPU, error rates, latency), use [alarms](/observability/alarms). A firing alarm opens an [incident](/observability/incidents), and a notification rule that watches incident events sends it to your channel.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## When to use notifications

Notification rules are most useful when your team needs to know about deployment activity or incidents without watching the CLI or Console. Common scenarios:

- **Production deploy alerts.** Notify a Slack channel when a production deploy fails, so the on-call engineer sees it immediately.
- **Automated deploy visibility.** When deployments happen automatically (for example through [GitOps](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console)), notification rules surface failures of preview and Git push deploys.
- **Incident paging.** Send incident opened, escalated and resolved events to the channel your on-call team watches.
- **Multi-team coordination.** Scope rules per project so each team receives only its own deployment events.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## When NOT to use notifications

If you only deploy occasionally and watch the CLI output yourself, you may not need notification rules. They become important once deployments happen automatically or across many projects and stages.

Notifications are also not the tool for runtime health monitoring. To alert when error rates spike, CPU saturates or latency crosses a threshold, use [alarms](/observability/alarms), which watch CloudWatch metrics on running resources.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## Event types

Each rule lists the events it watches. The **New notification rule** dialog groups them as follows:

| Group | Events |
|---|---|
| **Deployment** | Deploy started, Deploy succeeded, Deploy failed, Deploy rolled back |
| **Deletion** | Delete started, Delete succeeded, Delete failed |
| **Rollback** | Rollback succeeded, Rollback failed |
| **Git deployments** | Preview deploy succeeded, Preview deploy failed, Git push deploy succeeded, Git push deploy failed |
| **Scripts** | Script run succeeded, Script run failed |
| **Secrets** | Secret created, Secret updated, Secret deleted |
| **SSM parameters** | Parameter created, Parameter updated, Parameter deleted |
| **Incidents** | Incident opened, Incident escalated, Incident resolved |
| **Security** | New critical or high security findings |

A new rule starts with the failure events, the incident events and new security findings selected. A single rule can watch several event types, so related alerts can go to one channel through one rule.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## Managing notification rules

Open **Channels** in the Alerting group of the Stacktape Console and click a channel. Its page lists what the channel receives, one rule per row:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| **Events** | The events the rule sends, grouped by subject, for example "Incidents: opened, resolved" |
| **From** | The projects and stages the rule covers, for example "All projects · production stages" |
| **Added** | When the rule was created |

The Channels list summarises the same thing per channel in its **Receives** column.

To add a rule, click **New rule** on the channel's page, choose the event types and, optionally, projects and stages, then click **Add rule**. To delete a rule, use **Delete** in its row menu; the channel stays. Adding and deleting rules needs the `org:manage-notifications` permission (organization owners and admins); every member can see them.

A new Slack (Stacktape app) channel starts with default rules: incidents and failed deployments from every stage, successful deployments from production stages, and new security findings.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## Scoping notifications

Rules can be scoped to specific projects and stages. When a scope is left at its default, the page shows "All projects" or "All stages".

- **Project scoping** restricts the rule to specific projects. Only events from those projects send an alert.
- **Stage scoping** restricts the rule to specific stages, for example only `production`. This keeps dev and staging deploys from generating noise.

Project and stage scoping can be combined. Secret and SSM parameter events belong to the whole organization, so a rule that watches only those events has no project or stage scope.


> **Tip:** Create separate rules for different severity levels. For example, route failure events to a high-urgency Slack channel and success events to a low-noise webhook.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## Checking what was sent

[Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history) in the Alerting group lists every alert Stacktape sent to your channels, with the delivery outcome per channel. Each channel's page also shows its recent alerts. If an alert was not delivered, the delivery details name the error and link to the channel, where **Send test** checks it after you fix its settings. The old `/notifications` address opens Channels.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content:
## Notifications vs. alarms vs. budgets

Notifications, alarms and budgets serve different purposes. Notification rules and budgets send to Console [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels); an alarm sends to the `notificationChannels` listed on it in the configuration and opens an incident when it fires.

| Feature | Watches for | Defined in |
|---|---|---|
| **Notification rules** | Stacktape events (for example a failed deployment or an opened incident) | Console, on each channel's page |
| **[Alarms](/observability/alarms)** | CloudWatch metric thresholds (error rates, CPU, latency, queue depth) | Stacktape configuration, `alarms` list on a resource; created on deploy |
| **[Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets)** | AWS spending thresholds | Console, Budgets page |

Use notifications for operational awareness ("did the deploy finish?"), alarms for runtime health ("is the API throwing errors?") and budgets for cost control ("are we overspending?").

Stacktape creates the AWS budget when a budget is saved. Alarms are created when the stack that defines them is deployed.

docs.title: Notification Rules
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Notification Rules
headingPath: Can I route different events to different channels?
docs.content:
### Can I route different events to different channels?

Yes. Each channel has its own rules, so give each channel the events and scope it should receive. For example, send all deployment events to a low-noise webhook with one rule, and route only `production` deploy failures to a high-urgency Slack channel with another.

docs.title: Notification Rules
headingPath: Why didn't my notification get delivered?
docs.content:
### Why didn't my notification get delivered?

Open [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history), which lists every alert that was sent with its delivery status per channel. If a delivery failed, the cause is usually the destination [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels): an expired webhook URL or a misconfigured Slack integration.

docs.title: Notification Rules
headingPath: What is the difference between notifications and alarms?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between notifications and alarms?

Notifications watch for events that Stacktape records, such as a deployment failing or an incident opening. [Alarms](/observability/alarms) watch CloudWatch metrics on running resources, such as CPU usage, error rates, latency or queue depth.

docs.title: Notification Rules
headingPath: Do I need a separate alert channel for notifications and budgets?
docs.content:
### Do I need a separate alert channel for notifications and budgets?

No. The same [alert channel](/observability/alert-channels) can be used by notification rules and budgets. To get alarm alerts in that channel, add a rule that watches incident events: a firing alarm opens an incident.

docs.title: Notification Rules
headingPath: Can I get notified only for production deploys?
docs.content:
### Can I get notified only for production deploys?

Yes. Set the rule's stages to the stage names it applies to, such as `production`. Combine it with project scoping when only some projects should send alerts.

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
# Observability Overview

Stacktape surfaces logs, metrics, alarms, and issues through the CLI and Console — reading from the same AWS CloudWatch data your stack produces. In the Stacktape Console, each alert channel has rules that choose which events it receives, and Sent alerts records what was sent. Error tracking (the Console's Error tracking page) is on for every stage by default and is wired into each stack during deployment.

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Observability surfaces

Stacktape provides multiple observability surfaces for supported workloads and AWS resources in your stack. Each surface is accessible from the CLI, the Console, or through your Stacktape configuration — depending on the feature.

| Surface | CLI | Console | Config |
|---------|-----|---------|--------|
| [Logs](/observability/logs) | [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) | See [Logs](/observability/logs) | — |
| [Metrics](/observability/metrics) | [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics) | See [Metrics](/observability/metrics) | — |
| [Tracing](/observability/tracing) | — | Trace search and waterfall views | See [Tracing](/observability/tracing) |
| [Uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) | — | Live status, availability history, incidents | See [Uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) |
| [Synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests) | — | Run history with screenshots | See [Synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests) |
| [Alarms](/observability/alarms) | [`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarms) | Alarm state and history | See [Alarms](/observability/alarms) |
| [Incidents](/observability/incidents) | [`stacktape incident list`](/cli/incidents) and lifecycle commands | Correlated incident queue and evidence | — |
| [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) | [`stacktape error list`](/cli/errors-list), [`error resolve`](/cli/errors-resolve), [`error ignore`](/cli/errors-ignore), [`error reopen`](/cli/errors-reopen) | Error inbox with grouping and occurrence counts | On by default; `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` turns it off or limits stages |
| [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) | — | Create and manage channels | See [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) |
| [Notification rules](/observability/notifications) | — | Which events each alert channel receives | — |
| [Alert history](/observability/alert-history) | — | Unified log of all delivered alerts | — |
| [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) | — | — | See [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) |

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Logs

Stacktape has a logs surface for inspecting CloudWatch Logs produced by your stack. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) for ad-hoc log queries and live tailing from the terminal — filter by resource, time range, or keyword. The Console provides a persistent log viewer for browsing logs across resources and stages without leaving the browser. For full CLI options and details, see [Logs](/observability/logs).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Metrics

Stacktape provides a metrics surface for viewing AWS CloudWatch metrics produced by your resources. Use [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics) for quick terminal-based metric checks — useful during active debugging or in CI/CD scripts. The Console provides metric dashboards for ongoing monitoring across your stack. For full CLI options and details, see [Metrics](/observability/metrics).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Alarms

Alarms monitor CloudWatch metrics and fire when a threshold is breached. Define alarms per resource in your stack configuration and deploy to apply them. The Console shows their state and history. For the authoritative list of resource types that support config-time alarms, trigger types, and evaluation windows, see [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

**Config-time definition** — use the `alarms` property on supported resources to define threshold-based alarms directly in your Stacktape configuration. These alarms are version-controlled and deploy with your stack. For the full property reference and supported trigger types, see [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

**Legacy Console rules** — existing rules remain visible under **Legacy alarm rules**. Use `stacktape alarm export` to move them into stack configuration. The Console no longer creates or edits alarm rules.

**From the CLI**, use [`stacktape alarm list`](/cli/alarms) to inspect alarm state in a stack.

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Error tracking

Error tracking is an error inbox for your deployed workloads, shown on the **Error tracking** page in the Console. Use `error list` to inspect errors from the CLI and `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` to control capture. Instead of manually searching logs for exceptions, Stacktape detects common runtime error patterns, groups repeated occurrences into a single item, and surfaces them with the error message, stack trace, originating resource, project, stage, and occurrence count.

**How detection works** — on deployment, Stacktape adds CloudWatch Logs subscription filters to supported Stacktape-managed Lambda functions and `js-bundle` containers. Matching log events are sent to the Stacktape service Lambda in your stack, parsed, fingerprinted, and reported to the Console. Issues are grouped by fingerprint, project, and stage.

Detection is log-pattern based. It looks for common runtime error markers: Lambda invoke errors, unhandled promise rejections, exceptions, tracebacks, panics, fatal errors, and stack-trace lines for TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, and PHP.

**Turning it off or limiting stages**: error tracking is on for every stage of every stack by default. A stack turns it off or limits it to some stages with `deploymentConfig.errorTracking`; the change takes effect at the stack's next deployment. Organization owners and admins can also turn it off for every stack in **Error tracking settings** (the **Settings** button on the Error tracking page).

**From the CLI**, manage issues using [`stacktape error list`](/cli/errors-list), [`error resolve`](/cli/errors-resolve), [`error ignore`](/cli/errors-ignore), and [`error reopen`](/cli/errors-reopen). See the CLI reference pages for available options.

**High-volume protection** — Stacktape includes built-in safety limits. Stale log batches are ignored, each detector invocation handles a bounded number of matching errors, context lookups are capped, and the Console stores only recent occurrence examples while keeping the full occurrence count.

**Limitations** — Because detection starts from log messages, it can miss errors that don't match the recognized patterns and can also pick up application logs that merely look like errors. It is best for recurring runtime failures, not a complete observability or tracing system. On the next deployment, Stacktape skips issue detection for workloads with Stacktape log forwarding configured, user-managed packaging, edge functions, unsupported languages, and disabled projects or stages.

For setup, detection scope, and limitations, see [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Alert channels

Alert channels are the destinations where alarm and notification alerts get delivered. You create channels in the Stacktape Console, then use them in notification rules and budget alerts, or reference them from config alarms with `console-channel`.

Channels deliver alerts to destinations such as Slack, email, or a webhook. For deployment and incident notifications, select a pre-created channel. For alarms in config, use a `console-channel` reference or configure the integration directly on the alarm.

For supported integration types, setup instructions, and authentication details, see [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Notification rules

Notification rules alert you when deployment lifecycle events happen — a deploy succeeds, fails, or is canceled. Each rule specifies which events to watch and which channel to deliver the alert to.

Notification rules are managed in the Stacktape Console, on the page of the alert channel they send to.

For event types and scoping, see [Notification rules](/observability/notifications).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Sent alerts

The Console keeps one log of the alerts it sends: incidents, deploy and change notifications, and budget alerts. Use [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history) to see every alert your organization was sent and whether it reached its channels.

Stacktape also maintains separate focused histories:

- **Alarm history**: an alarm's state changes in CloudWatch (when it fired and recovered), opened from an alarm on the Alarms page
- **Budget history**: budget threshold alerts, under **Budgets → History**

Notification rule alerts are listed in [Alert history](/observability/alert-history) itself; the old `/notifications/history` address redirects there.

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## Log forwarding

Log forwarding streams logs from your workloads to an external observability platform using AWS Kinesis Data Firehose. Three destination types are supported: Datadog, Highlight.io, and custom HTTPS endpoint — see [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) for details on each. Failed deliveries are backed up to an S3 bucket automatically. For cost details, see [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview).

When log forwarding is configured on a workload, Stacktape skips issue detection for that workload — both features use a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter slot, and each log group has a limited number of slots.

For supported targets, configuration details, and provider-specific setup, see [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
## CLI vs Console

The CLI debug commands are designed for ad-hoc investigation — you're debugging a problem right now and want quick answers in your terminal. The Console is designed for ongoing monitoring — persistent views, alarm state and history, and team-wide visibility.

**Use the CLI when:**
- You're actively debugging a failing deployment or runtime error
- You want a quick metric check without leaving your terminal
- You need to query or filter logs
- You're scripting observability checks in CI/CD

**Use the Console when:**
- You need to monitor alarm state across your organization
- You want to manage issues as a team
- You need a record of sent alerts and whether they were delivered
- You're setting up notification routing for deployment events

Both work against the same underlying CloudWatch data and Stacktape issue store. They're complementary, not competing.

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Observability Overview
headingPath: Can I use Datadog or another external platform instead of CloudWatch?
docs.content:
### Can I use Datadog or another external platform instead of CloudWatch?

Yes. Stacktape's [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) streams logs to external platforms via Kinesis Data Firehose — three destination types are available (`datadog`, `highlight`, and `http-endpoint`). See the [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) page for supported targets and setup. CloudWatch metrics and alarms remain AWS-native — Stacktape doesn't replace CloudWatch, but you can forward the raw log data to your preferred platform for analysis and search.

docs.title: Observability Overview
headingPath: Do I need to instrument my code to get logs and metrics?
docs.content:
### Do I need to instrument my code to get logs and metrics?

No. Lambda functions and container workloads write stdout/stderr to CloudWatch Logs automatically. AWS provides infrastructure metrics (invocations, errors, CPU, memory, latency) without code changes. For application-level metrics beyond what AWS provides, consult the [AWS CloudWatch documentation on publishing custom metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/publishingMetrics.html).

docs.title: Observability Overview
docs.content:
### Where do I configure alarms?

Define alarms on each resource in your stack configuration and deploy. The Console displays deployed alarm state and history. Export existing legacy Console rules with `stacktape alarm export` before moving them into configuration. See [Alarms](/observability/alarms#migrating-legacy-console-alarm-rules).

docs.title: Observability Overview
headingPath: How does issue detection differ from log monitoring?
docs.content:
### How does issue detection differ from log monitoring?

[Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) is an automated error inbox. It detects, groups, and tracks recurring runtime errors with no setup, because it is on by default. Log monitoring (via [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) or the Console) gives you raw access to all log output. Issues answer "what's broken across my stack?" while logs answer "what happened at this specific time?"

docs.title: Observability Overview
headingPath: Why isn't issue detection picking up my errors?
docs.content:
### Why isn't issue detection picking up my errors?

Detection is log-pattern based and only recognizes common runtime error markers (unhandled exceptions, tracebacks, panics, fatal errors) for TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, .NET, Ruby, and PHP — errors that don't match these patterns are missed. It is also skipped entirely for workloads with Stacktape log forwarding configured, user-managed packaging, edge functions, unsupported languages, and disabled projects or stages. The log subscriptions are added during deployment, so a stack reports only after it has been deployed with Stacktape v4; **Error tracking settings** lists which deployed stacks are wired.

docs.title: Observability Overview
headingPath: Why does enabling log forwarding disable issue detection on a workload?
docs.content:
### Why does enabling log forwarding disable issue detection on a workload?

Both features rely on a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter, and each log group has a limited number of filter slots. When [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) is configured on a workload, Stacktape skips issue detection there to avoid exhausting those slots. If you need automated error grouping for a workload, leave log forwarding off for it.

docs.title: Observability Overview
headingPath: How much does observability cost on AWS?
docs.content:
### How much does observability cost on AWS?

For details on CloudWatch, Kinesis Data Firehose, and overall AWS spend management, see [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview).

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
# Synthetic Tests

A synthetic test runs your script on a schedule from AWS CloudWatch Synthetics in your own account and alerts you when a run fails. Where an [uptime check](/observability/uptime-checks) asks "does the endpoint respond?", a synthetic test verifies a whole flow: sign-in, checkout, a multi-step API sequence with assertions.

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
## When to use

Write a synthetic test for the handful of flows whose breakage costs you customers — typically sign-up, sign-in, and payment. One browser test per critical flow in production is the sweet spot; each additional test adds real monthly cost (see below).

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
## When NOT to use

- **"Is it up?"** — an [uptime check](/observability/uptime-checks) answers that for a fraction of the cost.
- **Pre-deploy verification** — synthetic tests monitor continuously; they don't gate deployments.
- **Load testing** — one run at a time, on a schedule.

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
## Configuration

```yaml
resources:
  checkoutFlow:
    type: synthetic-test
    properties:
      test:
        type: browser
        properties:
          scriptPath: ./e2e/checkout.canary.ts
      scheduleRate: rate(15 minutes) # default rate(5 minutes)
      timeoutSeconds: 60 # default 60
      memory: 1024 # default 1024
      environment:
        - name: BASE_URL
          value: https://app.example.com
      notificationChannels:
        - type: console-channel
          properties:
            channelName: on-call-slack
```

`test.type` is `browser` (drives a real Chromium browser with [Playwright](https://playwright.dev)) or `api` (HTTP calls with per-step timing; no browser, so runs are faster and cheaper).

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
## Failure alerts

Stacktape creates a CloudWatch alarm on the test's success rate. One failed run trips it; the next passing run resolves it. Between runs the alarm holds its last real state — a failing test on a sparse schedule stays failing until a run actually passes, and a new test's first passing run does not announce a recovery. With `notificationChannels` configured, both events are delivered like [alarm](/observability/alarms) notifications — including `console-channel` references — and appear in the Console's Sent alerts. Only actual failing runs alarm; a canary that stops running entirely does not page (its state is visible on the Synthetics page).

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
## Cost

CloudWatch Synthetics charges ~$0.0012 per run (first 100 runs each month are free), plus the underlying Lambda, S3 and CloudWatch Logs usage. A browser test at `rate(5 minutes)` runs ~8,900 times a month — roughly $11 in run charges and $15–20 all-in. An `api` test runs shorter and lands closer to $11–13. Slower schedules cost proportionally less: `rate(15 minutes)` is about a third of that.

docs.title: Synthetic Tests
docs.content:
## Limits

- Schedules between `rate(1 minute)` and `rate(1 hour)`, or a six-field `cron(...)` expression. For cron schedules, AWS rejects a timeout longer than the gap between runs.
- Run timeout between 3 and 840 seconds, never above the schedule interval.
- The bundled script must stay under 250 KB, and all of a stack's bundled scripts together under 600 KB — they ship inside the CloudFormation template.
- Environment variable names must start with a letter, use only letters, digits and `_`, and avoid the reserved `AWS_`/Lambda runtime names; all variables together must stay under 4 KB.
- Memory between 960 and 3008 MB (multiples of 64).
- Synthetic tests are skipped in [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview).
- Renaming a synthetic test replaces its canary, and the run history starts over.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
# Tracing

Tracing records the path of a request through your application: every operation it triggered — handler execution, SQL queries, HTTP calls to other services — how long each took, and where it failed. Stacktape instruments your functions with [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/) automatically; you enable it with one config property and deploy. Traces are stored in your own AWS account using X-Ray Transaction Search and explored on the Console's **Traces** page.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## When to use

Turn tracing on when you need to answer "why was this request slow?" or "where did this request fail?" — questions logs alone answer poorly because the evidence is scattered across services. Sampling makes it affordable to keep on permanently in production.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## When NOT to use

- **Counting and alerting on failures** — use [alarms](/observability/alarms) on error-rate metrics; traces explain individual requests, they don't aggregate.
- **Reading application output** — use [logs](/observability/logs). Spans record timing and structure, not your log lines.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## Configuration

Enable tracing stack-wide in `stackConfig`:

```yaml
stackConfig:
  tracing:
    enabled: true
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
```

Every `function` resource in the stack is instrumented (server functions nested inside web-framework resources like `nextjs-web` are not instrumented yet). Individual functions can override the stack default with their own `tracing` property:

```yaml
stackConfig:
  tracing:
    enabled: true
    samplingRate: 0.2
resources:
  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      # this function records every request regardless of the stack-wide sampling
      tracing:
        samplingRate: 1
  housekeeping:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/housekeeping.ts
      # opt this function out entirely
      tracing: false
```

`tracing` on a function accepts `false` (opt out), `true` (opt in with stack-wide sampling), or an object with its own `enabled` and `samplingRate`. A function without the property inherits the stack default.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
### Sampling

`samplingRate` is the fraction of requests to trace, between 0 and 1 (default 1 — every request). Keep it at 1 while traffic is small; lower it as traffic grows to control span-storage cost. Sampling is parent-based: once a request is sampled, every service it touches records its part, so distributed traces stay complete.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## What gets instrumented

For Node.js functions, Stacktape bundles a slim OpenTelemetry runtime directly into the function's code and wraps the handler at the bundle entry — no code changes on your side. This works identically for ESM and CJS output (ESM stays the default), instruments HTTP and `fetch` calls out of the box, and starts in a fraction of the time the AWS-managed layer needs. Spans are handed to the X-Ray daemon over UDP, so exporting adds no measurable latency to your invocations.

Python 3.10–3.13, Java 11/17/21, and .NET 8 functions are instrumented with the AWS-managed OpenTelemetry layer instead. A traced function on any other runtime is skipped with a deploy-time warning instead of failing the deployment; a layer-instrumented function is also skipped when it already uses a conflicting `AWS_LAMBDA_EXEC_WRAPPER` or a manually attached OpenTelemetry layer.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
### Container services

For a traced [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), private service, worker service, or multi-container workload, Stacktape adds an OpenTelemetry collector as an extra container in the task and points every container's OpenTelemetry SDK at it (`http://localhost:4318`) through standard `OTEL_*` environment variables. The application needs the OpenTelemetry SDK — any language works, and spans the SDK emits reach the collector without further configuration. Automatic zero-code instrumentation for containers is planned.

The collector is non-essential, hard-capped at 256 MB of the task's memory, and given a low CPU weight (128 shares): if it fails or exceeds its memory limit, it is killed and the application keeps running with tracing degraded. Small tasks (512 MB) get noticeably tighter with tracing enabled — consider one memory size up. EC2-based workloads (with `instanceTypes`) are not supported — their bridge networking cannot reach a sidecar on localhost — and are skipped with a warning.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
### Environment variables

Stacktape manages `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER`, `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG`, and the `stacktape.*` keys of `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` — values you set for these are overridden (with a warning), because the Console relies on them to attribute traces to projects and stages. Other OpenTelemetry variables are yours to override per function: `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` renames the service shown in trace views, and any `OTEL_*` variable you set wins over the Stacktape default.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## Account-level effects

The first deploy with tracing enabled switches on **X-Ray Transaction Search** for the whole AWS account and region. This is an account-level AWS setting, not a per-stack one:

- Spans from **all** X-Ray-instrumented workloads in the account — Stacktape-managed or not — are then stored in the `aws/spans` CloudWatch Logs log group.
- X-Ray creates the `aws/spans` log group with a 30-day retention, so spans are kept for 30 days. Stacktape does not change a retention that is already set; you can change it in CloudWatch Logs. Should X-Ray create the group without a retention, Stacktape sets the same 30 days instead of CloudWatch's default of keeping logs forever. An already-enabled Transaction Search setup is left exactly as found.
- Deleting the stack does **not** switch Transaction Search back off, because other workloads may rely on it.
- AWS takes several minutes to activate Transaction Search. The first deploy does not wait for it, so spans sent in those first minutes are not stored.

Span storage is priced by AWS at roughly $0.35 per GB ingested (plus CloudWatch Logs storage), and searching traces runs CloudWatch Logs Insights queries, which AWS bills by data scanned. With sampling and typical span sizes this is small; watch it on high-traffic stacks with `samplingRate: 1`.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## Viewing traces

The Console's **Traces** page searches recent traces per AWS account and region: filter by operation or service name, errors only, and time window. Opening a trace shows the waterfall — every span with per-service colors and timing — and each span's full attributes.

Because the `aws/spans` log group mixes spans from every project in the account, the Traces page requires an organization membership that is not limited to specific projects.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.content:
## Limits

- Tracing is skipped in [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview).
- AWS Lambda allows at most 5 layers per function; the tracing layer counts toward that limit.
- Very recent traces can take a minute or two to appear after the request runs.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
# Uptime Checks

Uptime checks probe your HTTP endpoints from multiple AWS regions and alert you when an endpoint stops responding successfully. The probes run inside your own AWS account — Stacktape provisions a small prober Lambda in each monitoring region, so there is no external monitoring vendor and no per-check subscription fee. The Console shows live status, availability and latency history, and an incident timeline for every check.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
## When to use

Add an uptime check to every public endpoint whose downtime you want to hear about before your users do: production APIs, customer-facing web apps, and webhook receivers. Checks are cheap (a few Lambda invocations per minute), so the practical default is one check per public-facing service in every production stage.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
## When NOT to use

- **Verifying business logic** — an uptime check asserts that an endpoint responds; it does not run flows like sign-in or checkout. Use a [synthetic test](/observability/synthetic-tests) for that.
- **Monitoring internal-only services** — probers reach endpoints over the public internet. A VPC-internal service is not reachable.
- **Catching application errors** — [error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) groups runtime errors from logs; an endpoint can serve 200s while a background job fails.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
## Configuration

An uptime check is a standalone resource. The only required property is `url`:

```yaml
resources:
  apiHealth:
    type: uptime-check
    properties:
      url: https://api.example.com/health
```

A full example with assertions, evaluation thresholds, and notifications:

```yaml
resources:
  apiHealth:
    type: uptime-check
    properties:
      url: https://api.example.com/health
      method: GET # GET or HEAD, default GET
      intervalSeconds: 60 # 30 or 60, default 60
      timeoutSeconds: 10 # default 10
      followRedirects: true # default true
      assertions:
        - type: status-code
          properties:
            accepted: [200, 204]
        - type: body-contains
          properties:
            value: '"status":"ok"'
      evaluation:
        consecutiveFailures: 3 # default 2
        consecutiveSuccesses: 2 # default 2
      regions: [eu-west-1, us-east-1, ap-southeast-1]
      notificationChannels:
        - type: console-channel
          properties:
            channelName: on-call-slack
```

Without `assertions`, a probe succeeds when the response status is 2xx or 3xx. Without `regions`, Stacktape probes from three regions: the stack's region plus two distant ones.

`notificationChannels` accepts inline channel definitions (Slack, MS Teams, Discord, email, webhook) or `console-channel` references to channels managed in the [Console](/observability/alert-channels). Without any channel, incidents still appear in the Console but nothing is delivered.

Set `enabled: false` to pause a check without deleting its history.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
## How it works

- On deploy, Stacktape provisions one shared prober Lambda per monitoring region in your account and stores each check's definition there. Probes run every 30 or 60 seconds.
- A check is marked down only when a quorum of regions (at least two, when the check probes from two or more) is failing at the same time — a region counts as failing for up to ten minutes after its last failing report — and the failure has persisted for `consecutiveFailures` consecutive evaluations. This prevents alerts from single-region network blips.
- Recovery follows the same rule symmetrically: `consecutiveSuccesses` consecutive successful evaluations.
- Down and recovery events open and resolve incidents, deliver to your notification channels, and are retried on delivery failure.
- If probing itself stops reporting (for example, the prober was deleted manually), the Console raises a monitoring-silent incident so a dead monitor never masquerades as a healthy endpoint.

Deleting the stack (or the check) removes the check's probing; the shared prober infrastructure stays idle in the account and costs nothing meaningful.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
## Limits

- Probed methods are `GET` and `HEAD`. Checks with request bodies are not supported.
- At most 100 uptime checks per stack, and at most 5 regions per check. A region's shared prober has a bounded probing budget per minute — with many slow or timing-out endpoints in one region (across all stacks), some probes can be skipped for that tick; keep high-`timeoutSeconds` checks few. A probe that cannot get its full configured timeout is dropped rather than reported as down, and a check that stops getting probed entirely raises a monitoring-silent alert.
- Response bodies are read up to 512 KB for `body-contains` assertions; the asserted text itself is capped at 2000 characters.
- Uptime checks are skipped in [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) — ephemeral dev stacks would only produce noise.

docs.title: Uptime Checks
docs.content:
## Viewing results

The Console's **Uptime** page lists every check with its live status. Opening a check shows availability and latency history per region and the incident timeline.

docs.title: Buildpack for Containers
docs.content:
# Buildpack for Containers

The `buildpack` packaging type (`BuildpackImagePackaging`) builds a container image from a project directory without a Dockerfile. Stacktape detects the language, framework, package manager, tool versions and start command from the project's own files, builds the image and uploads it to a managed ECR repository.

Detection and the build plan come from [Railpack](https://railpack.com), an open-source builder by Railway. Stacktape runs it for you; you do not install or configure it.

It applies to [web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [private services](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service), [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload), [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) and [AgentCore runtimes](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime).

docs.title: Buildpack for Containers
docs.content:
## When to use

Use `buildpack` when:
