docs.title: Billing and Subscription
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
docs.content:
### How does Stacktape pricing work?

Stacktape charges based on the AWS infrastructure costs it manages for you — not per seat, per deployment, or per request. The Free plan covers up to $100/month of managed AWS costs with no fee. The Flexible plan is priced as a percentage of managed AWS costs, with rate tiers shown on the Subscription Plans page, and includes unlimited deployments and stacks. Enterprise pricing is custom.

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
docs.content:
### What counts as "managed AWS costs"?

Managed AWS costs are costs for AWS infrastructure that Stacktape manages through your stacks. Stacktape does not charge for other AWS resources in your account that exist outside Stacktape-managed stacks.

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
headingPath: Who can manage billing in my organization?
docs.content:
### Who can manage billing in my organization?

Users with the `org:manage-billing` permission see the upgrade and downgrade controls on the Subscription Plans page. Payment management controls on the Billing page appear only when you have this permission. Users without this permission can still view both pages (except Viewers, who are redirected). See [team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for role management.

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
headingPath: What happens if I exceed the Free plan's $100/month limit?
docs.content:
### What happens if I exceed the Free plan's $100/month limit?

Deploys pause. Stacktape refuses new deploys and `stacktape dev` sessions of the organization until it upgrades to the Flexible plan or the next calendar month starts. Your running infrastructure is not touched, and deleting or rolling back stages still works. See [Free plan cost limit](#free-plan-cost-limit).

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
headingPath: Can I downgrade from Flexible to Free?
docs.content:
### Can I downgrade from Flexible to Free?

Yes. Open the Subscription Plans page and click **Downgrade to FREE** under the Free plan card. This calls the Console's cancellation flow and refreshes your organization data on success. You need the `org:manage-billing` permission to see the button.

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
headingPath: How do I get Enterprise pricing?
docs.content:
### How do I get Enterprise pricing?

On the Subscription Plans page, click the schedule-meeting button under the Enterprise plan card. This connects you with the Stacktape team to discuss custom pricing, SSO, SOC 2 compliance, and premium support options.

docs.title: Billing and Subscription
headingPath: Where can I find my invoices?
docs.content:
### Where can I find my invoices?

Open the Billing page in the Stacktape Console. It shows billing details, an invoices list, and a Paddle checkout container. Users with the VIEWER role cannot access this page.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
# Connecting Your AWS Account

Stacktape deploys infrastructure into your own AWS account using a secure cross-account IAM role. You connect an AWS account once in the Stacktape Console, and Stacktape handles credential management from that point — no manual AWS access keys required. Your projects and stacks can be deployed to any region.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
## Overview

The **AWS accounts** page (`/aws-accounts`) in the Stacktape Console lets you establish and manage the trust relationship between Stacktape and your AWS accounts. When you connect an account, Stacktape generates a link to an AWS CloudFormation Quick Create Stack page. The CloudFormation stack creates a cross-account IAM role that Stacktape assumes to interact with your AWS account — perform deployments, list logs, fetch metrics, and manage resources on your behalf. Credentials are temporary and short-lived — no permanent AWS access keys are stored or exchanged.

Each connected account appears in a table showing its name, AWS account ID, connection status, creation date, and primary regions. You can connect multiple AWS accounts to a single organization — for example, separate accounts for production and development.

Connecting your account is free. You only pay for the AWS resources that Stacktape deploys into your account. For a detailed breakdown of what permissions the cross-account role includes, see [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions).

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
## Walkthrough

You need the `org:manage-aws-accounts` permission in your Stacktape organization to connect an account.

1. **Open the modal** — In the Stacktape Console, open `/aws-accounts` and click **Connect AWS account**.
2. **Name the account** — Enter a label for the connection (e.g. "production" or "dev-account"). This name is for your reference only — the Console pre-fills a default like `aws-account-1`.
3. **Create the connection stack in AWS** — Click **Connect account in AWS console**. This opens the generated AWS connection link in a new tab. The modal shows an image of the AWS-side steps to follow.
4. **Wait for activation** — Return to the Stacktape Console. A newly created connection can appear as PENDING until the AWS CloudFormation stack finishes. While a PENDING account exists, the Console refetches account data every two seconds. When the backend returns the account as ACTIVE, the table shows ACTIVE.

> **Warning:** The connection CloudFormation stack must be created in the **eu-west-1** region. The Console opens a generated AWS link that targets the correct region. Your projects and stacks can be deployed to **any** region.

The connection modal contains two steps: an account name input field (Step 1) and an image illustrating the AWS-side steps to follow when creating the CloudFormation connection stack (Step 2).

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
## Connection States

Each connected AWS account has one of three states:

| State | Meaning | Action needed |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| **ACTIVE** (green) | Connection is working. Stacktape can deploy to this account. | None. |
| **PENDING** (orange) | The connection link was generated but the CloudFormation stack hasn't finished creating. | Use the "Finish the account connection" link shown in the Note column to complete stack creation in AWS. |
| **BLOCKED** (red) | The connection failed or was revoked. The status reason explains why. | Check the status reason in the Note column, fix the issue in AWS, and reconnect if needed. |

While a PENDING account exists on the AWS accounts page, the Console refetches account data every two seconds. When the backend returns the account as ACTIVE, the table shows ACTIVE.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content: ## Common Tasks

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
### Connecting multiple AWS accounts

Organizations commonly connect separate AWS accounts for different purposes — a production account with stricter controls and a development account for experimentation. Click **Connect AWS account** again and repeat the walkthrough for each additional account. Each connection is created through its own generated AWS CloudFormation flow.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Choosing the account for a CLI command
docs.content:
### Choosing the account for a CLI command

CLI commands that work with a deployed stack, such as `deploy`, `delete` and `rollback`, run in one connected account. The CLI picks it in this order:

1. `--aws-account <name>`, the account's name in the Console.
2. The account your local AWS credentials belong to: `--profile`, then `AWS_PROFILE`, then `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in the environment. The CLI reads the account ID from the profile's `sso_account_id` or `role_arn` when it can, and otherwise asks AWS STS.
3. The default saved with [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure).
4. Your organization's only connected account.

If the local credentials belong to an account that is not connected, the command stops before it changes anything and lists the connected accounts. It also stops when their account cannot be determined, for example when an SSO session has expired, and when a profile and environment keys point to different accounts. To deploy anyway, pass `--aws-account`, unset the profile, or connect the account.

`--aws-account` takes precedence over a profile; the CLI prints a line saying the profile is ignored. AWS credentials in environment variables are still used for the deployment when they are set, so they must belong to the selected account.

Each of these commands prints the account it uses, for example `AWS credentials loaded via Stacktape for account production (222222222222)`.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
### Revoking access

You can revoke Stacktape's access to your AWS account in two ways:

- **Delete the AWS account connection in the Stacktape Console** — removes the connection from Stacktape's side.
- **Delete the CloudFormation connection stack in the AWS Console** — removes the IAM role from your AWS account. If Stacktape later reports the connection as BLOCKED, check the status reason in the Note column.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Checking which regions an account uses
docs.content:
### Checking which regions an account uses

The AWS accounts table shows **Primary regions** for each connected account. The table displays the account's primary regions when checked, or "not checked" if regions haven't been evaluated yet. The connection modal also states that projects and stacks can be deployed to any region.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
### Account stuck in PENDING

If your account remains in PENDING state:

1. Use the **Finish the account connection** link in the Note column to reopen the generated AWS CloudFormation flow. If AWS reports a stack creation failure, inspect the failure in the AWS CloudFormation console.
2. Verify the stack is being created in the **eu-west-1** region — the Console's generated link targets the correct region automatically.
3. Users with the `org:manage-aws-accounts` permission see a delete control on connected-account rows. If you cannot complete the AWS-side stack, delete the account entry and start a new connection.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Cannot delete a connected AWS account
docs.content:
### Cannot delete a connected AWS account

Stacktape prevents deletion when projects reference the account in their GitOps deployment configurations. The error message lists the affected projects. Delete the GitOps deployment configurations from the listed projects, then retry the deletion.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
### Account shows BLOCKED

A BLOCKED state means the connection is no longer usable. Read the status reason in the Note column — for example, the IAM role may have been modified or removed. Fix the underlying issue in AWS. You can remove the Stacktape-side connection from the table if you need to recreate it.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: "You do not have permission to manage AWS accounts"
docs.content:
### "You do not have permission to manage AWS accounts"

This action requires the `org:manage-aws-accounts` permission. Ask your organization owner or admin to grant you the appropriate role. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for details.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content:
## Related Features

- [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions) — details on what the cross-account role can do
- [Organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) — how connected accounts relate to your project structure
- [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) — auto-deploy to connected accounts on push
- [Deploy your first stage](/getting-started/deploy-your-first-stage) — uses a connected account to run your first deployment

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Do I need to create AWS access keys for Stacktape?
docs.content:
### Do I need to create AWS access keys for Stacktape?

No. Stacktape uses cross-account IAM role assumption, not static access keys. The connection CloudFormation stack creates an IAM role that Stacktape assumes with temporary credentials. You never need to generate, rotate, or store AWS access keys for Stacktape to work.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Can I deploy to any AWS region after connecting?
docs.content:
### Can I deploy to any AWS region after connecting?

Yes. The connection stack must be created in `eu-west-1`, but that only controls where the connection CloudFormation stack is created. Your projects and stacks can be deployed to any region.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Is connecting my AWS account free?
docs.content:
### Is connecting my AWS account free?

Connecting the account is free. You pay only for the AWS resources that Stacktape later deploys into your account.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: How do I revoke Stacktape's access to my AWS account?
docs.content:
### How do I revoke Stacktape's access to my AWS account?

You have two options: delete the AWS account connection in the Stacktape Console (removes it from Stacktape's side), or delete the CloudFormation connection stack in the AWS Console (removes the IAM role from your account). Either one stops deployments to that account from working. After deleting the stack in AWS, Stacktape reports the connection as BLOCKED — remove it from the AWS accounts table and create a new connection to restore access.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Why is the "Connect AWS account" button disabled?
docs.content:
### Why is the "Connect AWS account" button disabled?

Connecting and deleting account connections requires the `org:manage-aws-accounts` permission. If the button (or the delete control on a connected-account row) is disabled, you don't currently have that organization permission. Ask your organization owner or admin to grant the appropriate role — see [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Why won't my account stay connected (stuck in PENDING)?
docs.content:
### Why won't my account stay connected (stuck in PENDING)?

PENDING means the connection link was generated but the CloudFormation stack in AWS hasn't finished creating. The Console refetches the account every two seconds and flips it to ACTIVE automatically once the backend reports it. If it stays PENDING, use the "Finish the account connection" link in the Note column to reopen the AWS flow, and verify the stack is being created in the **eu-west-1** region.

docs.title: Connecting Your AWS Account
headingPath: Why can't I delete a connected AWS account?
docs.content:
### Why can't I delete a connected AWS account?

Stacktape blocks deletion when projects reference the account in their GitOps deployment configurations; the error message lists the affected projects. Remove the GitOps deployment configurations from those projects, then retry the deletion.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
# Console Overview

The Stacktape Console is a web application for the organizations, projects and stages you deploy with Stacktape. It shows deployment activity, incidents, logs, metrics, traces, error tracking, security findings and AWS costs, and it manages members, alert channels, budgets, secrets, SSM parameters, AWS account connections and domains.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
## What the Console does

Projects represent your applications, typically one per Git repository. Each project can have multiple stages (isolated deployments such as `production`, `staging` or `dev`), each with its own resources. A stage is deployed from a Stacktape configuration that describes which resources to create.

From the Console you can:

- Review deployment activity and AWS costs across projects and stages
- Respond to [incidents](/observability/incidents), which group signals such as a failing uptime check, a firing alarm or a new error in a production stage
- Read [logs](/observability/logs), [metrics](/observability/metrics) and [traces](/observability/tracing), and see the state of [uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) and [synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests)
- Triage runtime errors on the [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) page
- Review security findings from each deployment and set [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) that are enforced on every deployment
- Create [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels), [notification rules](/observability/notifications) and [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets), and check delivery in [Alert history](/observability/alert-history)
- Manage sensitive values in AWS Secrets Manager and configuration values in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
- Connect [AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) and [custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
- Manage [members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) with role-based access control

The Console complements the [Stacktape CLI](/cli/deploy). You deploy with [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy), and [Git provider connections](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) can deploy automatically from your repositories. Alarms, uptime checks and synthetic tests are defined in the Stacktape configuration and go live when the stack is deployed. The Activity page lists recorded CLI operations: deploys, deletes, scripts, bucket syncs and other commands.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
## Console navigation

The sidebar starts with Overview and Incidents, followed by five groups. Some items appear only when your role has the required permission; see [Permission-gated navigation](#permission-gated-navigation). Incidents, Error tracking, Posture, Vulnerabilities and Alarms show a count badge when there is something to look at.

| Group | Pages | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| **Top** | Overview, Incidents | Default dashboard and the [incident](/observability/incidents) queue |
| **Organization** | Projects, Runners, Activity, Members, Costs | Projects and stages, the EC2 runners that run Git deploys and GitHub Actions jobs, CLI operation history, [members and roles](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control), [cost tracking](/managing-costs/dashboards) |
| **Observability** | Logs, Metrics, Traces, Uptime, Synthetics, Error tracking | [Logs](/observability/logs), [metrics](/observability/metrics), [traces](/observability/tracing), [uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks), [synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests), [runtime errors](/observability/error-tracking) |
| **Security** | Overview, Posture, Vulnerabilities, Exposure, Guardrails | Security score per stack, configuration findings, vulnerable packages, what the internet can reach, [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) |
| **Alerting** | Channels, Sent alerts, Alarms, Budgets | [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) and their [notification rules](/observability/notifications), [sent alerts](/observability/alert-history), [alarm state](/observability/alarms), [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets) (All budgets and History) |
| **Configuration** | Secrets, SSM parameters, AWS accounts, Domains | [Secrets](/configuration/secrets), SSM parameters, [AWS account connections](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), [custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains) |

The profile menu in the header opens Account (your account settings), API keys, Subscription plans, Billing, Third-party providers and Git connections.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
## The Overview route

The Overview page (`/overview`) is the Console's default route for the selected organization. Use the sidebar to open the detailed pages, such as Projects, Incidents, Costs or Error tracking.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
## Getting started

This walkthrough covers the path from first login to viewing a deployed stage.

1. **Sign in.** The Console opens on the Overview page (`/overview`).
2. **Connect an AWS account.** Open **AWS accounts** in the Configuration group and click **Connect AWS account**. Stacktape uses a cross-account IAM role, so you do not manage AWS credentials yourself. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account).
3. **Deploy a stage.** Run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy), or connect a Git provider from **Git connections** in the profile menu and set up [GitOps](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) for push-to-deploy.
4. **View your stage.** Open **Projects** in the Organization group and select your project to see its stages and deployment activity.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content: ## Common tasks

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Viewing deployment activity

Open **Activity** in the Organization group. The page lists Stacktape CLI operations across your organization, so you can see who ran deploys, deletes, scripts, bucket syncs and other recorded commands.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Managing secrets

Open **Secrets** in the Configuration group to manage sensitive values stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Secrets created here can be referenced in your Stacktape configuration. The page requires the `secrets:view` permission. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets).

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Managing SSM parameters

Open **SSM parameters** in the Configuration group to manage values stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use parameters for non-sensitive configuration your workloads need at runtime, such as feature flags or endpoint URLs. Click **New parameter** to add one. The page requires the `ssm-params:view` permission.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Setting up alarms

Alarms are defined in the Stacktape configuration, in the `alarms` list of a resource, and are created when the stack is deployed. The **Alarms** page in the Alerting group shows the current state of the CloudWatch alarms in your connected AWS accounts. See [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

Alarm rules created in the Console earlier are legacy. They are listed under **Legacy alarm rules** on the Alarms page and keep applying to matching deployments until the stack's configuration defines its alarms. Run `stacktape alarm export` to move them into your configuration.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Tracking runtime errors

The **Error tracking** page in the Observability group is an error inbox for your deployed workloads. Stacktape reads runtime errors from your logs and groups repeated occurrences into one entry per distinct error and resource. Error tracking is on for every stage by default; a stack turns it off or limits it to some stages with `deploymentConfig.errorTracking`. The page requires the `issues:view` permission. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Inviting members

Open **Members** in the Organization group and click **Invite member**. Each member has a role that determines what they can view and change. The page requires the `members:view` permission. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Setting budgets

Open **Budgets** in the Alerting group and click **New budget alert**. Each budget monitors one connected AWS account for the calendar month. Stacktape creates the AWS budget when you save it and removes it when you delete the alert. **History** under Budgets lists the budget alerts that were sent. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: Configuring alert channels and notification rules
docs.content:
### Configuring alert channels and notification rules

Channels are the destinations where alerts are delivered, such as a Slack channel, an email address or a webhook. Open **Channels** in the Alerting group and click **New alert channel**. The new channel's page opens; click **New rule** there to choose which events (for example a failed deployment, an opened incident or a changed secret) it receives. Adding rules requires the `org:manage-notifications` permission. **Sent alerts** lists every alert that was sent and its delivery status per channel.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
## Permission-gated navigation

The Console uses role-based access control. Sidebar items are hidden when your role lacks the required permission:

| Navigation item | Required permission |
|---|---|
| Incidents | `incidents:view` |
| Members | `members:view` |
| Costs | `org:view-billing` |
| Error tracking | `issues:view` |
| Security group (Overview, Posture, Vulnerabilities, Exposure, Guardrails) | `security:view` |
| Alarms | `org:manage-alarms` |
| Budgets | `org:manage-budgets` |
| Secrets | `secrets:view` |
| SSM parameters | `ssm-params:view` |
| Domains | `domains:manage` |

Overview, Projects, Runners, Activity, Logs, Metrics, Traces, Uptime, Synthetics, Channels, Sent alerts and AWS accounts are not filtered by permission in the sidebar. Every role that sees the Security group can read Guardrails; only owners and admins (`org:manage-guardrails`) can change them.


> **Warning:** If a sidebar item is missing, your role may not include the required permission. Ask your organization's owner or admin to adjust your access. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for role details.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Cost data is not appearing

Cost reports are generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports and may take up to a day to appear. If the Costs page shows no data, check that you have a connected [AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) and allow up to 24 hours for data to arrive.

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: An alarm does not exist in AWS
docs.content:
### An alarm does not exist in AWS

Alarms are created when the stack is deployed. After you add an alarm to a resource's `alarms` list, run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) for the target stage. Legacy Console alarm rules also take effect only on the next deployment of each matching stage.

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: The Error tracking page is empty despite errors in logs
docs.content:
### The Error tracking page is empty despite errors in logs

A stack reports errors only after it has been deployed with Stacktape v4, because the log subscriptions are added during deployment. Click **Settings** on the Error tracking page to open **Error tracking settings**: it shows whether error tracking is on for the organization and lists each deployed stack with whether its last deployment wired error tracking. Also check that the stack's `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` does not turn it off for that stage, and that the resource does not use `logging.logClass: infrequent-access`. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Sidebar items are missing

Some sidebar items are permission-gated. If you don't see an item (for example, Costs or Alarms), your role may not include the required permission. See the [permission-gated navigation](#permission-gated-navigation) table or ask your organization admin.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
## Related features

- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): required before any deployment
- [Organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages): how the Console organizes your work
- [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys): authenticate from the CLI and CI/CD
- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): invite members and manage roles
- [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription): subscription details
- [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console): deploy on push
- [Observability overview](/observability/overview): incidents, alarms, error tracking and notifications in depth

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: Do I need the Console to use Stacktape?
docs.content:
### Do I need the Console to use Stacktape?

No. [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) let you authenticate with Stacktape from the CLI or CI/CD pipelines, and `stacktape deploy` does the deploying. The Console adds member access, cost visibility, incidents, error tracking, security findings, budgets and guardrails on top. Most teams use both: the CLI (directly or through GitOps) for deploying, and the Console for visibility and operational control.

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?
docs.content:
### Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?

Yes. Stacktape uses a cross-account IAM role to manage resources in your AWS account, so you never hand over long-lived AWS credentials. Connect more accounts from **AWS accounts** in the Configuration group. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for the required role.

docs.title: Console Overview
docs.content:
### Where do I configure alarms?

In the Stacktape configuration, in the `alarms` list of each resource. The alarms are created when the stack is deployed. The Console's Alarms page shows their state. Alarm rules created in the Console earlier are listed under **Legacy alarm rules**; export them into your configuration with `stacktape alarm export`.

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: How does Stacktape track AWS costs, and why is the Costs page empty?
docs.content:
### How does Stacktape track AWS costs, and why is the Costs page empty?

The Costs page breaks down AWS costs by project and stage, generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports. New data can take up to a day to appear, so an empty page usually means a recently connected [AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) or reports that haven't arrived yet. See [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview) for budgets and optimization tips.

docs.title: Console Overview
headingPath: Why is a sidebar item missing for me?
docs.content:
### Why is a sidebar item missing for me?

The Console uses role-based access control, and several sidebar items are permission-gated. For example, Members requires `members:view`, Costs requires `org:view-billing`, and Alarms and Budgets require the matching `org:manage-*` permission. If an item is missing, ask your organization's owner or admin to adjust your role. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
# Organizations, Projects, and Stages

The Stacktape Console organizes work into three levels: organizations contain projects, and projects contain stages. A project represents a single application — typically one Git repository. A stage is an isolated deployment of that project (such as production, staging, or dev), with its own databases, functions, containers, and networking.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
## How the hierarchy works

The Console structures work in three nested levels. An organization sits at the top and contains projects. Each project contains stages — isolated deployments of that application.

1. **Organization** — groups projects, team members, and settings
2. **Project** — one application, usually one Git repository
3. **Stage** — an isolated deployment (production, staging, dev)

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Organizations

An organization groups related projects, team members, and settings. In the Console, everything you see is scoped to the currently selected organization — projects, costs, alarms, and team settings all belong to the active organization. Switching organizations shows a different set of projects.

An organization's setup commands run before every deployment on a build runner, for every project.

You can manage organizations from the CLI with [`stacktape org create`](/cli/org-create) and [`stacktape org list`](/cli/org-list).

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Projects

A Stacktape project represents a single application and usually maps 1:1 to a Git repository. Each project can have multiple stages — fully isolated deployments like `production`, `staging`, or `dev`.

The Projects page lists all projects in the selected organization. Each project card shows:

- **Project name** and connected Git URL (if any)
- **Number of deployed stages** — hovering the stage badge shows counts for alarming alarms, running stages, deployments in progress, errored stages, and not-yet-deployed stages
- **Last deployment time** (displayed as a relative timestamp like "2 hours ago")
- **Current month's cost** with a trend label. When previous-month cost is greater than zero, the label is a percentage change or `Flat`; otherwise it shows `No spend` or `New spend`

Projects are sorted by most recently updated stage, so active projects appear first. A filter input at the top narrows results by project name or Git URL using fuzzy search.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Stages

A stage is a running deployment of a project — a complete, isolated set of AWS resources. Common stage names include `production`, `staging`, `dev`, or `testing`. Stages are fully isolated and do not share resources with each other; examples include containers, functions, databases, and other deployed resources.

To deploy a stage, you need a Stacktape configuration that describes which resources (containers, functions, databases, etc.) to deploy. You can share the same Stacktape configuration across all stages of a project (most common), or maintain separate configurations per stage when environments need different resource shapes.


> **Info:** Stages are sometimes called "environments" in other tools. Stacktape uses "stage" as the canonical term, but they mean the same thing — an isolated deployment of your project. See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments) for configuration patterns.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content: ## Getting started

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Step 1 — Create a project

Projects start in the CLI. Run [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) in your repository; the first deploy creates the project, and it appears in the Console. **New project** in the Console shows these commands and opens the project once its first deployment starts.

You can also create an empty project with [`stacktape project create`](/cli/project-create).

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Step 2 — Create a stage

Inside the project view, click the **New stage** button in the left sidebar to open the stage creation form.

Once a stage is created, clicking it in the sidebar navigates to the deployment setup. If the project has a connected Git repository, the Console routes to `/projects/{project}/create-new-stage/{stage}`. If no Git repository is connected, the Console routes to `/projects/{project}/create-new-stage-using-cli/{stage}` instead.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Step 3 — Deploy

Use [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) for CLI deployment — see that page for required options — or trigger a deployment through [GitOps](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

```bash
stacktape deploy --project my-app --stage production --region eu-west-1
```

Once a stage has been deployed, clicking it in the sidebar navigates to that stage's overview route (`/projects/{project}/{stage}/overview`). The project details query refetches every 6 seconds except on the create-new-stage page, so deployment status updates while the page is open.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
## Common tasks

The Console provides shortcuts for day-to-day project management directly from the Projects page and the project overview sidebar.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Filtering and finding projects

On the Projects page, use the filter input to search by project name or Git URL. The fuzzy search narrows results as you type. Projects are sorted by the most recently deployed stage, so active projects appear first. When no projects exist yet, the page displays "No projects created yet." The **Create new project** button remains available in the page header.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Viewing stage details

Click a project card to open the project view. The left sidebar orders entries as: operation-only stages (in-progress or recently failed deployments), saved undeployed stages, deployed stages, and undeployed names without saved records. Dev-mode stacks are sorted after regular deployed stages within the deployed-stage portion. Clicking a deployed stage navigates to that stage's overview route (`/projects/{project}/{stage}/overview`).

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Configuring build runners

The **Runners** page lists the build runner of each project. Its **Setup commands** button opens the commands that
every project's deployments run before building; owners and admins (the `org:manage-runner-settings` permission) edit
them there. Each runner's **Settings** tab holds the project's own instance size, build cache limit, idle behavior, setup
commands and GitHub Actions settings.

See [Build runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) for details on runner lifecycle, instance sizing, and caching.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Configuring project settings

From the project view, click the gear icon next to the project name to open the settings dropdown. This menu is visible only to users with the `projects:update-settings` permission. Available options depend on your project setup:

| Setting | When visible | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Configure Git deployments** | Git repository connected | Opens the project's Git deployments page — see [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) for setup |
| **Configure Runner** | Always (within settings dropdown) | Opens the project runner configuration modal |
| **Configure GitHub Actions runner** | Git repository connected | Set up a [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners) |
| **Delete project** | User also has `projects:delete` permission | Remove the project from the organization |

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Redeploying a stage

When a redeploy is initiated from the project overview, the Console asks for confirmation of the target commit. After confirmation, the Console navigates to the deployment detail logs page (`/projects/{project}/{stage}/deployment-detail/{invocationId}?tab=logs`) where you can monitor build output. See [Build runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) for runner configuration.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Deleting a stage or project

Deployed stages are deleted from the CLI with [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete) — see that page for exact deletion semantics.

To delete a project, open the project settings dropdown (gear icon next to the project name) and select **Delete project**. The settings dropdown requires the `projects:update-settings` permission, and the **Delete project** option within it is shown only to users who also have the `projects:delete` permission. If the project still has deployed stages, the Console warns that it is advised to delete them before continuing and requires explicit confirmation.


> **Warning:** If a project still has deployed stages when you delete it, the Console warns that it is advised to delete them before continuing and requires explicit confirmation.


Non-deployed stages (created in the Console but never deployed) can be removed directly from the sidebar. This only removes the Console record — no AWS resources are affected because none were created. Failed stage entries can be dismissed from the sidebar; the confirmation says this removes deployment history for that stage.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
## Access control

The Stacktape Console uses roles and permissions to control what team members can do within an organization. Key actions on the Projects and project overview pages are gated by the following permissions:

| Permission | Controls |
|---|---|
| `projects:delete` | Deleting a project (shown inside the project settings dropdown, which requires `projects:update-settings`) |
| `projects:update-settings` | Accessing project settings (Git deployments, runner config, GitHub Actions runner) |
| `deployments:delete-non-production` | Controls delete and dismiss actions on stage entries in the project sidebar |
| `org:manage-runner-settings` | Editing the setup commands every project runs |

Users without the required permission do not see the corresponding UI controls — for example, the project settings gear icon is hidden from users who lack `projects:update-settings`.

For a complete breakdown of roles, how permissions map to roles, and how to invite team members, see [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
## Troubleshooting

Common issues when working with projects and stages in the Console.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Failed stage in the sidebar

If a deployment fails, the stage appears as errored in the sidebar. You can dismiss a failed stage using the context menu on that stage entry. The confirmation says dismissing will remove the deployment history for that stage, then refetches the project and operation lists. If a later deployment succeeds, the stage appears through the normal deployed-stage list.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Non-deployed stages in the sidebar

Stages created in the Console but never deployed appear in the sidebar as not-yet-deployed entries. You can delete these directly from the sidebar. This removes only the Console record — no AWS resources are affected because none were created.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Cost shows $0 for active stage

Cost data comes from AWS Cost and Usage Reports, which are generated daily and may take up to a day to appear. Newly deployed stages may show zero cost until daily report data arrives. When previous-month cost is greater than zero, the trend label shows a percentage change or `Flat`; otherwise it shows `No spend` or `New spend`.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content:
### Git repository not connected

A project created by a CLI deploy has no repository until you connect one. Its page shows "Git repository not connected" with a **Connect** button, which lists the repositories of your connected Git providers. Accepting the CLI's offer to deploy on push after a deploy connects the repository as well. Once connected, the project settings dropdown includes **Configure Git deployments**. Without a repository, new stages are deployed from the CLI.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: What is the difference between a project and a stage in Stacktape?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between a project and a stage in Stacktape?

A project represents a single application, usually mapped to one Git repository. A stage is an isolated deployment of that project — like production, staging, or dev. Each project can have multiple stages, and each stage has its own databases, functions, containers, and networking. Think of projects as "what you're building" and stages as "where it's running."

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: Should I use one configuration per project or one per stage?
docs.content:
### Should I use one configuration per project or one per stage?

Most teams share a single Stacktape configuration across all stages — the same `stacktape.ts` deploys to production, staging, and dev. This keeps environments consistent and reduces configuration drift. Use separate configurations per stage only when environments genuinely need different resource shapes (for example, a smaller database instance in dev). See [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments) for patterns.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: Why does my active stage show $0 cost?
docs.content:
### Why does my active stage show $0 cost?

Cost data comes from AWS Cost and Usage Reports, which are generated daily and may take up to a day to appear. A newly deployed stage will show $0/mo until the first daily report arrives, even if it is already running resources. The project card displays the current month's cost alongside a trend label (`No spend`, `New spend`, a percentage change, or `Flat`).

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: What is the difference between a Stacktape organization and an AWS account?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between a Stacktape organization and an AWS account?

A Stacktape organization is a grouping layer for projects, team members, and settings within the Console. An AWS account is where your actual infrastructure runs. You connect one or more AWS accounts to your Stacktape organization so deployments can create resources in those accounts. The two concepts operate at different layers — the organization controls who can do what in the Console, while the AWS account controls where resources are provisioned. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for setup.

docs.title: Organizations, Projects, and Stages
headingPath: When should I create multiple organizations?
docs.content:
### When should I create multiple organizations?

Create separate organizations when you need distinct team boundaries — for example, separating work between different clients, business units, or teams that should not share projects or settings. Most teams need only one organization. If everyone works on the same set of projects, a single organization with role-based access (see [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control)) is simpler to manage.

docs.content:

- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) — invite members, assign roles, and configure permissions
- [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) — auto-deploy stages when you push to connected branches
- [Stacks per Git branch](/ci-cd-and-gitops/stacks-per-git-branch-pattern) — map branches and PRs to stages dynamically

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
# Team and Access Control

The **Members** page in the Organization group of the Stacktape Console controls who can use your organization and
what they reach. Invite people, choose their role, projects and AWS accounts, require two-factor sign-in, give CI an
organization key that does not belong to a person, and see what stops working before you remove someone.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Overview

The page has up to four parts:

- **Two-factor sign-in** (Owners and Admins): whether members who sign in with a password must also use an
  authenticator app.
- **People**: everyone who has joined, with their role, what a Developer or Viewer reaches, two-factor status, when
  they were last active and when they joined. Search by name or email, filter by role, or show only members without
  two-factor or inactive for 30 days or more.
- **Invitations**: invitations that have not been accepted yet, who sent them, and when they expire.
- **Organization keys** (Owners and Admins): API keys that belong to the organization, for CI.

Click a member's name to open their page. Owners and Admins can open anyone's page; Developers and Viewers can open
their own.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Roles

| Role | Can do | Reaches |
|------|--------|---------|
| Owner | Everything, including deleting the organization, billing and appointing other Owners | Every project and every connected AWS account |
| Admin | Everything except deleting the organization | Every project and every connected AWS account |
| Developer | Deploy, delete non-production stages, manage secrets and parameters | Only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them |
| Viewer | Read projects, deployments, logs, incidents and members | Only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them |

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Project and AWS account access

A Developer or Viewer has two lists, set when you invite them and changed with **Edit access**:

- **Projects** decide which projects they see in the Console and which projects the CLI lets them deploy.
- **AWS accounts** decide where Stacktape gives them AWS access: CLI credentials for deploys, scripts and stack
  commands, deployments started from the Console, and the Console pages that read AWS directly (logs, metrics,
  secrets, parameters, debug sessions, redeploys and rollbacks, Investigate and Fix with AI).


> **Warning:** AWS access always covers the whole account. A Developer given the account `production` for the project `shop` can,
with the credentials the CLI receives, also reach other projects' stacks in `production`. Give a person an account
only if they may act in all of it. Agencies with one AWS account per client get a clean boundary by giving each
person only their clients' accounts.


A Developer with no AWS accounts can still see their projects in the Console, but the CLI refuses to deploy, and the
pages that read AWS say that their access does not include the account. Owners and Admins always reach every account.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Inviting members

1. Open **Members** and click **Invite members**.
2. Enter one or more email addresses, separated by commas or new lines (up to 20 at once).
3. Choose a role. For a Developer or Viewer, choose their projects and AWS accounts.
4. Click **Send invitations**.

Someone who already has a Stacktape account becomes a member at once. Anyone else gets an email and appears under
**Invitations** until they sign up. An address that is already a member, or that could not be invited, stays in the
field with the reason, so the rest are not lost.

An invitation works for 14 days after its email last went out. **Resend invitation** sends it again and starts the
14 days again; an expired invitation can be resent the same way. **Copy invite link** copies the sign-up link to
share another way; it only works for the invited address. **Cancel invitation** stops the link from working.

Personal organizations have exactly one member. To work with others, create a team organization; team organizations
have no member limit.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Organization keys for CI

A personal [API key](/stacktape-console/api-keys) acts as the person who created it and stops working when they leave
the organization. CI that uses one breaks when that person is removed. An organization key belongs to the
organization instead:

1. In **Organization keys**, click **New organization key**.
2. Name it after where it runs, for example `github-actions`.
3. Choose **Developer** with the projects and AWS accounts the pipeline deploys, or **Admin** for everything.
4. Copy the key from the next dialog; it is shown only once. Store it as the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret of your CI.

The list shows who created each key and when it was last used. Revoking a key stops every pipeline that uses it at
once. Organization keys cannot create organizations or connect AI subscriptions, which belong to people.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Requiring two-factor sign-in

Owners and Admins can require two-factor sign-in with **Require** in the Two-factor sign-in row. The confirmation lists
the members who sign in with a password only. After that, those members see only a screen that sends them to
[Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings) to add an authenticator app; the rest of the organization opens
again as soon as they do. Signing in with Google counts as two-factor. API keys, including the CLI and CI, keep
working.

You need two-factor sign-in on your own account before you can require it.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Removing a member

Open the member's row menu, or their page, and choose **Remove**. The dialog lists what stops working with them:

- their personal API keys, with when each was last used,
- their own AI subscriptions for incident runs,
- their Slack link.

If one of their keys was used in the last 7 days, the dialog says so, because CI may depend on it, and offers to
create an organization key first. Stacks they deployed keep running, their deployments stay in the history, and
organization keys keep working, including ones they created.

**Revoke API keys** in the row menu revokes a member's personal keys without removing them.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Last active

The Last active column shows the most recent of three times, listed separately when you hover it and on the member's
page:

- **Console**: their last visit, recorded at most once an hour.
- **CLI**: the last request with one of their personal API keys.
- **Last deploy**: the last deploy they started.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: "Your access does not include the AWS account"
docs.content:
### "Your access does not include the AWS account"

The member is a Developer or Viewer and the account is not in their AWS accounts. An Owner or Admin adds it with
**Edit access** on the Members page. The CLI shows the same reason, and `stacktape` lists only the accounts the member
can use.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
headingPath: The CLI stopped deploying for a Developer after an upgrade
docs.content:
### The CLI stopped deploying for a Developer after an upgrade

Developers and Viewers reach only the AWS accounts chosen for them. When this was introduced, each of them was given
the accounts their projects had deployed to; an account their projects never used must be added with **Edit access**.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
### Invite members is disabled

Either your role cannot invite (only Owners and Admins can), or this is a personal organization.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
### An invitation shows Expired

Its 14 days passed. Choose **Resend invitation**; the person can sign up for 14 more days.

docs.title: Team and Access Control
docs.content:
## Related features

- [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings): password and two-factor authentication
- [API Keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys): personal keys for the CLI
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): what Stacktape can do in an account
- [Organizations, Projects, and Stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages)

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
# Agent Mode in Dev


> **Warning - Preview — in active development:** Agent mode is usable today but still evolving. Verify available endpoints by calling `GET /` on the running agent server. Some details on this page may change between Stacktape releases.


Stacktape [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) can start an HTTP API server alongside your local workloads and databases. This **agent mode** gives AI coding assistants — and any HTTP client — programmatic access to check workload status, trigger rebuilds, read log file paths, query local databases, and call AWS SDK commands, enabling automated edit-test-fix loops without manual intervention.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## When to use

Agent mode is designed for workflows where an AI coding assistant drives the edit-test-fix loop. Enable it when:

- **AI-driven development** — You're using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, or another AI coding assistant to build your application. The assistant starts `stacktape dev --agent` as a shell command, then uses the HTTP API to check status, rebuild workloads, read the log file path, query local databases, call AWS SDK commands, and stop dev mode.
- **Automated test harnesses** — You want a script to verify application behavior during development by hitting the status, env, or database endpoints.
- **Database inspection without client tools** — You need to run SQL queries, check Redis keys, scan DynamoDB items, or search OpenSearch indices against local dev databases without installing separate database clients.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## When NOT to use

- **Manual development** — If you're editing code yourself and checking results in a browser, standard [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) without `--agent` is simpler. The TUI output is optimized for human reading.
- **Production observability** — Agent mode runs locally. For deployed stacks, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs), [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics), or the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).
- **CI/CD pipelines** — Use [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) directly in your pipeline. Agent mode is a development-time feature.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Starting agent mode

Add the `--agent` flag to the [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) command to start the HTTP API server alongside your workloads.

```bash
stacktape dev --agent --agent-port 9900 --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

| Flag            | Description                                                                              |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--agent`       | Enables the agent HTTP API server alongside dev mode                                     |
| `--agent-port`   | Port for the agent HTTP server                                                           |
| `--stage`       | Stage used for dev mode and the `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` directory                 |
| `--region`      | Session AWS region; `/aws/sdk` rejects any different region   |
| `--resources`   | Which workloads to run (`all` or comma-separated names)                                  |
| `--fresh-db`     | Reset local database data on startup                                                     |

Once ready, Stacktape prints the agent URL and a summary of available endpoints. Local database data persists in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` between runs — see [reset scope](/local-development/local-databases#resetting-local-data) before using `--fresh-db`. It resets prepared databases, including relay dependencies, and DynamoDB Local tables share storage.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Startup progress

A first start creates the account's dev network and the stage's dev stack and takes several minutes; a warm start takes seconds. While the agent starts, the command prints one JSONL `event` line per step with `"phase": "DEV_STARTUP"`, so an assistant can tell a long start from a hung one:

| `eventType`    | Reports                                                                                         |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEV_SESSION`  | The agent's port and token file first (`detail.kind: "dev-agent"`), the project, stage, region and config file the session resolved (`detail.kind: "dev-target"`), a heartbeat every 20 s, and "Dev session ready" |
| `DEV_NETWORK`  | Creating, updating or reusing the dev network                                                   |
| `DEV_BOX`      | Starting the dev box and connecting to it                                                       |
| `DEV_STACK`    | Creating or updating the dev stack; CloudFormation `UPDATE_STACK` events carry resource counts  |
| `DEV_WORKLOAD` | Each workload starting and running, or its error (`instanceId` is the workload name)            |
| `DEV_DATABASE` | Each local database starting and running, or its error                                          |

If the start fails, the final `result` line carries the failure's own code and hints, for example `CLI_DEV_STACK_CONFLICT` with how to resolve it. Dev mode never updates or deletes a stack it did not create. A dev stack in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` requires explicit deletion before another start; `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` permits another start. A stack still rolling back or in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` must finish or recover before an update can proceed. A Lambda build/deploy failure may leave the agent running with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES` and `ready: false`; inspect status and rebuild it.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Authentication

The agent listens on `127.0.0.1` only and accepts a request only when it carries the session's token. Each `stacktape dev --agent` run creates a new random token and stores it in `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token` in your home directory (`%USERPROFILE%\.stacktape\dev-agent-tokens\{port}.token` on Windows). Because the file is named after the agent's port, any of your tools can find it from any directory. Only your user can read the file. Stacktape deletes it when the agent stops, and an agent that starts later removes the files of agents that were killed. The startup message and the `AGENT_READY` result print the file path, never the token.

Every request must send the token in an `Authorization: Bearer` header. POST requests must also send `content-type: application/json`. The examples on this page use these shell variables:

```bash
AGENT=http://127.0.0.1:9900
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/9900.token)"
JSON='content-type: application/json'

curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/status
```

The agent refuses requests that a web page or another machine could send:

| Request                                                              | Response                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| No token or a wrong token                                            | `401 UNAUTHORIZED`           |
| A `Host` header other than `127.0.0.1:{port}` or `localhost:{port}`  | `403 FORBIDDEN`              |
| Any request with an `Origin` header (sent by browsers)               | `403 FORBIDDEN`              |
| A POST without `content-type: application/json`                      | `415 UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` |

The 401 response names the token file, so a coding assistant that forgot the header can recover on its own. [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop) and the [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) read the token file themselves. `dev stop` stops the agent of the project in the current directory; pass `--cwd <directory>` for another project directory and `--stage <stage>` when several stages run.


> **Tip:** AI coding assistants can call `GET /` on the agent server to receive a full endpoint listing dynamically. Use `GET /?compact=true` for a shorter LLM-oriented response — it includes the current phase, workload names, available local resources with their primary query/schema endpoints, core action templates (rebuild, logs, env, aws, stop), and a pointer to `GET /` for full docs.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Response format

Every agent endpoint wraps its result in a consistent JSON envelope so clients can handle success and error uniformly.

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "message": "OK",
  "data": {}
}
```

| Field     | Description                                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `v`       | Envelope version (currently `"1.0"`)                                                 |
| `ok`      | `true` on success, `false` on error                                                  |
| `code`    | Machine-readable status. Common values include `OK`, `NOT_FOUND`, `VALIDATION_ERROR`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`, `ALREADY_EXISTS`, `AUTH_ERROR`, and `READ_ONLY_VIOLATION` |
| `message` | Human-readable description (optional — most responses include it, but not all)       |
| `data`    | Endpoint-specific payload (optional — present when the endpoint returns structured data) |

Many not-found and validation errors include contextual hints in `data`, such as an `available` array of valid resource names or a `hint` string describing expected input. For example, referencing a non-existent workload returns the list of available workloads in `data.available` and a usage hint in `data.hint`. This makes it easy for AI agents to self-correct without extra calls.

Agent endpoints return a JSON envelope with `v`, `ok`, and `code` on every response; most successful responses also include `message` and endpoint-specific `data`. Response examples throughout this page may omit envelope fields like `v` for brevity.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content: ## Core endpoints

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Status

The `/status` endpoint reports the current agent phase and a map of workload names to their local URLs (if running) or status strings. AI agents should poll this endpoint after starting dev mode and wait for `"ready"` before testing workload URLs.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/status
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "phase": "ready",
    "ready": true,
    "failedWorkloads": [],
    "workloads": {
      "api": "http://localhost:3000",
      "worker": "running"
    },
    "sessionId": "0b6c…",
    "projectDirectory": "/home/me/my-app",
    "projectName": "my-app",
    "stage": "dev",
    "region": "eu-west-1",
    "pid": 12345
  }
}
```

`sessionId`, `projectDirectory`, `projectName`, `stage` and `region` identify the session; `dev stop` and the MCP server use them to find the agent of a project.

The `phase` value is one of `starting`, `ready`, `rebuilding`, `stopping`, or `stopped`. Phase becomes `ready` once dev mode has started every selected workload and local resource, and `/stop` moves it to `stopping`. The `ready` field is `true` only when the phase is `ready`, every workload is `running`, and the configuration file still matches the one the session started with. A container workload with a port is `running` once that port accepts connections, after a start and after a rebuild; one that does not within 120 seconds gets the status `error`. A workload that failed, crashed or failed to rebuild makes `ready` false and appears in `failedWorkloads` with its error, so an assistant waiting for `ready` never tests against a workload that is down or runs outdated code. When the configuration file changed, `ready` is false and `restartRequired` explains that dev mode has to restart (see [Rebuild](#rebuild)).

If a workload fails while `stacktape dev --agent` is starting, the command stops the session, prints each failed workload with its error and the log file path, and exits with a non-zero code.

For detailed information including uptime, per-workload type/port/error data, local resource status, and the log file path, use verbose mode.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" "$AGENT/status?verbose=true"
```

The verbose response replaces the workload string map with an array of objects containing `name`, `type`, `status`, `url`, `port`, and `error` fields, plus a `localResources` array, `uptime` in seconds, and the `logFile` path. Workload `status` is one of `pending`, `starting`, `running`, `error`, or `stopped`. Local resource status uses the same values.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Logs

The `/logs` endpoint returns the path to the JSONL log file on disk. Logs are **not** streamed through the HTTP response — AI agents should read the file directly using standard tools like `tail`, `grep`, or `jq`.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/logs
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "logFile": ".stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt",
    "format": "jsonl",
    "hint": "Use standard tools: tail -n 50 <logFile> | jq ."
  }
}
```

Each line in the log file is a JSON object with these fields:

| Field    | Example                      | Description                           |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `ts`     | `"2025-03-15T14:30:15Z"`    | When the line was produced. For a deployed function, the CloudWatch event time, not the time it was fetched |
| `source` | `"api"`, `"dev"`             | Workload or database that produced the line, or `dev` for dev mode itself |
| `level`  | `"info"`, `"warn"`, `"error"` | Severity level                      |
| `msg`    | `"Server started on :3000"`  | Log message content, without terminal colors |

Lines with `"source":"dev"` record dev mode's own lifecycle: startup steps, file changes, rebuilds started, finished or failed with the error, dev stack updates and dev box state. Grep them to see what dev mode did, for example whether a rebuild failed:

```bash
grep '"source":"dev"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

A restart keeps the previous session's lines. Each session appends to the file and starts with a `"msg":"Dev session started"` line whose `session` field names its session ID, project directory and stage. A file over 10 MB moves to `<file>.1` when the next session starts.

Deployed dev functions keep their source maps and run with `--enable-source-maps`, so stack traces in the log point at your source files rather than the bundle.

View the last 50 lines:

```bash
tail -n 50 .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter for errors only:

```bash
grep '"level":"error"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter by a specific workload:

```bash
grep '"source":"api"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

This file-based approach is intentional — AI coding assistants already have file-reading tools, and `tail -f` provides real-time streaming without polling overhead.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Environment variables

The `/env/{workload}` endpoint returns the environment variables available to a specific workload. For Lambda functions, variables are fetched from the deployed AWS function configuration. A function that uses a local database shows that database's `STP_*` variables with the address of the [dev box](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases), through which the function reaches it. For containers and frontends, variables are read from the local runner state. A container whose image failed to build still shows the environment it would get. A workload that failed before dev mode prepared its environment, for example because the dev stack did not deploy, returns `WORKLOAD_NOT_STARTED` with its error.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/env/api
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "workload": "api",
    "type": "function",
    "source": "aws",
    "envVars": {
      "STP_NOTES_TABLE_TABLE_NAME": "my-project-dev-notesTable",
      "AWS_REGION": "eu-west-1"
    },
    "count": 2
  }
}
```

Secret values are masked. The agent replaces the values of variables read from `$Secret` or `$SsmParam`, of variables whose names mark them as secret (such as `PASSWORD`, `TOKEN`, `KEY`, `SECRET` or `AUTHORIZATION`, which includes the AWS credentials of container workloads), and the password inside connection strings, for example `postgresql://[redacted:credentials]@localhost:5432/app`. Host names, private IP addresses, ports, database names and plain settings stay readable. A deployed dev function reaches a local database at the private address of the dev box, such as `10.230.4.17`, so its `/env` shows that address. Public IP addresses are masked as `[redacted:ip]`. Your workloads still receive the real values.

Local databases never use the deployed database's secret. When the configured password is a directive such as `$Secret('db.password')`, dev mode generates a local password, keeps it in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/{resource}/password`, and gives that same password to the container, the deployed dev functions and local workloads.

This endpoint is useful for debugging [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) wiring. If an expected `STP_*` variable is missing, the workload's `connectTo` array likely doesn't reference the target resource. The response also includes the `source` field — `"aws"` for Lambda functions (fetched from the deployed function configuration) or `"local"` for other tracked workload types (currently container, hosting-bucket, and nextjs-web workloads, read from the local runner state).

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Rebuild

After editing application code, trigger a workload rebuild to pick up the changes. Rebuilding a specific workload is faster than rebuilding all of them — AI agents should target only the workload whose code changed.

Rebuild a specific workload:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" -d '{}' $AGENT/rebuild/api
```

Rebuild all workloads at once:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" -d '{}' $AGENT/rebuild/all
```

The request answers after the workload has been rebuilt and, for a Lambda function, its new code deployed. A rebuild that fails, for example because of a syntax error, answers with `ok: false`, the code `REBUILD_FAILED`, the build error, the failed workloads and the log file path:

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": false,
  "code": "REBUILD_FAILED",
  "message": "Rebuild failed. api: Build failed: Unexpected ;",
  "data": {
    "failedWorkloads": [{ "name": "api", "error": "Build failed: Unexpected ;" }],
    "logFile": ".stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt",
    "hint": "The failed workloads keep the status error. A failed function keeps its deployed code, and a container's error says whether its previous build still serves requests. Fix the error and rebuild again."
  }
}
```

The workload then has the status `error` and `/status` reports `ready: false` until a rebuild of it succeeds. Its previous code may still answer requests, so a test that passes while the workload is in `error` does not test your change.

When the rebuilt workload's files are also used by other workloads, such as a shared package in a monorepo, and changed after those workloads were last built, the result names them in `staleWorkloads` with the changed files, and the message says so: `Rebuilt api. quote, report also use changed files (packages/shared/src/index.ts) and still run the previous build; rebuild them or rebuild all.` With `--watch`, a change rebuilds every workload that uses the file.

A rebuild deploys code only. When the Stacktape configuration file changed since dev mode started, the rebuild does nothing and answers with the code `CONFIG_CHANGED_RESTART_REQUIRED`. Stop dev mode and start it again: the start updates the dev stack with the new configuration. Formatting and comments do not count as a change. The refused workloads keep their status and their previous build keeps serving; `ready` stays false and `restartRequired` explains why. If you revert the configuration instead, the next rebuild, or with `--watch` the configuration check, rebuilds them.

With `--watch`, dev mode rebuilds a workload when one of its source files changes, through the same path, so a failed build sets the same `error` status and writes the error to the log file. It also watches the configuration file and sets `restartRequired` when it changes. `stacktape dev --agent --watch` reports the session started only after the watcher is running, so an edit made right after the start is rebuilt.

A workload builds one rebuild at a time. A request for a workload that is rebuilding waits for that build and then builds the current files, and further requests made meanwhile join it. Only the last build sets the workload's status, so the status always reflects the newest files.

Running `stacktape dev --agent` again while the session runs reports the same workloads, URLs and database ports as the start did. When the session waits for a restart, the command fails with `CLI_DEV_RESTART_REQUIRED`. When a workload in it failed, the command fails with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES`, and while it still starts, with `DEV_SESSION_NOT_READY`; the session keeps running and the result's `data` carries it with `ready: false` and `failedWorkloads`.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Liveness check

`GET /health` returns the current agent phase and can be used as a simple liveness check. Unlike `/status`, `/health` does not include workloads or local resources — it only returns `ok` and the current agent `phase` inside the standard envelope. Use `/status` for full workload details.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/health
```

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Resource health checks

Check the health of a specific local resource (database, cache). The agent monitors local resources automatically, but this endpoint triggers an immediate check and returns the result.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/health/myDb
```

The response includes `name`, `type`, `port`, `host`, and the `status` value returned by the local health monitor. If the resource name doesn't match any running local resource, the error response includes an `available` array listing valid resource names.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Stop

Gracefully shut down dev mode, all workloads, and all local resources.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" -d '{}' $AGENT/stop
```

Calling stop when the agent is already stopping or stopped returns success without side effects.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Database endpoints

Agent mode exposes database endpoints for PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis, DynamoDB and OpenSearch. Most operate on local instances. DynamoDB `query`, `scan`, `schema` and `sample` can also read a table deployed by the dev stack and mark responses `deployed: true`; `get`, `put`, `delete` and `reset` require a local table. `GET /` lists endpoint groups for running local resources. Errors include available resource names where applicable.

The `{name}` path parameter in every database endpoint matches the resource name in your Stacktape configuration. If you reference a name that doesn't exist, the error response includes an `available` array listing the valid resource names.


> **Warning:** The PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis command/query endpoints accept an optional `confirm` field. The startup documentation warns that destructive operations require `{"confirm": true}` in the request body — without it, the request is rejected. The DynamoDB and OpenSearch delete handlers do not accept a `confirm` parameter; they require the key or document identifier fields shown below.
