docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### PostgreSQL

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) with a PostgreSQL engine in your Stacktape configuration.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/postgres/myDb/query \
  -d '{"sql": "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10"}'
```

| Endpoint                          | Method | Description                    | Parameters                            |
| --------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `/postgres/{name}/query`          | POST   | Execute SQL                    | `{sql, limit?, timeout?, confirm?}`   |
| `/postgres/{name}/schema`         | GET    | Column types and constraints   | `?tables=t1,t2` (optional filter)     |
| `/postgres/{name}/tables`         | GET    | List all tables                |                                       |
| `/postgres/{name}/explain`        | POST   | Query execution plan           | `{sql, analyze?}`                     |
| `/postgres/{name}/indexes`        | GET    | Index definitions              | `?table=name` (optional filter)       |
| `/postgres/{name}/stats`          | GET    | Table statistics               | `?table=name` (optional filter)       |
| `/postgres/{name}/sample`         | GET    | Sample rows from a table       | `?table=name&limit=5`                 |

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### MySQL

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) with a MySQL or MariaDB engine in your Stacktape configuration. The endpoint path uses `/mysql/` for both MySQL and MariaDB resources.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/mysql/myDb/query \
  -d '{"sql": "SHOW TABLES"}'
```

| Endpoint                        | Method | Description                    | Parameters                                             |
| ------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `/mysql/{name}/query`           | POST   | Execute SQL                    | `{sql, limit?, timeout?, confirm?}`                    |
| `/mysql/{name}/schema`          | GET    | Column types and constraints   | `?tables=t1,t2` (optional filter)                      |
| `/mysql/{name}/tables`          | GET    | List all tables                |                                                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/explain`         | POST   | Query execution plan           | `{sql, format?}` (format: `"traditional"`, `"json"`, or `"tree"`) |
| `/mysql/{name}/indexes`         | GET    | Index definitions              | `?table=name` (optional filter)                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/stats`           | GET    | Table statistics               | `?table=name` (optional filter)                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/sample`          | GET    | Sample rows from a table       | `?table=name&limit=5`                                  |

A PostgreSQL or MySQL query that writes rows (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) returns the number of rows it changed in `affectedRows`, as the database driver reports it. `rowCount` is the number of rows returned, or the number of changed rows when the statement returns none.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Redis

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) in your Stacktape configuration. The `cmd` field accepts a Redis command as a single string (e.g. `"GET mykey"`, `"SET user:1 '{\"name\":\"Alice\"}'"`).

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/redis/myCache/command \
  -d '{"cmd": "GET session:user123"}'
```

| Endpoint                       | Method | Description                  | Parameters                       |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `/redis/{name}/command`        | POST   | Execute any Redis command    | `{cmd, confirm?}`               |
| `/redis/{name}/keys`           | GET    | List keys matching pattern   | `?pattern=*&limit=100`          |
| `/redis/{name}/get`            | GET    | Get value by key             | `?key=name`                     |
| `/redis/{name}/ttl`            | GET    | Get TTL for a key            | `?key=name`                     |
| `/redis/{name}/info`           | GET    | Server info                  | `?section=memory` (optional)    |
| `/redis/{name}/type`           | GET    | Get type of a key            | `?key=name`                     |

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### DynamoDB

`query`, `scan`, `schema` and `sample` support both local tables and tables deployed by the dev stack (responses include `deployed: true`). `get`, `put`, `delete` and `reset` require a local [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb). Key parameters (`pk`, `sk`) are objects mapping attribute names to values — for example, `{"userId": "123"}`.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/dynamodb/notesTable/scan \
  -d '{"limit": 10}'
```

| Endpoint                           | Method | Description                  | Parameters                                    |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/query`           | POST   | Query by partition/sort key  | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?, index?, limit?}`       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/scan`            | POST   | Full table scan              | `{filter?, limit?}`                           |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/get`             | POST   | Get single item              | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?}`                       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/put`             | POST   | Put an item                  | `{item: {...}}`                               |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/delete`          | POST   | Delete an item               | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?}`                       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/schema`          | GET    | Table key schema and indexes |                                                |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/sample`          | GET    | Sample items                 | `?limit=5`                                    |

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### OpenSearch

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for an [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) in your Stacktape configuration. Query bodies follow standard OpenSearch query DSL.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/opensearch/searchDomain/search \
  -d '{"query": {"match": {"title": "serverless"}}, "limit": 10}'
```

| Endpoint                             | Method | Description                  | Parameters                           |
| ------------------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `/opensearch/{name}/search`          | POST   | Search documents             | `{query: {...}, index?, limit?}`     |
| `/opensearch/{name}/get`             | GET    | Get document by ID           | `?index=idx&id=docid`               |
| `/opensearch/{name}/put`             | POST   | Index a document             | `{index, id?, doc: {...}}`           |
| `/opensearch/{name}/delete`          | POST   | Delete a document            | `{index, id}`                        |
| `/opensearch/{name}/indices`         | GET    | List all indices             |                                      |
| `/opensearch/{name}/mapping`         | GET    | Get index mapping            | `?index=idx`                         |
| `/opensearch/{name}/analyze`         | POST   | Analyze text with tokenizer  | `{text, analyzer?, index?}`          |
| `/opensearch/{name}/count`           | GET    | Count documents              | `?index=idx` (optional)              |

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Reset and seed local databases

An end-to-end test needs a known database state. Resetting deletes the data of the local databases and keeps their schema, so a test can start from empty tables without restarting dev mode. A seed script then writes the rows the test expects.

```bash

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Every local database, keeping the settings table
docs.content:
# Every local database, keeping the settings table
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/reset/all -d '{"confirm": true, "keepTables": ["settings"]}'

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
# One database
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/reset/myDb -d '{"confirm": true}'

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Run the seed script from the config
docs.content:
# Run the seed script from the config
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/scripts/seed/run -d '{}'
```

| Endpoint                  | Method | Description                                                         | Parameters                   |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `/reset/{name}`           | POST   | Delete the data of one local database, or of all with `/reset/all` | `{confirm: true, keepTables?}` |
| `/scripts/{script}/run`   | POST   | Run a `local-script` from the config against the local databases    | `{timeoutSeconds?}`          |

A reset requires `{"confirm": true}` and changes only databases that dev mode runs on your machine; any other name returns `NOT_FOUND`. What it does per database type:

- **PostgreSQL**: one `TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY` of every table in the database's own schemas, so identity columns start again at 1. Tables that extensions own, such as PostGIS's `spatial_ref_sys`, stay.
- **MySQL and MariaDB**: `TRUNCATE` of every table of the configured database, which also resets `AUTO_INCREMENT`. A database without `dbName` uses the MySQL system database `mysql`. The reset refuses it, like the other system databases `sys`, `performance_schema` and `information_schema`, because they hold the server's users and state; set `dbName` on the engine to reset the application's data.
- **Redis**: `FLUSHALL`.
- **DynamoDB**: deletes every item; the table and its indexes stay.
- **OpenSearch**: not supported. `/reset/all` skips it and names it in `skipped`; start dev mode with `--fresh-db` to delete its data.

Migration history tables stay in every SQL database, so the schema and the migration tool still agree after a reset: `_prisma_migrations`, `__drizzle_migrations`, `knex_migrations`, `kysely_migration`, `pgmigrations`, `migrations`, `mikro_orm_migrations`, `SequelizeMeta`, `schema_migrations`, `flyway_schema_history`, `databasechangelog`, `alembic_version`, `django_migrations`, `goose_db_version`, `__EFMigrationsHistory` and their lock tables. `keepTables` names more tables to keep. A kept table that references a reset table through a foreign key stops the reset with an error instead of being emptied with it.

The seed is a script from the `scripts` section of your config. It runs as a [`beforeDev` hook](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) would: its `connectTo` resources resolve to the local databases of this session, and the response carries its output. It is stopped after `timeoutSeconds` (default 50, at most 280) and then returns `SCRIPT_TIMEOUT`. Dev mode runs the config it started with: a script added to the config file since then returns `CONFIG_CHANGED_RESTART_REQUIRED` until dev mode restarts.

The seed endpoint refuses scripts that reference a deployed resource it knows about. It checks every string of the script, including directives nested in `$Format` and directives inside commands: `connectTo` and `$ResourceParam` must name databases running locally, and `$CfResourceParam`, `$StackOutput`, `$CfStackOutput` and `$CfFormat` are refused. Bastion scripts and scripts that assume a workload's role are refused. After the directives resolve, a script whose environment or commands contain the host or endpoint of one of the stack's deployed databases is refused before it runs.


> **Warning:** A seed script is not a sandbox. It runs on your machine with your AWS credentials, so it can still reach deployed data in ways the check cannot see: a value read with `$Secret`, a URL written literally in the script or in an `.env` file it loads, or an AWS SDK call. Keep seed scripts pointed at the connection that dev mode gives them.


```typescript
scripts: {
  seed: {
    type: 'local-script',
    properties: {
      executeCommand: 'npx prisma db seed',
      // STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING points at the local database
      connectTo: ['mainDatabase']
    }
  }
}
```

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## AWS SDK access

Agent mode provides access to read-only AWS SDK commands through the `/aws/sdk` endpoint. It sends only the reviewed read-only operations that [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call#safety-model) accepts; any other operation, including the Secrets Manager and SSM value reads, is rejected before a request is sent. Environment variable values and Cognito client secrets come back redacted, CloudFormation templates come back as their structure without any value, while other reads, such as log events and S3 objects, return application data as it is. The endpoint uses the dev agent IAM role. The role only reads, and only the resources of this dev stack in the session region: it identifies them by the stack-name tag CloudFormation puts on every resource, or by their identifiers in the template. CloudWatch metric and alarm reads cover the whole session region, because metrics belong to no stack. The HTTP endpoint accepts only reviewed read operations and adds resource filtering for Batch, whose read actions IAM cannot limit to the stack. If the role is missing or cannot be assumed after the IAM-propagation retry, the request fails; it never falls back to the developer's credentials. Restart dev mode to update the stack and role when needed.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/aws/sdk \
  -d '{"service": "lambda", "command": "ListFunctions", "input": {"MaxItems": 10}}'
```

The request body accepts `service` (required), `command` (required), `input` (optional, defaults to `{}`), and `region` (optional, must equal the session region if supplied; another region is rejected). Use [`stacktape aws call`](/cli/aws-call) with an explicit target for a different region. If `service` or `command` is missing, the agent returns a validation error with a hint showing the expected request shape.

To list all supported services and example commands:

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/aws/sdk/services
```

`GET /aws/sdk/services` returns a successful envelope whose payload lists the accepted operations for each supported service, nested under `data.data` in the response. Use the running endpoint response as the authoritative list of valid `service` and `command` values before constructing `/aws/sdk` calls. The service list in the startup message and on this page is a summary; the endpoint response is always up to date.

Common AWS SDK calls for AI agents:

| Use case                  | Service            | Command              | Example input                                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Read Lambda logs          | `logs`             | `FilterLogEvents`    | `{"logGroupName": "/aws/lambda/fn", "filterPattern": "ERROR"}` |
| Scan a DynamoDB table     | `dynamodb`         | `Scan`               | `{"TableName": "tbl", "Limit": 10}`                           |
| List S3 objects           | `s3`               | `ListObjectsV2`      | `{"Bucket": "bkt", "Prefix": "uploads/"}`                     |
| Check a queue's backlog   | `sqs`              | `GetQueueAttributes` | `{"QueueUrl": "https://…/q", "AttributeNames": ["All"]}`       |
| Describe a stack          | `cloudformation`   | `DescribeStacks`     | `{"StackName": "my-stack"}`                                    |


> **Info:** The startup message lists supported `service` identifiers: `lambda`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `logs`, `cloudformation`, `cloudwatch`, `sqs`, `sns`, `sfn`, `eventbridge`, `secretsmanager`, `ssm`, `sts`, `iam`, `ec2`, `ecs`, `ecr`, `rds`, `ses`, `cognito`, `apigatewayv2`, `xray`, `kinesis`, `firehose`, and more. Call `GET /aws/sdk/services` on the running agent for the complete, up-to-date list.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Typical AI agent workflow

The core value of agent mode is the **automated feedback loop**: an AI agent writes code, checks if it works, reads any errors, fixes them, and rebuilds — all without human intervention.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Flow
1. **Write config**: AI writes or edits stacktape.ts based on your requirements
2. **Start agent mode**: AI runs stacktape dev --agent to boot workloads and databases
3. **Write application code**: AI implements handlers, services, and frontend code
4. **Rebuild and test**: AI calls POST /rebuild/{name}, checks status, reads logs, queries databases
5. **Fix and iterate**: AI reads error logs, fixes code, rebuilds — repeating until everything works
6. **Deploy**: Once working locally, AI deploys to AWS with stacktape deploy

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
### Tips for AI agent integrations

- **Poll status before testing** — Wait for `"phase": "ready"` before making requests to workload URLs. Workloads may still be compiling during the `starting` phase.
- **Use compact docs** — Call `GET /?compact=true` at the start of a session to discover available endpoints with minimal token usage. The full `GET /` listing is more detailed but token-heavy.
- **Rebuild selectively** — `POST /rebuild/{name}` rebuilds only the named workload. Use it instead of `/rebuild/all` when you changed code in a single workload.
- **Check env vars early** — `GET /env/{workload}` reveals whether [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) is wired correctly before you start debugging application code.
- **Read logs from the file** — The `/logs` endpoint returns a file path. Use `tail`, `grep`, or `jq` to filter the JSONL log file. Use `tail -f` for real-time streaming.
- **Inspect schemas before writing queries** — Call the `/schema` or `/tables` endpoint to discover table and column names before writing SQL or DynamoDB queries.
- **Use database endpoints for verification** — After writing data through your API, query the database directly to confirm it was stored correctly.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## MCP server integration

For MCP-based assistant setup, see the [Stacktape MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) page. If your AI assistant supports the Model Context Protocol (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf), the MCP server provides a higher-level integration layer. Agent mode's HTTP API is the lower-level alternative that works with any tool capable of making HTTP requests. The MCP `stacktape_dev` tool calls this API for the assistant, so it never handles the token file: its `status`, `logs`, `rebuild`, `query`, `tables`, `reset_db`, `seed`, `env`, `aws` and `stop` actions map to the endpoints on this page. Without a session ID it acts only on sessions of its own project directories, so an assistant in one worktree cannot rebuild or reset another worktree's session by accident.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content:
## Security

The agent can run SQL against your local databases, rebuild and stop workloads, and call AWS read operations with the dev agent's credentials. Only programs running as your user on this machine can call it:

- It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so other machines on your network cannot connect.
- Every request needs the session token from `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token`, which only your user can read.
- It refuses requests with an `Origin` header or a foreign `Host` header, so a web page cannot call it, even through DNS rebinding.
- POST requests must be JSON, which a web page cannot send to another site without the browser asking the agent first.

Do not forward the agent port to other machines, and do not paste the token into chats or logs.

The `/aws/sdk` endpoint fails closed when the dev agent role is missing or cannot be assumed; it never falls back to developer credentials. This does not make every read stack-scoped: CloudWatch metrics/alarm and API Gateway reads can reach other resources in the account and session region. CloudWatch Logs uses stack-name log-group ARN patterns. The endpoint accepts only reviewed read operations and adds resource filtering for Batch. See [AWS SDK access](#aws-sdk-access) for the boundary.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Should I use agent mode or the Stacktape MCP server?
docs.content:
### Should I use agent mode or the Stacktape MCP server?

Both work with assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf. Agent mode is a plain HTTP API that any tool can call with `curl` or HTTP libraries — no protocol integration needed, so it suits custom tooling or any client that can make HTTP requests. The [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) uses the Model Context Protocol standard that those assistants support natively, providing a more integrated, higher-level layer. If your AI tool supports MCP, prefer the MCP server; reach for agent mode when you need raw HTTP access.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: What databases can I query through the agent API?
docs.content:
### What databases can I query through the agent API?

Agent mode exposes typed HTTP endpoints for five local resource types started by dev mode — PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch — so agents can inspect schemas, run queries, and verify data without installing separate database client tools. Each type has its own endpoint group (SQL engines get `query`/`schema`/`tables`/`explain`/`indexes`/`stats`/`sample`, plus key-value and document operations for Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch). `GET /` lists only the endpoint groups for resources currently running in the session.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Is my data persisted between agent mode sessions?
docs.content:
### Is my data persisted between agent mode sessions?

Yes. The startup message confirms local database data is stored in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` and survives restarts. To empty the databases while dev mode runs, call [`/reset`](#reset-and-seed-local-databases); it keeps the schema. The `--fresh-db` flag deletes the data directories when dev mode starts, including the schema.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Are destructive database operations safe during AI sessions?
docs.content:
### Are destructive database operations safe during AI sessions?

The PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis query/command endpoints accept an optional `confirm` field. The startup documentation warns that destructive operations require `{"confirm": true}` — without it, the request is rejected. `/reset` always requires it. DynamoDB and OpenSearch delete handlers do not accept a `confirm` parameter; they require the key or document identifier fields directly. All of these endpoints reach only the databases dev mode runs locally, except that the DynamoDB `query`, `scan`, `schema` and `sample` endpoints also read a table the dev stack deploys (a remote resource). Their answer then has `deployed: true`, and the write endpoints refuse that table.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: What happens if a workload fails?
docs.content:
### What happens if a workload fails?

If a function fails to build or deploy while `stacktape dev --agent` starts, the session keeps running and the function keeps its previous code. The command exits with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES`, names the function and its error, and its result carries the session with `ready: false`. Fix the code and call `POST /rebuild/{name}`. Any other workload that fails during the start stops the session, and the command exits with `CLI_DEV_WORKLOAD_FAILED`; fix the code and start again. After the start, a workload that crashes or fails to rebuild does not stop the session: `/status` reports it in `failedWorkloads` with its error, and `ready` stays false. Fix the code and call `POST /rebuild/{name}` to retry without restarting the session.

docs.title: Agent Mode in Dev
headingPath: Why does an `/aws/sdk` call fail or return access-denied?
docs.content:
### Why does an `/aws/sdk` call fail or return access-denied?

The `/aws/sdk` endpoint uses the dev agent IAM role. Most resource permissions are limited to the stack, but CloudWatch metrics/alarm and API Gateway reads are account-wide within the session region; CloudWatch Logs reads use stack-name log-group ARN patterns. Only Batch gets additional resource filtering at the HTTP endpoint. A missing role or failed AssumeRole makes the call fail; it never falls back to your credentials. IAM can also deny a resource the role cannot read. Restart dev mode to update a missing or outdated role. A call is also rejected, without reaching AWS, when the operation is not a reviewed read-only one; the error lists the operations accepted for that service. The endpoint supports a broad set of services (`lambda`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `logs`, `cloudformation`, `sqs`, `sns`, `sfn`, and more); call `GET /aws/sdk/services` for the authoritative, up-to-date list of valid `service` and `command` values before constructing a call.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
# MCP Server Setup


> **Warning:** Preview — in active development. The Stacktape MCP server is under active development. Some operations may not work end-to-end in all environments, and behavior may change as the server stabilizes.


The Stacktape MCP server gives AI coding assistants structured access to Stacktape documentation, CLI commands, project inspection, and dev mode control. Instead of copying CLI output back and forth, your assistant calls Stacktape tools directly and receives typed JSON responses it can reason about.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Quick start

```bash
stacktape mcp add
```

[`mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) finds the coding agents on your machine and asks which ones to connect, with the installed ones preselected. For each agent you pick, it adds the Stacktape MCP server for your user, then starts the server once to check that it works. Start a new session (or reload the window) in your agent and ask: “Use Stacktape to show what this project deploys.”

A working integration exposes `stacktape_incident`, `stacktape_docs`, `stacktape_project`, `stacktape_cli`, and `stacktape_dev`. For an incident, the assistant starts with `stacktape_incident` and reads logs, metrics and other diagnostics through `stacktape_cli` directly. Mutating commands are planned with `action: "plan"` and run only after you approve them.

To undo the setup, run [`stacktape mcp remove`](/cli/mcp-remove).

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## When to use

Use the MCP server when your AI coding assistant supports the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). The structured tool interface is better than raw CLI output for several workflows:

- **Deploying or deleting stacks** — the assistant plans the command, validates arguments against CLI metadata, and executes with safety gates, all through tool calls.
- **Debugging** — query [logs](/cli/logs), [metrics](/cli/metrics), [alarms](/cli/alarms), [database contents](/cli/query-sql), or [DynamoDB items](/cli/query-dynamodb) during a conversation. The assistant gets structured JSON instead of parsing terminal output.
- **Configuration help** — the assistant searches Stacktape's bundled documentation index for resource types, config syntax, and deployment patterns without opening a browser.
- **Dev mode** — start, monitor, rebuild, and stop [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) sessions from within your AI conversation.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## When NOT to use

Skip the MCP server if your AI client does not support the Model Context Protocol — use the [Stacktape CLI](/cli/deploy) directly or the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview) instead. For long-running deployments, prefer the CLI when you want to watch the command directly in your own terminal. MCP command responses are consolidated and may be truncated. The MCP server runs CLI commands as subprocesses and returns a consolidated response; if an optional caller-specified timeout is exceeded, the subprocess is terminated and an error is returned.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Supported agents

`mcp add` sets up these agents. Every agent starts `stacktape mcp` itself, as a local process on your machine.

| Agent | How `mcp add` adds the server |
|-------|-------------------------------|
| Claude Code | `claude mcp add --scope user` |
| Codex (CLI, IDE extension and app) | `codex mcp add`; edits `~/.codex/config.toml` when the `codex` command is missing |
| Cursor | Edits `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| VS Code (GitHub Copilot) | Edits the user `mcp.json` of your default profile |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | Edits `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` |
| Windsurf (Devin Desktop) | Edits the existing `mcp_config.json`, or creates `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenCode | Edits `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` or `opencode.json` |

An agent counts as installed when its command is on your PATH, or its app or settings folder exists. In a named VS Code profile, add the server from that profile with **MCP: Open User Configuration** (see [Manual setup](#manual-setup)). Any other MCP client that can start a local stdio server works too; see [Other MCP clients](#other-mcp-clients).


> **Info:** The server speaks the current MCP revision (`2026-07-28`) and the earlier 2025 revisions (`2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`), so it works with agents that have not moved to the new protocol yet. The confirmation form for destructive commands works in both: on older revisions it arrives as a standard elicitation request.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## What `mcp add` changes

- **User level only.** Entries go into your own agent configuration, never into the project, so nothing reaches your repository or your teammates. Claude Code and Codex are changed through their own `mcp add` commands; Claude Code's `~/.claude.json` is never edited directly.
- **Edits in place.** In JSON and JSONC files, `mcp add` changes only the `stacktape` entry. Your comments, other servers and formatting stay as they are, and the previous file is kept next to it as `<file>.bak.<timestamp>`. A file it cannot parse is left untouched and reported.
- **The command it writes.** When `stacktape` is on your PATH, the entry runs `stacktape mcp`, so upgrades keep working. When you installed Stacktape with the install script, the entry uses the binary's full path (`~/.stacktape/bin/stacktape`), because agents started from the Dock or Start menu often do not see your shell's PATH. Otherwise it writes the running binary's full path and tells you to run `mcp add` again if that file moves.
- **A check at the end.** `mcp add` starts the configured command, completes an MCP handshake and lists the tools. It reports a failure with the server's own error output.

Running `mcp add` again is safe: entries that already match are reported as already set up and left untouched. If a project contains its own Stacktape entry (for example a committed `.mcp.json` from an older Stacktape), that agent uses the project entry inside that project, and `mcp add` tells you where it is.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Non-interactive setup

```bash

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Name the agents and skip the question
docs.content:
# Name the agents and skip the question
stacktape mcp add --coding-agents claude-code,cursor

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Set up every installed agent (CI images, dotfiles, scripts)
docs.content:
# Set up every installed agent (CI images, dotfiles, scripts)
stacktape mcp add --yes
```

With `--yes` or `--agent`, `mcp add` sets up every installed agent. When it finds none, it changes nothing and exits with an error that shows how to name the agents.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Manual setup

To configure an agent by hand, point it at the `stacktape` command with the single argument `mcp`. Optionally set `STACKTAPE_MCP_CLIENT_NAME` to the agent's name, as `mcp add` does; Stacktape uses it to label operations started from that agent.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Tab: Claude Code


```bash
claude mcp add --scope user stacktape -- stacktape mcp
```

Use `--scope project` instead to write a `.mcp.json` that your team commits and shares.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Tab: Codex


```bash
codex mcp add stacktape -- stacktape mcp
```

This writes the entry to `~/.codex/config.toml`, which the Codex CLI, IDE extension and app share:

```toml
[mcp_servers.stacktape]
command = "stacktape"
args = ["mcp"]
```

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
MCP Server Setup
MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Tab: Copilot CLI


```bash
copilot mcp add stacktape -- stacktape mcp
```

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
MCP Server Setup
MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Other MCP clients

Any client that starts a local stdio server works: the command is `stacktape` and the arguments are `["mcp"]`. To call the tools from scripts or the command line, [mcporter](https://github.com/openclaw/mcporter) can register it with `mcporter config add stacktape --command stacktape --arg mcp`.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Moving from the hosted MCP server
docs.content:
### Moving from the hosted MCP server

Stacktape 3 also offered a hosted MCP server, added to agents as a URL. Stacktape 4 replaces it with `stacktape mcp`, which runs locally with your own CLI login. Remove the old URL entry from your agent and run `stacktape mcp add`.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Available tools

The MCP server exposes five tools. Each tool uses an `action` parameter to group related operations, keeping the tool surface small while giving assistants access to incidents, docs, project inspection, CLI commands, and dev mode control.

| Tool | Actions | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| `stacktape_incident` | `show`, `list` | Fetch an incident's full context in one call, or find incidents by project, stage and status |
| `stacktape_docs` | `search`, `get` | Search or fetch Stacktape documentation by query, route, resource type, definition name, property name, or heading path |
| `stacktape_project` | `scan`, `orient` | Inspect the local workspace for Stacktape config files, package scripts, dependencies, and suggested CLI defaults |
| `stacktape_cli` | `list`, `describe`, `plan`, `run` | Discover CLI commands, validate arguments, build execution plans, and execute non-interactive commands through safety-classified gates |
| `stacktape_dev` | `plan`, `start`, `status`, `logs`, `rebuild`, `rebuild_all`, `query`, `tables`, `reset_db`, `seed`, `env`, `aws`, `stop` | Plan and control [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) sessions, and inspect and reset their local databases |

Every completed tool call returns a `stacktape.mcp.tool-result.v1` JSON envelope as structured content and as an identical text block. The envelope includes `ok`, `code`, and `message`, with operation-specific fields under `data`. This lets clients consume typed results while keeping the response readable in clients that primarily render text content.

Use the canonical names in each tool schema. CLI invocation arguments and `stacktape_dev` args accept supported CLI aliases, including common snake_case and kebab-case forms. This does not apply to every outer field of every tool: use `incidentId`, `resourceType`, `propertyName` and other schema names exactly.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Incident tool

`stacktape_incident` is where an assistant starts an [incident](/observability/incidents) investigation. `action: "show"`
with an `incidentId` returns the incident handoff as markdown, the same document
[`incident show`](/cli/incidents-show) prints. It contains the incident's signals with their evidence, release and
configuration changes, the timeline, earlier related incidents, the AI assessment, the reports of any hosted AI runs
and read-only next steps.
`action: "list"` finds incidents by `projectName`, `stage` and `status` (`ACTIVE` by default, `ALL` for resolved history
as well) and returns at most `limit` of them (default 25).

The tool runs those CLI commands with your local Stacktape login, so the Console applies your organization and project
access. It is read-only. The assistant then reads logs, metrics, alarms and stack state with `stacktape_cli`.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Docs tool

`stacktape_docs` searches a documentation index bundled with the Stacktape CLI — no network access required. Use `action: "search"` with a `query` to find configuration syntax, resource types, deployment patterns, or troubleshooting guidance. Use `action: "get"` with a `route`, `definitionName`, `propertyName`, `sourcePath`, or `headingPath` to fetch an exact section.

Search supports three modes: `answer` (default) returns a synthesized answer with references, `reference` returns matched references without content, and `snippet` returns code-focused excerpts.

Key selectors and limits:

| Parameter | Actions | Type | Description |
|-----------|---------|------|-------------|
| `query` | `search` | string | Search query (required for `search`). |
| `mode` | `search` | `answer` \| `reference` \| `snippet` | Response mode. Default: `answer`. |
| `maxItems` | `search` | number | Max search results. Default: 3. |
| `docKind` | both | `docs-page` \| `config-reference` | Filter to a specific docs artifact kind. |
| `resourceType` | both | string | Filter or select by resource type, e.g. `function`. |
| `route` | `get` | string | Exact docs route, e.g. `/config-reference/function`. |
| `definitionName` | `get` | string | Exact TypeScript definition name from config reference. |
| `propertyName` | `get` | string | Exact config property name to extract. |
| `sourcePath` | `get` | string | Exact source path from a previous docs reference. |
| `headingPath` | `get` | string[] | Exact heading path array from a previous docs reference. |
| `maxChars` | `get` | number | Max content characters. Default: 16,000. |
| `includeFullPage` | `get` | boolean | Set `true` to fetch all content for a long route. |

For long route-only `get` requests, when more than 20 docs-page sections match and `includeFullPage` is not set, the server returns available heading paths instead of the full route content — the assistant passes one back to get the specific section.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Project tool

`stacktape_project` with `action: "scan"` discovers Stacktape config candidates (`.ts`, `.js`, `.yml`, `.json`), parses `package.json` scripts that invoke Stacktape commands, detects lockfiles, and returns suggested defaults for `configPath` and `currentWorkingDirectory`. This is the first tool an assistant should call when entering an unfamiliar Stacktape project.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `cwd` | string | Server process cwd | Absolute path to the Stacktape project root. Pass this whenever the assistant knows it. |
| `maxFiles` | number | 8 (`orient`: 12) | Maximum ranked files to return per category. |
| `includeDetails` | boolean | `false` | When `true`, includes full package script commands and unabridged candidate metadata. |

The `orient` action returns the same scan data with stronger next-action guidance for the assistant.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### CLI tool

`stacktape_cli` covers the non-interactive CLI surface: [deployments](/cli/deploy), [deletions](/cli/delete), [previewing changes](/cli/diff), [rollbacks](/cli/rollback), diagnostics ([`logs`](/cli/logs), [`metrics`](/cli/metrics), [`alarm list`](/cli/alarms), [`query sql`](/cli/query-sql), [`query dynamodb`](/cli/query-dynamodb), [`query redis`](/cli/query-redis), [`query opensearch`](/cli/query-opensearch), [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call)), incidents (`incidents`, `incident show`, `incident watch`), [secrets](/configuration/secrets) (`secret set`, `secret get`, `secret delete`), parameters (`param get`), stack info (`status`, `stack list`), and deployment scripts (`script run`).

The actions:

1. **`action: "list"`** — discover available commands, optionally filtered by `category` or `safety` level.
2. **`action: "describe"`** — get full metadata for a specific command (allowed arguments, safety class, confirmation policy). For `aws call`, it also lists the accepted AWS SDK operations per service.
3. **`action: "plan"`** — build a read-only execution plan for a mutating command. Pass `cwd` with the absolute path to the Stacktape project root when the assistant has it — `plan` uses it to scan config files and `package.json` scripts. The action infers defaults, validates arguments against CLI metadata, and returns a suggested `action: "run"` payload with a shell command preview. No credentials are required for planning.
4. **`action: "run"`** — execute a command as a CLI subprocess. Read-only, diagnostic and local commands run directly with validated arguments. Mutating commands require `confirm: true`. Destructive commands require direct user confirmation through the client's confirmation form (see [Safety model](#safety-model)).

Common parameters accepted by `plan` and `run`:

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `command` | string | CLI command name, e.g. `deploy`, `logs`, `secret get` |
| `cwd` | string | Absolute path to the Stacktape project root for project scanning |
| `args` | object | CLI arguments as a camelCase key-value object |
| `stage` | string | Target Stacktape stage |
| `region` | string | Target AWS region |
| `projectName` | string | Stacktape project name |
| `awsAccount` | string | Connected Stacktape AWS account name |
| `configPath` | string | Stacktape config path relative to `currentWorkingDirectory` |
| `currentWorkingDirectory` | string | Working directory for resolving config and app files |
| `resourceName` | string | Resource name for diagnostics commands |
| `scriptName` | string | Deployment script name for `script run` |
| `secretName` | string | Secret name for secret commands |
| `secretValue` | string | Secret value for `secret set` (masked in tool output) |
| `secretFile` | string | Path to a file containing the secret value |
| `fullDeploy` | boolean | Deploy every change through CloudFormation instead of updating changed code directly |
| `confirm` | boolean | Required for mutating commands. Destructive commands also require direct user confirmation through the client's confirmation form; this flag alone cannot authorize them. |
| `timeoutMs` | number | Command timeout in milliseconds for `run` |

The `list` action also accepts `category` (e.g. `deployment`, `diagnostics`, `secrets`) and `safety` (e.g. `readOnly`, `mutating`, `destructive`) to filter results.


> **Warning:** Plan mutating commands with `action: "plan"` before `action: "run"`. Commands marked as `sensitiveOutput` in CLI metadata have their output masked before being returned. The MCP planning guidance specifically warns assistants not to display `secret get` or private `param get` values in chat — run those in your own terminal to avoid exposing values in the conversation transcript.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Dev tool

`stacktape_dev` manages [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) lifecycle without requiring a terminal. The dev mode agent listens on a loopback HTTP port (default `7331`) for control commands. The tool reads the agent's session token from the token file the agent reports at start and sends it with each request; the token never appears in tool output.

- **`plan`** scans the project and returns suggested start arguments without starting anything. Its `data.stacktapeDevStart.arguments` is a complete `start` call, with the project directory in `args.cwd`. `plan` defaults `stage` to `dev` and infers `projectName`, `region`, `awsAccount`, `currentWorkingDirectory`, and `configPath` from deploy scripts and project scan when available. With `configPath` or `currentWorkingDirectory` set, only deploy scripts of that project count; when the best scripts would deploy different targets, the plan uses none of them. A dev-mode plan is only complete when `stage`, `region`, and `configPath` are resolved; otherwise the tool returns `MISSING_ARGS` with next steps. Since `stage` defaults to `dev`, the most common missing arguments are `region` and `configPath`.
- **`start`** launches dev mode as a subprocess. Pass `projectName`, `stage`, `region`, `configPath`, and optionally `awsAccount`, `agentPort`, `currentWorkingDirectory`, `resources`, `skipResources`, `watch`, `remoteResources`, `freshDb` or `takeOver`. It returns `data.session.devSessionId` at once and sends a progress notification for each startup step: the dev network, the dev box, the dev stack deployment with resource counts, and each workload and database. It waits up to `waitSeconds` (default 50) for the start to finish. A first start that creates the dev network and the dev stack takes several minutes; `start` then returns `DEV_STARTING` with the latest progress while the start continues, so an MCP client's per-call timeout does not end it. A successful start returns no `rawTail`: the CLI's output there is the banner for people. When another session already runs dev mode for the stage, `start` returns `DEV_STAGE_RUNNING_ELSEWHERE` with the other session's user, machine and directory. `takeOver: true` moves the stage to the new session: deployed functions then reach the databases on this machine, and the other session stops itself.
- **`status`** returns the current state of the running session. While the session starts, it waits up to `waitSeconds` (default 50) for the start to finish, then returns the ready status, the start's error, or `DEV_STARTING` with the latest progress. A start that fails in the background keeps its error, code and hints for the next call about that session.
- **`logs`** returns the newest structured log entries (`limit`, default 100). Pass the returned `nextCursor` as `cursor` to read only lines written since, `level` (`info`, `warn`, `error`) for a minimum level (without `since` or `cursor`, only the current session's lines), `since` (an ISO time or a duration such as `10m`) and `workload` to filter. Entries with `source: "dev"` are dev mode's own lifecycle: rebuilds, file changes, dev stack updates and dev box state. Secret values of the workloads' environments, passwords in connection strings, and recognizable credentials (`password=...`, `Authorization: Bearer ...`, known token formats) are masked. An entry longer than one result is cut and marked with `truncatedFromChars`; the whole line stays in `logFile`.
- **`rebuild`** triggers a rebuild of a single workload (pass `workload` name). **`rebuild_all`** triggers a rebuild of every workload.
- **`tables`** lists what the local databases hold: tables for PostgreSQL and MySQL, keys for Redis, the key schema for DynamoDB and indices for OpenSearch. Without `resource` it covers every local database.
- **`query`** runs `sql` on PostgreSQL or MySQL, a Redis `command` such as `GET session:1`, or a DynamoDB query (`pk`, optional `sk` and `index`) or scan (`filter`). `resource` names the database and can be omitted when only one runs. Only statements the server fully understands run directly: reads that call no function the application defined, `INSERT ... VALUES`, `CREATE TABLE` with column definitions, `CREATE INDEX`, and `UPDATE` or `DELETE` whose own `WHERE` clause refers to a column (`WHERE true` or `WHERE 1 = 1` does not count). Any other SQL, such as `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`, `INSERT ... SELECT`, `CREATE TABLE ... AS`, a data-modifying `WITH`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` or `DO`, and the Redis `FLUSHALL`, returns `DESTRUCTIVE_OPERATION` until it is repeated with `confirm: true`. Comments, quoted text and quoted identifiers never change that decision, and SQL the server cannot read with certainty (an unterminated quote, a backslash inside a quoted string, a MySQL executable comment) also needs confirmation.
- **`reset_db`** gives the assistant a known database state without restarting dev mode; a reset of a small database takes milliseconds, a `freshDb` restart about 13 seconds. With `confirm: true` it deletes every row of the PostgreSQL and MySQL tables, every Redis key and every DynamoDB item of `resource`, or of every local database when `resource` is omitted. Tables, indexes and migration history tables such as `_prisma_migrations` stay, so the application needs no new migration. PostgreSQL identity columns and MySQL `AUTO_INCREMENT` counters start again at 1. `keepTables` names more tables to keep. OpenSearch is not supported; start dev mode with `freshDb` to delete its data.
- **`seed`** runs a `local-script` from the config's `scripts` section (`script`, default `seed`) with the local database connections and returns its output. It stops the script after `timeoutSeconds` (default 50, at most 280), with every process the script started, including ones that left its process group; if one survives, the result lists it in `survivingPids`. Output and errors are masked like `env` masks the script's environment. When the output is larger than one result, the result keeps the last lines and names a log file with all of them, and still reports whether the script succeeded. A script added to the config after dev mode started returns `CONFIG_CHANGED_RESTART_REQUIRED`: dev mode runs the config it started with, so it has to restart first. See [Reset and seed local databases](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#reset-and-seed-local-databases) for the script.
- **`env`** returns the environment of a `workload` with secret values masked, or `WORKLOAD_NOT_STARTED` when the workload failed before dev mode prepared its environment. **`aws`** calls a reviewed read-only AWS SDK operation (`service`, `command`, `input`, optional `region` equal to the session region) with the dev agent's role. Most resource permissions are limited to the stack, but CloudWatch metrics/alarm and API Gateway reads are account-wide in the session region; CloudWatch Logs uses stack-name log-group ARN patterns. Only Batch gets additional resource filtering at the live HTTP endpoint. A missing role or failed AssumeRole fails the live agent call without falling back to developer credentials, as [`/aws/sdk`](/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev#aws-sdk-access) does. For 15 minutes after a start failed, `aws` with that start's `devSessionId` still reads its stack. No dev agent runs, so the call goes through [`stacktape aws call`](/cli/aws-call) with the project, stage and region the start resolved and its AWS profile. This separate CLI diagnostic path reads through the stack's read-only debug role and fails instead of falling back to the selected user credentials; a stack whose first deploy failed before it had outputs allows only CloudFormation reads of that stack. Without a `devSessionId`, it reads a failed start of this project only when one matches `stage`, and otherwise asks for the ID. A start that failed before it resolved its stage returns `DEV_TARGET_UNKNOWN`.
- **`stop`** terminates the active session.

`query`, `tables` and `reset_db` reach databases that dev mode runs on your machine. The one exception is a DynamoDB table that the dev stack deploys, because it is in `remoteResources` or a deployed function's stream trigger needs it. `query` and `tables` with that table's name in `resource` scan, query or describe the deployed table, read-only, and the result has `deployed: true`, the table name and the region. `reset_db` refuses it with `NOT_LOCAL_RESOURCE`. Any other deployed resource returns `NOT_LOCAL_RESOURCE` or `NOT_FOUND`; read it with the `aws` action. `seed` refuses scripts with a known reference to a deployed resource: a `connectTo` or resource directive anywhere in the script, or a deployed database's host in its resolved environment or commands. It also refuses bastion scripts and scripts that assume a workload's role. A seed script still runs with your AWS credentials and is not a sandbox: it can reach deployed data through `$Secret`, a literal URL, an `.env` file or the AWS SDK.

`args` is typed in the tool's input schema, with a description of every argument, so an assistant does not have to guess names such as `freshDb` or `awsAccount`.

Multiple dev sessions can be active for different projects, worktrees or ports. Pass the `devSessionId` returned by `start` as `args.devSessionId` to `stop`; it never guesses which session you intended. The other actions may omit the handle only when exactly one session of the MCP server's own projects runs. A session counts as the server's own when the server started it, or when its project directory is the server's working directory, is inside it, or is inside one of the client's [roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/client/roots). Some clients start the server in your home directory. A working directory or root that is your home directory, a directory that contains it (such as `/home`, `/Users` or `C:\Users`) or a filesystem root counts only for a project in exactly that directory. Paths are compared after following symbolic links, and without regard to case on Windows and macOS.

Another worktree's session is never picked by accident. Without `devSessionId`, `rebuild`, `rebuild_all`, `reset_db`, `seed` and a `query` that writes return `DEV_SESSION_ID_REQUIRED` for a session outside the server's projects, even when `cwd` names its directory. Read-only actions accept `cwd` to read another project's session. A `query` sent that way runs read-only in the database: PostgreSQL and MySQL run it in a read-only transaction, and Redis accepts only commands that read. A statement that writes through a function is refused too. Every refusal lists the running sessions in `data.activeDevSessions`, each with its `devSessionId` and `projectDirectory`. With several eligible sessions, omission returns `AMBIGUOUS_DEV_SESSION`; an unknown or unreachable handle returns `NOT_FOUND`.

Before the tool picks a session, it drops sessions whose agent no longer answers, for example after `stacktape dev stop` in a terminal. An agent that does not answer within 3 seconds stays known: a call that would pick it returns `DEV_AGENT_NOT_RESPONDING` instead of waiting.

A session that another one took over keeps answering `DEV_STAGE_TAKEN_OVER`. The answer names the new holder (user, machine and directory) and says the stage was moved on purpose. It tells the assistant to ask the user before moving the stage back, because taking it back stops the other session, which may be a person's or another agent's work. Calls without `devSessionId` return that until a `start` succeeds, so they never reach the session that replaced it.

Sessions survive a restart of the MCP server. Every agent reports its `devSessionId` and project directory, and the tool finds running agents through their token files, so a new MCP server process answers `status`, `logs` and `stop` for sessions an earlier one started.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Safety model

The MCP server classifies every CLI command into a safety level and enforces per-level gates:

| Safety level | Behavior | Examples |
|-------------|----------|---------|
| `readOnly` | Executes without confirmation | `diff`, `status`, `stack list`, `logs`, `metrics`, `alarm list`, `incident show` |
| `diagnostic` | Executes without confirmation | `query sql`, `query dynamodb`, `query redis`, `query opensearch`, `aws call` |
| `local` | Executes without confirmation | `synth`, `validate`, `package` |
| `mutating` | Requires `confirm: true` in the `run` call | [`deploy`](/cli/deploy), [`secret set`](/cli/secret-set), [`rollback`](/cli/rollback) |
| `destructive` | Requires direct user confirmation for the exact command and target; agent-supplied `confirm: true` alone is not sufficient | [`delete`](/cli/delete), [`secret delete`](/cli/secret-delete) |
| `interactive` | Rejected by the MCP server — must be run in the user's own terminal | [`login`](/cli/login), [`dev`](/cli/dev) (use `stacktape_dev` instead), `bastion shell` |

For destructive commands, the MCP server asks the user directly through their AI client's confirmation form: an input-required round trip on the `2026-07-28` revision, a standard elicitation request on the 2025 revisions. The confirmation is short-lived, bound to the exact command, arguments, and project directory, and can be used only once. A declined, expired, replayed, or target-mismatched confirmation does not execute the command. If the client does not support confirmation forms, the command fails closed and the assistant is told to ask the user to run the command in their own terminal.


> **Warning:** Diagnostic commands run without a confirmation prompt because the MCP server accepts only read operations for them: read-only SQL statements (`SELECT`, `WITH`, `VALUES`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE`, `EXPLAIN`), the read operations of the Redis, DynamoDB and OpenSearch query commands, and [reviewed read-only AWS SDK operations](/cli/aws-call#safety-model) for `aws call`. Anything else is refused. The data they return can still be sensitive, so think about what you let an assistant read from production.


Commands marked as `sensitiveOutput` in CLI metadata have their output masked before being returned. The MCP planning guidance specifically warns assistants not to display `secret get` or private `param get` values in chat. `param get` returns a private parameter as `<<OMITTED>>`: the server refuses `showSensitiveValues` for it and for `deploy`, so run `stacktape param get --show-secrets` in your own terminal for the value. A `secret set` plan does not repeat `secretValue`: its `shellCommand` asks for the value in your terminal. The MCP server also redacts known credential patterns (Stacktape API keys, GitHub tokens, Slack tokens, database connection strings with passwords) from all tool responses.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Authentication

The MCP server reuses the local Stacktape CLI authentication state. It is not a separate identity provider, and planning does not require Stacktape credentials. Commands that run the underlying CLI may also require whatever AWS access that CLI command normally requires. The `stacktape_cli` planning action rejects raw Stacktape credential CLI arguments (such as `apiKey` or `STACKTAPE_API_KEY`), and the MCP instructions tell assistants not to collect API keys in chat.

- **Docs search, project scanning, CLI listing, description, and planning** work without any authentication.
- **`stacktape_cli` with `action: "run"` and `stacktape_dev`** execute the underlying Stacktape CLI flow and may require the same project, stage, region, AWS account, and profile setup as the CLI command. If execution fails with an authentication error, the MCP guidance tells the assistant to ask you to run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) in your own terminal.

For CI environments, the MCP server's safety guidance tells assistants to ask users to configure a dedicated `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret outside the conversation instead of pasting credentials into chat.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## How it works

The MCP server starts when your AI client launches the `stacktape mcp` command as a child process using stdio transport. The startup sequence is:

1. The client spawns `stacktape mcp` as a child process.
2. The client and server agree on a protocol revision (`2026-07-28` or one of the 2025 revisions), and the client lists the five tools.
3. The bundled documentation search index initializes asynchronously. If indexing fails, operational tools remain available and `stacktape_docs` reports the indexing error.
4. The assistant sends MCP tool calls over stdin; the server executes them and returns structured JSON over stdout.

For CLI execution, the MCP server validates the command against CLI metadata, applies safety policy, spawns a Stacktape CLI subprocess, and forwards progress notifications while retaining a bounded event history for the final consolidated response. Cancelling the MCP call terminates the subprocess tree and returns `CANCELLED`; timeouts return `TIMEOUT`. A missing, malformed, or duplicate final CLI agent result fails closed instead of guessing whether the command succeeded. Tool responses are capped at 30,000 characters. Large `rawTail` output is shortened by keeping the beginning and end. Other large payloads are compacted by dropping or shrinking bulky fields (such as truncating answer text, limiting reference and snippet counts, and shortening data content). If compaction is still insufficient, the server returns `RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE`.

For docs queries, search runs against a local index. No network calls are made.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Verifying the setup

`mcp add` already starts the server and lists its tools. To check that the agent itself connects:

- **Claude Code:** `claude mcp get stacktape` shows `Status: ✔ Connected`.
- **Codex:** `codex mcp list` lists `stacktape` as enabled.
- **OpenCode:** `opencode mcp list` shows `✓ stacktape connected`.
- **Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf:** the MCP section of the settings shows `stacktape` with its five tools.

Then ask a question that needs the docs, for example “How do I deploy a Lambda function with Stacktape?”. The assistant should call `stacktape_docs`.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
## Upgrading

The MCP server ships inside the Stacktape CLI. After [`stacktape upgrade`](/cli/upgrade) or an npm update, the next session your agent starts uses the new server. No separate MCP update is needed.

Run [`stacktape mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) again to add another agent, or after moving the CLI when `mcp add` wrote its full path.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content: ## Troubleshooting

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: The agent shows no Stacktape tools
docs.content:
### The agent shows no Stacktape tools

Run `stacktape mcp add` again: its final check starts the server with the exact configured command and prints the error if that fails. If the check passes but the agent still shows nothing, restart the agent. Agents started from the Dock or Start menu may not see your shell's PATH; install Stacktape with the install script, or put the full path to `stacktape` in the agent's config.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: A config file cannot be parsed
docs.content:
### A config file cannot be parsed

`mcp add` leaves a file it cannot parse untouched and names it. Fix the syntax error, or restore the most recent `.bak.<timestamp>` copy, and run `mcp add` again.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Operations require authentication

Docs search, project scanning, and CLI metadata actions (`list`, `describe`, `plan`) work without authentication. `stacktape_cli` with `action: "run"` and `stacktape_dev` execute the underlying Stacktape CLI flow. If execution fails with an authentication error, run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) in your terminal. Some commands also require a configured [AWS profile](/cli/aws-profile-create).

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: An agent is not listed as installed
docs.content:
### An agent is not listed as installed

`mcp add` looks for the agent's command on your PATH and for its app and settings folders. Pick the agent in the list anyway, or name it with `--coding-agents`, and `mcp add` writes its configuration.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Dev session not found

If `stacktape_dev` returns `NOT_FOUND` for `status`, `logs`, `rebuild`, `rebuild_all`, a database action or `stop`, and its message does not name a database or script, no dev agent of yours is running, or the session's local agent port is no longer responding. Call `start` to create a new session.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content:
### Concurrent deployment conflicts

The MCP server spawns separate CLI subprocesses for each operation, so it does not interfere with other Stacktape commands you run in a terminal. However, running concurrent deployments to the same stack from both MCP and a terminal causes AWS CloudFormation conflicts. Avoid overlapping deploys to the same project and stage.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
docs.content: ## FAQ

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Which AI assistants work with the Stacktape MCP server?
docs.content:
### Which AI assistants work with the Stacktape MCP server?

[`stacktape mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) sets up Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, GitHub Copilot CLI, Windsurf and OpenCode. Any other MCP client that can start a local stdio server also works: point it at `stacktape mcp`.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Does the MCP server store or transmit my credentials?
docs.content:
### Does the MCP server store or transmit my credentials?

The MCP server runs locally and reuses the local Stacktape CLI authentication state. Commands executed through `stacktape_cli` and `stacktape_dev` follow the underlying CLI's normal authentication and AWS access behavior. The `stacktape_cli` planning action rejects raw Stacktape credential CLI arguments, and the MCP instructions tell assistants not to collect API keys in chat. Commands flagged `sensitiveOutput` (such as `secret get` and private `param get`) have their output masked, and the server also redacts known credential patterns (API keys, tokens, database connection strings with passwords) from all responses before returning them to the AI client. Even so, sensitive values are best retrieved by running the command in your own terminal rather than through an AI conversation.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: What works without an AWS account or login?
docs.content:
### What works without an AWS account or login?

Docs search, project scanning, and CLI metadata operations (`list`, `describe`, `plan`) work with no AWS account or Stacktape login — planning never requires credentials, so an assistant can explore commands and build execution plans offline. Only `stacktape_cli` with `action: "run"` and `stacktape_dev` execute the underlying CLI flow; if that fails with an authentication error, the guidance tells the assistant to ask you to run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) in your own terminal. Some commands also require a configured [AWS profile](/cli/aws-profile-create).

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Is the MCP server safe for production workflows?
docs.content:
### Is the MCP server safe for production workflows?

The MCP server is in preview. Docs, project scanning, CLI listing, description, and planning are read-only. The server classifies every CLI command into a safety level: `readOnly`, `diagnostic`, `local`, `mutating`, `destructive`, or `interactive`. Mutating commands require `confirm: true`, destructive commands require direct user confirmation for the exact command and target when the client supports confirmation forms, and interactive commands are rejected. Diagnostic commands like [`query sql`](/cli/query-sql) run without confirmation because the server accepts only read operations for them. Treat MCP-initiated deployments with the same care as manual CLI deployments.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: What happens if a deployment times out through MCP?
docs.content:
### What happens if a deployment times out through MCP?

CLI commands run as subprocesses. The caller can specify a `timeoutMs` value; if exceeded, the MCP server terminates the subprocess and returns an error. MCP dev startup can continue for up to 30 minutes. Each `start` or `status` call normally waits up to 50 seconds before returning progress while startup continues. The daemon is also reaped after 10 minutes without output; that silence limit is separate from the total startup budget. For long-running deployments, run them directly via the [CLI](/cli/deploy) where you get real-time streaming output.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: What is the difference between plan and run in stacktape_cli?
docs.content:
### What is the difference between plan and run in stacktape_cli?

`action: "plan"` creates a read-only execution plan: it scans the project, reads `package.json` scripts for defaults, validates arguments, and returns the recommended `action: "run"` payload — without executing anything or requiring credentials. `action: "run"` executes the command. Read-only and diagnostic commands can run directly. Mutating commands are planned first, then run with the planned payload after the user approves.

docs.title: MCP Server Setup
headingPath: Why was my tool response truncated or rejected as too large?
docs.content:
### Why was my tool response truncated or rejected as too large?

Tool responses are capped at 30,000 characters. The server first shortens large `rawTail` output by keeping the beginning and end, then compacts other large payloads (truncating answer text, limiting reference and snippet counts, shortening data content). If compaction is still not enough, it returns `RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE`. For long-running deployments with heavy output, run them directly via the [CLI](/cli/deploy) where you get full streaming output instead.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
# Using Stacktape with AI


> **Warning:** Preview — in active development. The Stacktape MCP server is under active development. Available tools, safety behavior, and integration details may change between releases.


Stacktape includes built-in support for AI coding assistants through an MCP server for deploying, inspecting, and debugging stacks from your editor; an agent mode that exposes an HTTP API for iterative local development; and an [`mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) command for registering the MCP server with supported editors. AI coding assistants can also use Stacktape docs and project context to help draft or edit `stacktape.ts` configuration files.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
## Start here

For most users, the shortest path is:

```bash
stacktape mcp add
```

It connects the coding agents installed on your machine (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Copilot CLI, Windsurf and OpenCode) to Stacktape: it adds the Stacktape MCP server to each one you pick, then checks that the server starts. Start a new session in your agent and ask it to “use Stacktape to show what this project deploys.” The agent gets five tools: `stacktape_incident`, `stacktape_docs`, `stacktape_project`, `stacktape_cli` and `stacktape_dev`. See [MCP server setup](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) for what it changes, manual setup and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
## The AI-assisted development workflow

An AI coding assistant working with Stacktape follows a build-test-deploy loop. The assistant writes your infrastructure config, starts a local dev environment, implements application code, reads logs to fix errors, and deploys when everything works. What makes this effective is the **feedback loop** — the AI observes what's happening and iterates until the stack works correctly.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
## Flow
1. **Generate config**: AI writes stacktape.ts from your requirements or existing codebase
2. **Start dev mode**: Agent mode launches local workloads with an HTTP API
3. **Write application code**: AI implements handlers, services, and business logic
4. **Test and iterate**: AI reads logs, queries databases, triggers rebuilds, and fixes errors
5. **Deploy**: AI deploys the working stack to AWS via the MCP server


The assistant writes or edits the config in step 1 using Stacktape docs for reference. Agent mode powers steps 2–4. The MCP server orchestrates step 5 and provides documentation context throughout.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
## MCP server

The Stacktape MCP server gives AI coding assistants direct access to Stacktape operations through the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). Instead of asking the assistant to run raw shell commands itself, the MCP server plans and runs Stacktape CLI operations through structured tools with validation, safety gates, and credential handling. The server runs locally via stdio transport and reuses your existing Stacktape CLI authentication.

The server exposes five tools:

| Tool | Purpose | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `stacktape_incident` | Fetch an incident's context or find incidents | Start an incident investigation with signals, evidence, release changes, history and the AI assessment |
| `stacktape_docs` | Search and fetch Stacktape documentation | Config syntax, resource types, deployment patterns, troubleshooting |
| `stacktape_project` | Inspect a local Stacktape project | Discover config files, parse package.json scripts, infer CLI defaults |
| `stacktape_cli` | List, describe, plan, and run CLI commands | Deploy, preview changes, read logs, query databases, manage secrets |
| `stacktape_dev` | Control dev mode lifecycle | Start, stop, check status, read logs, rebuild workloads |

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
headingPath: How assistants use the MCP server
docs.content:
### How assistants use the MCP server

An assistant investigating an incident starts with `stacktape_incident`, which returns the incident's context in one call. It then reads what it needs through `stacktape_cli`: read-only, diagnostic and local commands such as `logs`, `metrics`, `status` and `aws call` run directly with `action=run` and validated arguments, without a plan or your confirmation. `action=list` and `action=describe` help it find commands and their arguments.

This is the local path: your assistant on your machine. For a hosted run instead, the Console can start a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Grok or OpenCode) on the project's runner to investigate an incident or propose a fix as a draft pull request, funded by your organization's API key with the agent's provider or your own subscription. See [AI assessment, investigation and fixes](/observability/incident-ai).

Changes follow a plan-then-execute pattern. Before a mutating command, the assistant calls `stacktape_cli` with `action=plan`, which scans your project, resolves config files, validates arguments, and returns a run payload. It then calls `action=run` with that payload, adding `confirm: true` only after receiving explicit user approval in the same conversation. Destructive commands go further — the assistant cannot supply confirmation on its own; the MCP server requires direct user confirmation through the client's confirmation form before execution. This flow prevents the assistant from running changes with wrong arguments or against the wrong stage.

The `stacktape_docs` tool gives the assistant access to the full Stacktape documentation index. When you ask "how do I add a DynamoDB table?" or "what's the syntax for connecting resources?", the assistant searches the docs and returns grounded answers with code examples — rather than guessing from training data.

The `stacktape_dev` tool controls dev mode lifecycle without requiring an interactive terminal. The assistant can start agent mode, read logs, trigger workload rebuilds, and stop the session — all through structured JSON rather than terminal output parsing.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
### Safety model

The MCP server categorizes every CLI command by safety level and enforces appropriate gates:

| Safety level | Behavior | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `readOnly` | Runs without confirmation | `status`, `stack list`, `logs`, `metrics` |
| `diagnostic` | Runs without confirmation | `query sql`, `query dynamodb`, `query redis`, `query opensearch` |
| `local` | Runs without confirmation | `synth`, `validate`, `package` |
| `mutating` | Requires explicit user approval (`confirm: true`) | `deploy`, `secret set`, `domain add` |
| `destructive` | Requires direct user confirmation for the exact command and target | `delete`, `secret delete` |
| `interactive` | Rejected — must use user's terminal or `stacktape_dev` | `dev`, `init` |

Read-only commands run without confirmation. Diagnostic database commands also run without confirmation, because the server accepts only read operations for them and refuses anything else. Mutating commands require the user to explicitly approve execution in the current conversation. Destructive commands go further: the assistant cannot supply confirmation on its own. Instead, the MCP server presents a confirmation dialog directly to the user, and the operation proceeds only if the user confirms the exact command and target. If the MCP client does not support confirmation forms, destructive commands are refused entirely and the user is told to run them in their own terminal.

Interactive commands like [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) and [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) require a terminal UI and are rejected by `stacktape_cli`. Dev mode lifecycle is handled through the dedicated `stacktape_dev` tool instead.

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
### Credential handling

The MCP server rejects raw Stacktape credential arguments passed through the AI assistant, masks sensitive output (secrets, passwords, API keys, connection strings) before returning results, and instructs assistants not to read credential files or ask for API keys in chat. The MCP server reuses the Stacktape CLI authentication state. If execution fails with an auth error, the server directs the user to run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login) in their own terminal. For CI, configure a dedicated `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret outside the conversation rather than passing credentials through chat or MCP arguments.

For full setup instructions, see the [MCP server setup guide](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup).

docs.title: Using Stacktape with AI
docs.content:
## Agent mode

Agent mode is a variant of Stacktape's [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) designed for programmatic control by AI coding assistants. It starts a long-lived local process via `stacktape dev --agent` and exposes an HTTP API on a configurable loopback port (default 7331). Every request must carry the session token stored in `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token`. While standard dev mode uses an interactive terminal UI, agent mode returns structured JSON responses. When the MCP `stacktape_dev` tool plans agent mode, it defaults the stage to `dev` and can infer `configPath` from the project scan, but the final start arguments must include `stage`, `region`, and `configPath`.

Agent mode controls Stacktape dev mode through HTTP endpoints for status, logs, rebuilds, stop, and local database inspection. It provides structured JSON endpoints for:

- **Status checks** — workload health, ports, and readiness phase (`starting`, `ready`, `rebuilding`, `stopping`, `stopped`)
- **Log reading** — HTTP `GET /logs` returns the local JSONL file path. Read the file for raw HTTP integration; MCP `stacktape_dev` with `action: "logs"` reads it and provides cursor pagination and filters
